title: Can the "Answer Independence" Claim in Conversational AI Advertising Be Verified? Construct Decomposition and the Derivation of Audit Requirements
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Can the "Answer Independence" Claim in Conversational AI Advertising Be Verified? Construct Decomposition and the Derivation of Audit Requirements
detail.abstract: When OpenAI introduced advertising into ChatGPT in 2026, it declared "Answer independence"-ads do not influence answers-as an official principle. This study takes that claim itself as the object of analysis, asking what must be measured to verify it and whether external observers can do so. Drawing on construct validity in measurement theory, we decompose "answer independence" into five sub-constructs-content invariance (C1), mention neutrality (C2), tone neutrality (C3), omission neutrality (C4), and longitudinal stability (C5)-and assess the verification conditions and external verifiability of each, building on the algorithm auditing literature. Verifiability proves asymmetric across constructs: C1 and C3 are partially verifiable, C2 is verifiable only conditional on sponsor disclosure, C4 is unverifiable in principle absent a stipulated completeness criterion, and C5 is practically unverifiable without access to training pipelines. We further observe a mismatch between the scope of the claim and the scope of its grounds: while the claim itself is broad enough to cover all five constructs, the grounds offered for it (system separation and labeling) address only the easily verifiable layer. From this matrix we derive three audit requirements-sponsor disclosure, counterfactual access, and third-party pipeline auditing-and connect them to existing institutional precedents including advertising substantiation doctrines in U.S. and Korean law, third-party measurement accreditation, and researcher data access under the EU DSA. As, to our knowledge, the first framework to decompose a platform's independence claim through a measurement-theoretic lens and systematically grade its external verifiability, this study argues that the debate over conversational AI advertising should turn not on the truth of the claim but on its verifiability.

title: Gray-market Trade with Product Information Service in Global Supply Chains
affiliations: Kobe University - Graduate School of Business Administration

detail.title: Gray-market Trade with Product Information Service in Global Supply Chains

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Production Economics, volume 147, 2014[10.1016/j.ijpe.2013.08.019]

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the economic effects of a product information service when potential consumers, who are segmented by their taste, exist in gray markets. Specifically, we construct an economic model that considers a multinational firm (MNF) who expands business to a country and chooses whether to provide information service regarding product characteristics. If receiving the information, consumers in a specific segment, whose taste suits the characteristics, have positive utility from consuming the product, while those in other segments have no utility. By contrast, consumers in all segments have positive expected utility before consuming the product without information. With these settings, we demonstrate that there arises the equilibrium that the MNF provides no information service when gray-market trade, i.e., parallel trade, is allowed in the country, leading to lower consumer welfare than when it is prohibited. A primary finding in the equilibrium is that such a situation arises especially when potential consumers are less segmented. In this situation, the regulator in the country should ban the parallel imports so as to enhance consumer welfare. The result is counterintuitive and notable, because one might intuitively infer that gray-market trade is less desirable when customers are more minutely segmented and the product information service is thus more specific and necessary.

title: Dual-channel Supply Chain Operations
affiliations: Kobe University - Graduate School of Business Administration

detail.title: Dual-channel Supply Chain Operations
detail.abstract: The rapid development of information and communication technology has induced today's general manufacturing companies in various industries to use direct sales channels as well as indirect sales channels via distributors for their product sales to end-consumers. This combined use of the two types of sales channels is referred to as a dual-channel supply chain or simply a dual channel, and the management and operations of this process by a firm are called dual-channel supply chain operations. Reflecting the growing number of manufacturers adopting such arrangements, dual-channel supply chain operations have become a core subject in the operations management (OM) literature. In this chapter, the author provides an overview of recent studies associated with dual-channel supply chain operations, thereby identifying key topics of focus and outlining future research directions that are worthy of investigation. Consequently, the chapter shows that, given the current real-world business environment, dual-channel supply chain operations are undoubtedly an essential current and prospective research subject that will continue to command significant attention from both researchers and practitioners.

title: Power Structure and Profitability in a Three-Echelon Supply Chain Facing Stochastic Demand
affiliations: Kobe University - Graduate School of Business Administration

detail.title: Power Structure and Profitability in a Three-Echelon Supply Chain Facing Stochastic Demand
detail.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how the order in which supply chain members demand their respective margins, which is often called power structure, influences their profitability in a three-echelon supply chain facing stochastic demand. We consider a typical three-echelon supply chain consisting of an upstream firm, a midstream firm, and a downstream firm. Previous supply chain models examining power structure have shown the conventional result that a supply chain member that sets a price or margin earlier generates a higher profit in a deterministic environment; that is, firms achieve higher profits in the order of the first-mover, the second-mover, and the third-mover who set margins in a three-echelon chain. Here, the first-mover, second-mover, and third-mover mean the supply chain member who sets its margin first, second, and third, respectively. Our stochastic model suggests the starkly contrasting result that the expected profit under demand uncertainty is higher in the order: (i) in a wide range of circumstances, the third-mover, the first-mover, and the second-mover who demand margins or (ii) in a narrower range of circumstances, the third-mover, the second-mover, and the first-mover. That is, the range of exogenous parameters leading to the first case is broader than that leading to the second case. The result indicates that the first-mover advantage is completely lost and, instead, the last-mover advantage always arises in a stochastic environment. Currently, power in supply chains tends to shift from upstream firms to downstream firms. However, our results warn a supply chain member in a stochastic environment that if assuming leadership to set its price or margin just because it has the power to do so, the member can ultimately harm itself and reduce its own profit.

title: Visual Identity as the Neurocognitive Filter of China's Automotive Expansion From Industrial Scale to Symbolic Legitimacy

detail.title: Visual Identity as the Neurocognitive Filter of China's Automotive Expansion From Industrial Scale to Symbolic Legitimacy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests and no personal or institutional relationships that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it did not involve human participants, patients, animals, clinical intervention, or identifiable personal data.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural model of China’s global automotive expansion in which visual identity is not treated as a decorative terminal layer, but as Gate Zero: the neurocognitive prior through which all subsequent evidence of quality, price, technology, safety, service, and status is interpreted. Four external analyses provide the industrial, financial, market-absorption, and OEM-strategy layers of the model. The author’s prior visual-semiotic work provides the fifth and causally prior layer: the hypothesis that a brand emblem functions as a synthetic social phenotype, producing rapid affective appraisal, trust or distrust, approach or avoidance, and halo-based trait attribution before deliberate product evaluation begins. The model distinguishes physical presence from market penetration, final-customer absorption, operating-system maturity, financial conversion, and symbolic legitimacy. It argues that China has achieved genuine industrial scale and strategic supply-chain leverage, yet the conversion of that power into durable global automotive authority remains uneven. The paper proposes a falsifiable sharedmechanism hypothesis: that rapid appraisal of unfamiliar brand emblems and rapid appraisal of human faces rely on the same, or functionally equivalent, computational sequence of configural recognition, affective valence, salience assignment, trust inference, halo transfer, and behavioral disposition. An experimental program is specified to test spontaneous and preconscious effects, cross-domain neural decoding, mediation through affect and trust, and downstream effects on consideration, willingness to pay, and choice. The resulting framework recasts the decisive contest in global automotive power: industrial capacity reaches the consumer only after it passes through a visual-affective filter.

title: Entry Deterrence Through Credible Commitment to Transfer Pricing at Direct Cost
affiliations: Kobe University - Graduate School of Business Administration

detail.title: Entry Deterrence Through Credible Commitment to Transfer Pricing at Direct Cost
detail.abstract: This paper examines the choice between direct and absorption costing in a cost-based transfer pricing system for duopolistic firms competing with product market prices. Existing literature has shown that the adoption of an absorption costing system, which drives up the intrafirm transfer price, strategically dominates direct costing for the two firms, regardless of whether the transfer price is publicly observable, thereby constituting a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE). However, we demonstrate that direct costing can strategically dominate absorption costing when one of the two firms is an incumbent, whereas the other is a potential entrant. Stated differently, the well-known result in the strategic cost allocation problem reverses if we consider entry threats. More specifically, we show that if the incumbent credibly commits to an observable transfer price, the upfront adoption of a direct costing system enables the incumbent to deter the entry of the potential rival in the SPNE. As a commitment device for the observable price, we consider the regulation of transfer prices that usually exists in oligopolistic network industries. We show that a regulator that pursues social welfare maximization approves direct costing but not absorption costing. Therefore, the firms and the regulator can share a mutual interest in the adoption of a direct costing system, a state thus sustained as the SPNE. This result yields managerial accounting implications for a divisionalized firm facing the threat of potential competitors entering the market in that the firm can use this accounting system to help monopolize the market.

title: Achieved Knowledge versus Schooled Knowledge Degrees, Intelligence, and the Trial of Reality in the AGI Era
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Achieved Knowledge versus Schooled Knowledge Degrees, Intelligence, and the Trial of Reality in the AGI Era
detail.abstract: Modern universities have rigorous procedures for certifying schooled knowledge through coursework, examinations, supervised research, publication, peer review, and institutional progression. They lack an equally general procedure for examining achieved knowledge: knowledge embodied in a realized, durable, verifiable, attributable, and transferable achievement. School remains indispensable for formation, method, judgment, and intellectual inheritance. The problem is not schooling itself, but its near-monopoly over academic recognition. This paper proposes a parallel examination architecture for Degrees in Transformative Achievement. Candidates submit multimodal achievement records and undergo independent verification, attribution and contribution audits, knowledge extraction, ethical review, a human-contribution audit, and a multi-format Achievement Viva. Three categorical gates precede nine dimensions assessed through written reasons, networkaware contribution inquiry, and precedent-anchored judgment of level. Staged anonymity reduces status bias, while the power test postpones final examination when a candidate controls witnesses or verification. The degree grants neither a professional license nor political authority. The paper's primary contribution is the examination itself. Generative AI makes polished symbolic output easier to produce and less informative as a standalone signal of independent human capability. Under those conditions, verified and attributable achievement may become relatively more informative, although it remains vulnerable to capital, hidden labor, machine assistance, and fabricated evidence. Schooled knowledge survives academic examination; achieved knowledge must also survive the trial of reality. A university adequate to the future should be able to examine both.

title: AI Premium
affiliations: LUISS University - Department of Economics and Finance, University of Rochester and Yale University, Yale University - Cowles Foundation

detail.title: AI Premium
detail.abstract: Using 380 trillion tokens of realized AI consumption across more than four hundred large language models from the licensed proprietary OpenRouter dataset covering approximately 2 percent of current global monthly AI token consumption, we analyze how AI affects firms, markets, and workers. Leveraging the unprecedented size, scope and granularity data, we construct the AI Factor from growth in tokens, dollars, and users, estimate firm-level AI Betas from stock return comovement, and characterize the AI Premium. First, we build a high-frequency AI factor and decompose it into salient components. Second, we show that firms whose returns covary more positively with the AI factor--high AI beta firms--earn higher subsequent returns, and the AI premium is large and heterogeneous. A value-weighted long-short strategy earns 64.1 basis points per week, and the premium is large for loadings on the intensive, frontier-oriented margin of AI consumption--closed-source models, paying and seasoned users, and long prompts--but not on casual or open-weight use. Third, the premium reaches beyond technology firms into consumer-facing and capital-heavy parts of the economy, but is absent in emerging markets, including China. Fourth, the AI exposure is more positive in nonroutine interactive work and more negative in analytical, scientific, and operations-control skills--an occupation one standard deviation higher in interaction-and-communication content has 0.36-standard-deviation higher market-implied AI exposure. Additionally, we provide early evidence of the rise of the agentic economy.

title: Why Global FMCG Brands Succeed in Some Countries and Fail in Others: Cultural Adaptation and Consumer Preferences in India and South Korea: A Comparative Study of Nestlé’s Maggi and Kellanova’s Pringles
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Why Global FMCG Brands Succeed in Some Countries and Fail in Others: Cultural Adaptation and Consumer Preferences in India and South Korea: A Comparative Study of Nestlé’s Maggi and Kellanova’s Pringles
detail.abstract: This study investigates the strategic factors driving the uneven market performance of multinational fastmoving consumer goods (FMCG) brands across culturally and economically distinct regions. While existing international marketing literature extensively debates global standardization versus local adaptation, there remains a critical gap in understanding why identical brand equity yields deep market penetration in one Asian market while remaining a niche offering in another. Grounded in the theoretical framework of glocalization, this paper presents a qualitative comparative case study of Nestlé's Maggi and Kellanova's Pringles across two contrasting environments: India (an emerging, value-driven market) and South Korea (a mature, trend-driven economy). Utilizing secondary data from corporate disclosures, market research indices, and academic literature spanning up to 2026, the study evaluates four core determinants: cultural preferences, localized consumption behavior, pricing models, and packaging strategies. The findings reveal that Maggi achieved intergenerational market leadership in India through deep flavor localization ("masala" profile) and low unit pricing (LUP) models, yet faced structural barriers in South Korea due to a highly saturated domestic ramyeon market and conflicting category expectations. Conversely, Pringles established a premium, high-margin position in South Korea by aligning with urban convenience-store retail layouts and experience-oriented "kidult" marketing, but remains restricted to a niche demographic in India due to mass-market price elasticity. The study concludes that international FMCG success depends less on global brand recognition than on the structural alignment between strategic positioning and the localized consumption logic of the target market. These insights offer actionable blueprints for multinational firms executing cross-border entry strategies.

detail.abstract: Standard marketing models assume buyers are constrained by budgets. At the ultra-high-net-worth threshold — defined by the Capgemini Research Institute (2025) as $30 million or more in investable assets — this constraint disappears, and with it the foundational logic of conventional acquisition theory. This paper argues that when liquid capital eliminates financial loss as a meaningful concern, decision-making reorganizes around four non-monetary risks: cognitive bandwidth, reputational standing, peer-group exclusion, and generational legacy. Simultaneously, because these individuals are saturated with high-end pitches, standard transformative marketing language fails to register. This paper develops a composite value function with logistic saturation bounding to formalise this structural migration, derives the limiting behavioural conditions as W → ∞, and proposes two empirically testable experimental designs through which the model's key parameters — including the trajectories of λ_fin(W) and λ_status(W) — can be estimated from observed UHNWI decision behaviour.

title: Twenty Percent of What? The Hidden Base of Digital Tipping

detail.title: Twenty Percent of What? The Hidden Base of Digital Tipping
detail.abstract: Digital tipping screens routinely present suggested gratuity percentages without disclosing the amount or base items on which those percentages will be calculated. Depending on merchant settings and point-of-sale systems, the tip base may include taxes, discounts, service charges, or even the full amount of a split check. This Comment argues that such undisclosed tip bases can constitute deceptive practices under Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act. A displayed percentage is an affirmative numerical representation because it necessarily refers to an underlying base. When that base is not properly disclosed, the resulting representation may create a misleading net impression, particularly in time-pressured checkout environments where consumers have limited ability to verify the calculation.

title: Examining the Impact of AI-based Personalised Marketing on Australian Bank Customers

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study examines the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled personalised marketing on customer experience in the Australian banking sector, specifically among Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) customers. Methodology: A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was a data-gathering tool that obtained data on 151 Generation Y (aged 29-44) CBA customers in Victoria. Relative advantage, complexity, and compatibility (constructs of Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory) and trust are constructs measured by the use of a structured questionnaire. Analyses were conducted in descriptive statistics, reliability tests, correlation and multiple regression. Findings: Relative advantage was a positive predictor of customer experience with the best predictive value (=0.706), compatibility (=0.226) and trust (=0.175), whereas complexity had considerable negative predictive value (=-0.276). This model attributed 77.4 percent of the variance; all the hypotheses were accepted. Originality: The study addresses a gap in the Australian-specific empirical research into the topic of AI personalisation in the banking sector by implementing the DOI theory to customer perceptions, presenting new information on the determinants of AI uptake and experience. Research limitations/implications: The study is limited to the sample of Gen-Y Victorian CBA customers, i.e. 29-44 aged individuals, and therefore cannot be generalised. Future research would benefit by expanding the demographic scope and using longitudinal designs. Practical implications: Practical implications Banks must focus on practical advantages, allow consistency with customer practices, make interfaces simple to diminish complexity, and build trust based on visible practices to maximise AI-enabled customer encounters.

title: Does Generative AI Make Startup Ideas Alike? Evidence from Product Hunt
affiliations: and Case Western Reserve University - Weatherhead School of Management

detail.title: Does Generative AI Make Startup Ideas Alike? Evidence from Product Hunt
detail.abstract: Founders increasingly use generative AI to develop new products. Because a market's stock of distinct ideas shapes what it can build next, we ask whether generative AI broadens or narrows the ideas that founders bring to it. We study 291,314 product launches posted to Product Hunt from January 2018 to April 2026. After ChatGPT's release, launches become more concentrated around common category concepts, and the share of distinctive launches falls by more than a third, from 25% to 16%. Using an outcome-blind LLM ideation-exposure index, we find that the post-ChatGPT increase in similarity is larger in categories where general-purpose LLMs can more effectively assist product ideation. First-time teams introduce more distinctive ideas than experienced teams, but similarity rises within both groups, and holding founder composition fixed leaves the exposure gradient essentially unchanged. These findings are consistent with independent founders drawing on a common input and converging toward common category concepts. Generative AI may thus expand individual entrepreneurs' ability to develop products while narrowing the range of ideas that entrepreneurial entry supplies to the market.

title: Dead Reckoning: Counting Your Customers Who Never Say Goodbye
affiliations: The Wharton School

detail.title: Dead Reckoning: Counting Your Customers Who Never Say Goodbye
detail.abstract: Firms in non-contractual commerce face the challenge of knowing how many customers they actually have because their customers can stop buying without ever saying they have left. Buy-Till-You-Die models address this problem by estimating each customer's probability of being alive, a quantity usually called P(alive) and used in essentially every major software tool for generating dashboards, defining churn, calculating customer equity, and valuing the enterprise. We show that this practice confounds two distinct quantities. Within the beta-geometric family of models, P(alive) is the infinite-horizon limit of an observable family of finite-horizon probabilities of repeat purchase. Every finite-horizon estimate, such as the probability of repeat purchase within 12 months, is a forecast of a verifiable event. The limit at infinite time can only be estimated by extrapolation, a customer count obtained by dead reckoning. The implied customer count is therefore only partially identified: realized returners are the lower bound, and estimation conventions determine the reported point estimate above that. The consequences are significant. In our empirical setting, on a seven-year transaction panel for 31,683 unique customers, model specifications with nearly identical observable forecasts estimate the number of "alive" customers at values ranging from 3,654 to 27,734, a difference of 7.6x. A default weighting parameter set in customer base software swings the count 42 percent. Five years of subsequent purchases further falsify the maximum-likelihood count from below. The main patterns we find can be replicated on the CDNOW benchmark, with a 2.4x spread in point estimates of the size of the customer base. Most of what practice calls miscalibration is instead a category error: summed P(alive) overshoots the realized eighteen-month returners by 2.25x, while the same model's own eighteen-month forecast errs by just 1.18x. The remedy is to report and maintain an auditable horizon count, say the number of actual repeat customers within 18 months, estimate return probabilities at a stated horizon, audit them across scoring dates and horizons, recalibrate them as customer cohorts drift, and report the total customer count, if it must be reported at all, as a confidence interval rather than a point.

title: Exploring Digitalization in Facility Management: Towards a Research Agenda
affiliations: , Polytechnic University of Milan, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Students and Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Students

detail.title: Exploring Digitalization in Facility Management: Towards a Research Agenda
detail.abstract:
Background and aim. Digitalization in facility management (FM) services is an emerging phenomenon. The sector tends to prioritize the adoption of technology to address immediate concerns rather than effectively framing fundamental problems, hindering the creation of a comprehensive strategy. There is a lack of reflection on the complex relationship between digital technologies and FM services, highlighting the necessity for new conceptualizations to address implementation challenges. Our paper aims to identify categories that facilitate research and knowledge exchange between academia and industry to enhance the understanding of digitalization and its strategies within FM.

Methods. We conducted workshops with academics and industry representatives focusing on (i) classification and conceptualization of digital technology applications in FM, (ii) the effects of digital technologies in FM, and (iii) standardization and scaling up digital solutions within organizations and the industry.

Results. The article advances understanding of digital technologies' potential for use in FM. (i) We classify digitalization based on business development, technology, and value chain perspectives. (ii) We identify technology considerations, such as incentives, return on investment, and efficiency, as well as barriers, including collaboration, contextual factors, and cultural challenges. Human-centric solutions are proposed to address these barriers. (iii) We discuss standardization challenges, including SME perspectives, ISO fragmentation, cybersecurity, data management, software integration, and path dependence.

Practical implications. Conceptualizations co-created by industry and academia contribute to the establishment of a relevant research agenda and the facilitation of digital technology implementation. Type of paper. Research (short) Keywords.

title: Do Product Market Reforms Work? Assessing Regulatory Changes Impacting Competition
affiliations: Norwich Business School, University of East Anglia and University of East Anglia (UEA) - School of Economics

detail.title: Do Product Market Reforms Work? Assessing Regulatory Changes Impacting Competition

declarations.funderStatement: Royal Economic Society funding was received

detail.abstract: We create a new dataset that characterizes studies of product market reforms implemented from 1932 to 2011. We examine the size and origins of differences in estimated impacts based on an OECD classification scheme for potentially competitive restrictions of regulation. The median impact from switching to a pro-competitive environment is a 19 per cent price decline. Competition-restricting regulations that are directed at specific societal objectives, such as health, safety, education, the environment, and financial stability, have lower price increases than the price declines from regulatory changes creating greater competition. The findings support the view that special interests obtain large benefits from favorable regulation. These findings can help policymakers when balancing the effects of competition-enhancing regulatory reform against other societal objectives.

detail.abstract:
We present a first iteration of stylized facts for the circular economy (CE) as a way to synthesize the knowledge compiled into interesting, relevant, and empirically grounded general statements. This compilation is the result of a collaborative review, synthesis, and stylization effort on CE knowledge. It makes the existing CE literature digestible to a variety of audiences while also highlighting strengths and weaknesses of research and implementation to-date. 

Each stylized fact is self-contained, using the established technical language of the field. It is accompanied by a statement of evidence, which links to the relevant literature compiled by the authors of the individual facts and multiple internal reviewers from the author team. The stylized facts presented here explore five critical dimensions of the CE: 1. Stock-flow-service nexus and stock growth; 2. Material cycles and R strategies; 3. Global supply chains and environmental impacts; 4. Economic and social challenges and opportunities, including CE business models; and 5. Policy and regulation. We group all facts into these five categories. Neither the list of topics nor the list of facts is exhaustive.

The facts and arguments presented here can serve as the synthesized empirical foundation that can be translated into different forms of science communication, such as teaching material, video lectures, animations, infographics, policy briefings, and more. Such materials could be used across scientific communities, practitioners, and the wider public. By presenting a concise, system-wide perspective, the stylized facts aim to improve understanding of what the CE is, what it can deliver, and where its fundamental limits lie, thereby supporting  more informed decision-making and dialogue across research, policy and practice communities.

title: Implementing Generative AI for Proactive Network Performance Monitoring, Anomaly Detection, and Solution Provisioning
affiliations: Softility

detail.title: Implementing Generative AI for Proactive Network Performance Monitoring, Anomaly Detection, and Solution Provisioning
detail.abstract: The increasing complexity of modern cyberphysical environments, driven by 5G and IoT-enabled networks, necessitates intelligent and proactive approaches for network performance monitoring, anomaly detection, and automated response provisioning. Traditional reactive systems are often inadequate for timely threat identification and mitigation. This paper proposes a generative AI-driven framework that integrates Variational Autoencoders (VAE), Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), TimeGAN, and Diffusion models to learn complex network traffic distributions and detect anomalies in real time. The framework is evaluated using CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15, and synthetic datasets with rigorous preprocessing, feature engineering, and SMOTEbased class balancing. Experimental results show that TimeGAN achieves superior performance with accuracy up to 0.9887 and F1-score of 0.9618 on CICIDS2017 and 0.9626 on UNSW-NB15, along with low false positive rates and efficient detection latency. The proposed system also incorporates proactive risk prediction and zero-day attack detection, enhancing early warning capabilities. Overall, the framework demonstrates high robustness, scalability, and effectiveness for next-generation intelligent cybersecurity systems.

detail.abstract:
Background. Healthcare organizations are deploying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to surface knowledge from enterprise data across clinical, administrative, and operational functions. RAG systems introduce a class of runtime governance exposure that data-at-rest controls do not fully address: information is retrieved, assembled into context, embedded in prompts, transformed during generation, and surfaced in responses, with each stage creating distinct policy-conformance risks. In regulated healthcare environments, existing candidate enforcement mechanisms, including model alignment, prompt instructions, and post-hoc review, are structurally insufficient as the primary enforcement layer because they cannot produce perinteraction governance guarantees that are independent of probabilistic model behavior.

Objective. This paper proposes a runtime control pattern for healthcare RAG that places deterministic policy enforcement in the orchestration layer surrounding the language model, external to the model and independent of its behavior. The pattern specifies how governance rules are operationalized at runtime across six deterministic gates aligned with the retrievalaugmented generation lifecycle.

Key Messages. The paper introduces four contributions. First, a staged control fabric that organizes deterministic enforcement by gate, applying the lowest-cost control sufficient for the interaction's risk tier and escalating only when policy, sensitivity, or exception conditions require it. Second, a policy compilation principle that translates governance rules into executable artifacts before runtime, enabling each gate to enforce pre-approved policy decisions rather than interpret policy at runtime. Third, a six-gate runtime control pattern and associated runtime control matrix covering pre-retrieval, retrieval-time, context-assembly, prompt-construction, response-time, and post-response stages. Fourth, a failure-mode vocabulary naming enforcement leakage, boundary inversion, and verification gap as the primary architectural patterns that undermine deterministic enforcement.

Conclusions. The contribution is conceptual-architectural. No empirical validation is presented. The pattern specifies a runtime enforcement layer for regulated healthcare RAG systems; runtime auditability, evidence logging, source traceability, and human attestation are treated in the next paper in this series.

title: The DMA's Contribution to EU Digital Sovereignty

detail.title: The DMA's Contribution to EU Digital Sovereignty
detail.abstract:
Within the scope of core platform services, the Digital Markets Act (DMA) can contribute to the EU’s digital sovereignty. Since the gatekeepers of core platform services in the EU are currently mostly based in the United States and China, the DMA’s objective of making their position more contestable could, if successful, provide more room for providers from the EU or from other jurisdictions than those in which the gatekeepers are based. The growth of such alternative providers would reduce the ability of a single non-EU jurisdiction to control core platform services provided in the EU.

However, merely making these positions more contestable will not ensure EU digital sovereignty. In fact, most of the competitors of gatekeepers of core platform services are based in the same jurisdiction (mostly the US) as the gatekeepers themselves. If these competitors benefit most from increased contestability, this will not reduce the EU’s dependence on that jurisdiction. To enhance EU digital sovereignty, additional supply and demand-side measures should be taken to facilitate the growth of European providers of digital services.

title: How do Ransomware Groups Choose Their Targets? An Empirical Analysis
affiliations: University of Tulsa - Tandy School of Computer Science, University of Tulsa - Tandy School of Computer Science and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR)

detail.title: How do Ransomware Groups Choose Their Targets? An Empirical Analysis

declarations.funderStatement: Gandal and Moore gratefully acknowledge support from the US National Science Foundation (NSF) Award No. 2452738

detail.abstract: Ransomware groups vary in the types of organizations they compromise, yet little empirical work has examined whether these differences extend to the technology stacks of victims. We analyze 5,190 ransomware incidents across 151 groups, linking each victim to its observed technology stack from the SWDB Company Intelligence database. We find that some enterprise software is associated with greater ransomware risk than others, and that this association is often stronger for technologies carrying more known vulnerabilities. Next, by analyzing leaked chat logs of leading ransomware groups, we present direct evidence that some groups choose their victims based on observed technology use and revenue data gathered through opensource intelligence. Finally, examining the full population of victims, we find that some groups concentrate on particular technologies and revenue profiles, while others appear more opportunistic, with a victim profile close to the overall population.

title: Correct-by-Construction Factor Computation: A Verifiably Point-in-Time Engine for Tradeable Signals
affiliations: and Sky Alpha

detail.title: Correct-by-Construction Factor Computation: A Verifiably Point-in-Time Engine for Tradeable Signals
detail.abstract: Empirical factor research suffers from a reproducibility problem and a deployment problem, and both are fundamentally problems of engineering. Pipelines that compute firm-level signals routinely admit look-ahead bias. They do so through restated fundamentals, through the gap between a filing's date and its public availability, and, more subtly, through cross-sectional estimation that presumes a firm's peers are observable before they have all reported. Such pipelines are also typically too slow and too monolithic to refresh on a point-in-time (PIT) basis at the cadence live portfolios require. We present PITROVE, a factor-computation engine built on a single principle: PIT correctness is a verifiable construction invariant, not a claim. The engine couples a declarative, self-describing predictor specification with a non-bypassable validation gate that admits a signal to the feature store only if it satisfies five invariants: temporal causality, finiteness, key-uniqueness, nondegeneracy, and freshness. The engine attaches most accounting signals by an announcement-date backward join, which closes availabilitytiming leakage; for same-period cross-sectional signals it applies a stronger statutory-deadline release rule that blocks both restatement leakage and the incomplete-cross-section leakage naive as-of joins miss, demonstrated on the abnormal-accruals construction. We evaluate PITROVE using the Open Asset Pricing catalogue as a standardized, reproducible workload, the role TPC benchmarks play for database systems. From it we instantiate 150 of the 212 predictors as 160 daily signals over 2,222 Taiwan-listed securities and roughly 8.0 million firm-day observations each. Checked individually, every one of the 160 series records zero look-ahead violations, zero non-finite values, and zero duplicate keys, and the engine rebuilds the entire library, roughly 1.3 billion signal values, from raw data in approximately sixteen minutes. We are explicit that this certifies integrity rather than profitability. A controlled experiment shows that the engine's statutory-deadline rule removes a systematic cross-sectional bias that a naive announcement-date join leaves in place, cutting the error in a known signal by 37%; this is the root-mean-square error in a controlled synthetic simulation, and the ranking-relevant gain is smaller. A real-Taiwan run of the same ablation on two cross-sectional signals reorders early-filing firms into different deciles (~47% for abnormal accruals), but by no more than a same-size random subsample does, so the leakage-specific component is not detectable above finite-sample noise; the long-short portfolio effect is likewise statistically indistinguishable from zero, indicating that this leakage adds estimation noise rather than spuriously inflating performance. We ship the ablation harness and a full reproducibility artifact so that both the guarantee and its economic stakes are auditable. As an end-to-end demonstration that one codebase serves both research and production, a net-of-fee momentum signal generated by the engine compounds at 26.3% annually (Sharpe 1.24) against 12.0% for the market over twenty-one years, with a Sharpe ratio above one in every fiveyear sub-period. The contribution is the verifiable, portable, production-scale engine; the anomalies are merely its workload.

title: ArgorixLang: Compiled Governance, Sovereign Agent Metadata, and Offline-Verifiable Runtime Evidence
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: ArgorixLang: Compiled Governance, Sovereign Agent Metadata, and Offline-Verifiable Runtime Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they are contributors to the ArgorixLang research artifact and related implementation. No personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations are known to have influenced the study. The paper is claim-bounded and distinguishes implemented mechanisms, declarative metadata, proposed architecture, and properties not claimed.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve patients, clinical participants, or human-subject experimentation. The empirical analysis was based on an authorized artifact snapshot of runtime-generated request directories. Publication authorization was provided for the runtime material, and the study applied data minimization by aggregating identifiers, avoiding prompt reconstruction, and reporting only bounded artifact-level observations. Formal ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted by the authors using their own institutional, technical, and research resources.

detail.abstract: Agent systems increasingly combine model calls, tools, data movement, and inter-agent protocols, but their governance assumptions are commonly expressed outside the executable artifact. This paper presents ArgorixLang, a compiled language and runtime in which agent capabilities, policy, sovereign metadata, provider boundaries, and evidence requirements are explicit program constructs. We distinguish four claim classes throughout: implemented mechanisms, declarative metadata, proposed architecture, and properties not claimed. We study an authorized corpus of 33 runtime request directories using a reproducible, observational pipeline. Twenty-seven directories contain all five expected artifacts and six contain source only. All 27 complete evidence bundles pass offline digest and crossartifact verification of bytecode, trace, and security report, including a ledger digest recomputed from trace events and matched against the report's LedgerSummary; source integrity is outside bundle verification. At the same time, all 27 detailed policy reports set passed=false, require review, and record 44 unknown-rule violations each, despite a favorable top-level security_checks label. Thus bundle integrity does not imply policy approval, security, or certification. The corpus contains 7,155 ledger events and 1,188 detailed policy violations. The bounded injected.content field is present in 0 of 27-that is, none of the 27-complete, valid traces; six source-only directories have no trace and are not assessable, precluding prompt-level qualitative analysis. We describe the compiler, failclosed runtime, Agent Passport metadata, a declarative encoding of the unpublished ATrust conceptual protocol, its relationship to DCP-AI, and trace/report/bundle generation. The results demonstrate reproducible artifact production and offline integrity checking under the observed configuration; they do not demonstrate real identity authentication, credential verification, cryptographic handshakes, blockchain immutability, post-quantum security, compliance certification, or production isolation.

title: Evaluating the Implementation of Digital Rights in Platforms’ Terms and Conditions under the EU Digital Services Act

detail.title: Evaluating the Implementation of Digital Rights in Platforms’ Terms and Conditions under the EU Digital Services Act
detail.abstract: This paper examines how digital rights are operationalised, communicated, and implemented within platform governance frameworks under the EU Digital Services Act (DSA). While the DSA introduces a rights-based model centred on transparency, accountability, and user protection, there remains limited empirical evidence on how these rights are translated into platform practices. Drawing on a dataset of Terms of Service and Community Guidelines from twenty-nine platforms operating in the EU, this study adopts a mixed-methods content analysis approach. The analysis evaluates the accessibility and implementation of key procedural digital rights, including clarity of rules, enforcement transparency, and the availability of appeal mechanisms. Readability metrics are used to assess whether users can meaningfully access and understand these rights, while qualitative coding examines how platforms define harms, justify moderation, and structure enforcement. The findings reveal systematic variation across platform types, suggesting that digital rights under the DSA are unevenly realised in practice. Rather than functioning as uniform safeguards, user rights are mediated by platform design, business models, and regulatory exposure. By conceptualising platform policies as data infrastructures of governance, the paper demonstrates how the accessibility and effectiveness of digital rights can be empirically assessed through policy texts. The findings contribute to ongoing debates on the limits of rights-based digital regulation, highlighting the need for stronger oversight, improved comparability across platforms, and greater attention to the conditions under which users can meaningfully exercise their rights in data-driven environments.

title: Off-Balance-Sheet Utilization of Decentralized Compute-Sharing Protocols: True Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) Distortion and the Implicit Tail-Risk Premium in Credit Default Swap Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Off-Balance-Sheet Utilization of Decentralized Compute-Sharing Protocols: True Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) Distortion and the Implicit Tail-Risk Premium in Credit Default Swap Markets
detail.abstract: The proliferation of decentralized compute-sharing protocols-comprising blockchain-mediated GPU rental markets, tokenized inference networks, and distributed training consortia-has introduced a novel class of operational expenditure that systematically evades conventional on-balance-sheet recognition under both IFRS 16 and ASC 842 frameworks. This paper investigates whether such off-balance-sheet utilization materially distorts the True Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) of technology-intensive enterprises, and examines the degree to which credit default swap (CDS) markets price an implicit tail-risk premium attributable to this hidden operational leverage. We develop a formal accounting taxonomy distinguishing tokenized compute expenditure from conventional cloud procurement and demonstrate, through a multi-sector panel of 214 firms across the 2019-2024 period, that off-balance-sheet compute intensity correlates with a statistically significant FCFF overstatement of between 8.3% and 22.7%, conditional on firm leverage quartile and AI-workload concentration. Employing a structural credit-risk model augmented with a stochastic compute-liability factor, we derive a closed-form expression for the tail-risk premium embedded in five-year CDS spreads and find that markets demand an implicit premium of 14-47 basis points per unit of unrecognized compute leverage, with pronounced convexity at distress boundaries. These findings have material implications for credit analysts, valuation practitioners, and regulatory bodies considering the adequacy of existing lease-capitalization standards for intangible-infrastructure arrangements.

title: Classification of Blockchain Network Governance Types: Focusing on the Current State of Blockchain Network Governance and Accessibility

detail.title: Classification of Blockchain Network Governance Types: Focusing on the Current State of Blockchain Network Governance and Accessibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, animals, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper clarifies the definition of blockchain network governance and separates blockchain network governance layers into community layer and technical layer. Existing studies on blockchain governance have defined blockchain governance as all elements that include decision-making and cooperation within the platform, so it is not possible to closely analyze and evaluate the decision-making process that occurs at each layer. Therefore, according to this paper, the technical layer is defined as the layer where consensus is generated passively by algorithms or should not be changed arbitrarily due to the common characteristics of public blockchain technology (immutability, transparency, decentralization), and the community layer is defined as the layer where discussions that can affect the entire blockchain platform, including changes to the protocol, occur.
  In addition, through the cases of the EIP-779 hardfork and the Bitcoin BlockSize War, it focuses on the causes of sharp conflicts in blockchain network governance, such as information asymmetry, low accessibility, and the lack of secondary rules, which make it difficult to secure the legitimacy of decisions made in the network. The paper classifies blockchain network governance into four types based on on-chain utilization. It proposes an evaluation method to assess governance type and accessibility, aiding users in identifying a network’s governance type and recognizing shortcomings in its governance function.

title: The Reflexive Self-Referential Paradox of Suppressing Stuttering Anticipation - Constrained Optimization, Shadow Values, and a Testable Channel Framework

detail.title: The Reflexive Self-Referential Paradox of Suppressing Stuttering Anticipation - Constrained Optimization, Shadow Values, and a Testable Channel Framework

keywords.keywords: stuttering anticipation; developmental stuttering; thought suppression; self-monitoring; speech initiation.

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper analyzes a reflexive instruction in which a speaker attempts not to predict that they will stutter and may monitor whether the prediction has disappeared. Let S denote the prediction that the speaker will stutter during the next relevant speech initiation. Under idealized, faithful, and reflexive execution, suppressing S or verifying its absence requires the system to discriminate states containing S from states not containing S. Consequently, S must enter the task as an object of suppression, a recognition criterion, a failure condition, or a control parameter. Execution is incompatible with the strong success condition that S never becomes task-relevant. The term reflexive self-referential paradox refers here to the joint unsatisfiability of execution and strong success conditions, rather than to a semantic truth-value contradiction. A constrained optimization model is then introduced. The agent can adjust target monitoring m and content-directed activity a; anticipation strength q is an auxiliary state variable generated by baseline anticipation, direct cueing, monitoring-induced reactivation, and content-directed activity. The value function V (r, s, B, x) is the lowest feasible anticipation frontier given task intensity r, baseline anticipation s, cognitive resources B, and context x. The envelope theorem yields V r = ω r + λ * mr + ν * ρ r , and, under local interior conditions, the first-order conditions refine this into V r = ω r + ϕ m mr + ν * (c m,m mr + ρ r).

title: Residents’ Satisfaction Survey on the Primary Health Care Services of Barangay Pay-As, Kadingilan, Bukidnon
affiliations: and Central Mindanao University

detail.title: Residents’ Satisfaction Survey on the Primary Health Care Services of Barangay Pay-As, Kadingilan, Bukidnon
detail.abstract: Primary health care (PHC) is the cornerstone of an effective health system, providing accessible, equitable, and community-=based healthcare services that promote disease prevention, health promotion, and improved quality life. Measuring residents' satisfaction is an essential indicator of service quality because it reflects whether healthcare services meet the needs and expectations of community. Guided by the Expectation-Confirmation Theory, this study assessed residents' satisfaction with the implementation of primary health care services in Barangay Pay-as, Kadingilan, Bukidnon. Specifically, the study determined the reasons for providing primary health care services, identified the services availed by the residents and their expectations, measured their level of satisfaction, and examined the factors influencing satisfaction. The study employed a descriptive mixed-methods research design involving 77 residents who had availed themselves of at least one primary health care service offered by the Barangay Pay-as Health Center. Quantitative data were collected through a validated researcher-developed questionnaire, while qualitative data were gathered through interviews to support and enrich the quantitative data, whereas thematic analysis was employed for the qualitative responses. The findings revealed that residents were very satisfied (4.55 weighted mean) with maternal checkup , child immunization (4.67), family planning (4.63), and consultation and dispensing of medicines (4.56). Hypertension and diabetic maintenance services received a satisfied (4.32 weighted mean) rating primarily due to intermittent shortages of maintenance medicines and delays in medical supply distribution. Overall, residents expressed a very high level of satisfaction (4.55). Satisfaction was strongly influenced by the quality of healthcare services, healthcare providers' interpersonal skills, accessibility and continuity of care, promptness of service delivery, and the cleanliness and comfort of the health center. The findings indicate that while the Barangay Pay-as Health Center effectively delivers primary health care services, strengthening medicine availability and enhancing technical competencies through continuous professional development can further improve service quality and residents' satisfaction.

title: Inequalities in Spatial Accessibility to General Practitioners across Transport Modes in Germany: A Nationwide, High-Resolution Cross-Sectional Modelling Study
affiliations: Robert Koch Institute, Robert Koch Institute, Robert Koch Institute and

detail.title: Inequalities in Spatial Accessibility to General Practitioners across Transport Modes in Germany: A Nationwide, High-Resolution Cross-Sectional Modelling Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (grant 01EL2350C).

detail.abstract:
Background: German demand planning measures primary care access largely by car and neglects residents who walk, cycle, or rely on public transport. We quantified inequalities in spatial accessibility to general practitioners (GPs) by transport mode, urbanicity, and area-level socioeconomic deprivation.

Methods: This cross-sectional study linked the 2022 German Census ($100\mathrm{m}$ grid; 82·57 million residents) to all statutory GPs (2024), assessing travel times by walking, cycling, public transport, and car against mode-specific thresholds. County-level mode shares and morbidity-adjusted demand entered a multi-modal floating catchment area method with modes competing for shared supply. Accessibility was expressed as spatial access ratios (SPAR; national mean 1·00), and inequality decomposed with the population-weighted Theil T index.

Findings: Virtually all residents (>99·98\%) could reach a GP within a 24-minute drive. Without a car, 6·83 million (8·27\%) could not reach any GP within the thresholds, rising to 30·39\% in rural small-town and village areas, with no consistent deprivation gradient. Population-weighted median SPAR was 1·40 (IQR 0·96--2·15) for driving, 0·34 (0·11--0·89) for public transport, 0·17 (0·08--0·34) for cycling, and 0·06 (0·03--0·11) for walking. Nested Theil decomposition (T=0·54) attributed 61·52\% to transport modes, 18·57\% to urbanicity within modes, and 2·66\% to deprivation.

Interpretation: High physician density and universal coverage are necessary but not sufficient for equitable spatial access. Because transport mode dominates inequality in spatial accessibility, statutory planning should incorporate multi-modal reachability and accessibility standards. Improving patient mobility or bringing care closer to patients may reduce inequality more than redistributing GPs alone.

title: Natural Language Processing (NLP) Analysis of the Bank of Algeria's Communiques
affiliations: Research Center for Economics Applied to Development and

detail.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP) Analysis of the Bank of Algeria's Communiques
detail.abstract: This research applies text mining and natural language processing (NLP) methods to examine the communicative tactics of the Bank of Algeria through its annual reports from 2002 to 2022. Techniques such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for topic modeling and sentiment analysis with the Loughran-McDonald dictionary were employed to identify main themes and emotional tones. The remarkable changes in the bank's communication indicate the effects of oil price shocks, the global financial crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Initially, this was about economic expansion and monetary policy, but later it became focused on inflation targeting as well as financial stability in times of economic turbulence. Negative sentiment during this period indicates a cautious approach according to sentiment analysis results. Readability tests using the Coleman-Liau readability index also suggest that although the texts are complicated, they remain clear for efficient communication with both the public and employees operating in the marketplace. This is an area where literature lacks because no one has ever studied how Bank of Algeria reports can be analyzed utilizing these advanced techniques in text mining and NLP, as far as we have been able to find so far.

title: Every Sixty Days: The Customer-Initiated Accommodation and the Disability That Cannot Initiate

detail.title: Every Sixty Days: The Customer-Initiated Accommodation and the Disability That Cannot Initiate

keywords: American Council of the Blind v. Paulson

detail.abstract: For a large population of disabled people, electricity is not a utility service. It is the delivery medium of a legally required accommodation. An augmentative communication device is speech for a person who does not speak; an alarm is medication adherence for a person whose disability impairs prospective memory; a timer is executive function. When the power goes off, the accommodation goes off. The ventilator and the communication device are on the same circuit for the same reason, and no state disconnection rule sees the second one. This Article argues that state utility commissions have built every disability protection against disconnection on a single architecture, and that the architecture is inaccessible by reason of disability. The customer must know the protection exists, initiate the request, obtain third-party documentation, submit it inside a window, and renew it before it lapses. Those five acts describe one capacity, and that capacity is what cognitive, intellectual, and neurodevelopmental disability impairs. The regime conditions the benefit on the one thing the beneficiary cannot reliably do. Illinois supplies the worked example. Under 83 Ill. Adm. Code 280.160, a licensed physician must certify that disconnection will aggravate or create a medical emergency; the certificate protects the account for sixty days; and a person whose disability is permanent must therefore obtain and submit six certifications every year, for life. If the customer certifies late, the payment arrangement demands one fourth of the arrears rather than one twelfth. The installment triples. Lateness is the impairment. Pennsylvania supplies the proof of failure: when an evaluator finally measured whether a comparable program reached the households at the bottom, the answer was that roughly eighty percent of them received unaffordable bills under the program built to make bills affordable. The argument does not rest on disparate impact, which Alexander v. Choate declined to extend to all action disparately affecting people with disabilities. It rests on what Choate preserved: that a benefit may not be defined in a way that effectively denies meaningful access, and that a facially neutral criterion survives only where it does not turn on a trait the protected class is less capable of meeting. The Article locates the correct defendant, which is the commission and not the utility, and shows that Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison Co. points at the agency rather than away from it: a commission that orders a practice, rather than approving one a utility proposed, has put its own weight behind it. And it identifies a reliance defect in ratemaking. Commissions have expressly credited customer assistance programs when setting an authorized return on equity. None has asked whether the programs reach the customers whose hardship they are credited with mitigating.

title: Anticipation and Adaptation: Cost-Sharing Responses and Mortality Among the Oldest-Old
affiliations: Waseda University, , Waseda University and Waseda University

detail.title: Anticipation and Adaptation: Cost-Sharing Responses and Mortality Among the Oldest-Old

publicationDetails.detailsText: WINPEC Working Paper Series No. E26010 July 2026

detail.abstract: We study a Japanese reform that doubled coinsurance rates for higher-income enrollees aged 75+, using administrative data linking insurance claims to tax records for essentially the entire oldest-old population over 26 months. Patients exhibit a last-minute anticipatory surge before implementation, then persistently reduce utilization by cutting visit frequency rather than treatment intensity. Responses follow a gradient of service discretionarity, and a binding expenditure cap shields the most medically intensive patients from the reform's financial impact. Despite utilization reductions, 15-month mortality shows no adverse effect. Carefully calibrated cost-sharing, paired with effective safety nets, can achieve fiscal objectives without detectable health costs among the oldest-old.

title: Koyaanisqatsi: The Anthropocene Assault on Animal Kinship, Animal Suffering, Māyā, and the Kolmogorov Non-Warrant of Human Dominion - A Treatise on the Animal Condition in the Anthropocene

detail.title: Koyaanisqatsi: The Anthropocene Assault on Animal Kinship, Animal Suffering, Māyā, and the Kolmogorov Non-Warrant of Human Dominion - A Treatise on the Animal Condition in the Anthropocene

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Work is self-funded

detail.abstract: This paper develops the animal-specific ‘non-warrant’ framework and applies it to the human systems by which animals are confined, bred, forcibly reproduced, separated from kin, tortured, experimented upon, transported, commodified, humiliated, killed, and hidden behind names such as livestock, stock, pest, model organism, production animal, research subject, humane slaughter, welfare compliance, food security, sustainability, legal ownership, and market necessity. Its central object is not animal rights as an extension of human legal categories, nor animal welfare as a measurement problem within existing systems, but the stronger claim by which the Anthropocene human order asserts authority over animal Wamákȟaŋškaŋ. The treatise defines that claim as the animal-domination warrant, and, in its most concentrated form, as the animal-imprisonment warrant. The argument proceeds by first demoting the human claimant. Human cognition is treated as a proper subset of the living system; human models are reductions; science is a tool rather than an oracle; no species enjoys metaphysical privilege; and beings excluded from human forums require representation. The treatise then defines the animal-Whole as the animal considered not merely as body, output, biomass, welfare score, toxicity endpoint, or population unit, but as sentient experience, bodily integrity, movement, fear, pain, kinship, mother-child relation, reproductive process, lineage, future branch-space, ecological participation, genetic future, recursive evolutionary effect, and human-return field. The formal contribution is the Animal Imprisonment Non-Warrant Theorem. Using conditional Kolmogorov complexity and model-package analysis, the treatise argues that no finite, non-oracular, non-hard-coded human package can supply scientifically warranted authority to imprison, breed, torture, experiment upon, separate, commodify, humiliate, or kill animals where the claim-relevant animal future remainder remains uncontained. Such a package includes not only data, variables, equations, protocols, and validation rules, but also the lexical-categorical frame, residual apparatus, bridge from past to future, and institutional uptake. Description, diagnosis, warning, restraint, rescue, and repair may survive; future-authorising animal domination does not. The required consequence is withdrawal of the warrant and abolition of animal murder, torture, imprisonment, reproductive seizure, commodification, humiliation, and suffering for human purposes.

title: Substitution, Not Speculation: Why the Artificial Intelligence Investment Cycle Need Not Be a Bubble, and Why Its Robustness Accelerates the Commoditization of the Build

detail.title: Substitution, Not Speculation: Why the Artificial Intelligence Investment Cycle Need Not Be a Bubble, and Why Its Robustness Accelerates the Commoditization of the Build
detail.abstract: The 2025-2026 debate over an "AI bubble" has generated much heat and little classificatory clarity. This paper does not argue that valuations are modest, that froth is absent, or that no capital will be destroyed. It argues something narrower: the prevailing analogy to the dot-com episode of 1999-2001 misclassifies the object being repriced, and once that error is corrected the cycle need not be read as a bubble at all. Dot-com was the speculative repricing of a medium: the internet transports, stores, and recombines value created elsewhere but performs no productive work itself. The present cycle reprices a production factor: a synthetic, scalable, increasingly capable substitute for qualified human labor. The distinction is not rhetorical. A medium is valued on the expectation that others will build productive activity upon it, a long, contingent link, easily over-extrapolated, which is why media bubbles are common; a factor is valued on the marginal product it delivers directly, and the link between an AI system and the cognitive task it performs (drafting, translating, coding, reviewing) is immediate and measurable. Building on the author's Commoditization Stack and Data-Driven Platform of Platforms (DPoP) frameworks, the paper advances four propositions. First, the concentration of venture capital in frontier laboratories is a rational repricing of a labor-substituting factor, not mania. Second, weakness in SaaS valuations is not a symptom of an AI bubble but a confirmation of the commoditization gradient: layer-4 application software is being substituted by agentic AI as the Stack predicts. Third, AI's dual-use character and centrality to state strategy place it in a different risk class than commercial speculative assets. Fourth, the cycle's genuine pathologies (circular vendor financing, the enterprise deployment gap, energy constraints, the contested economic life of AI hardware) are best read as the friction of a mispriced-but-real factor market, not evidence of a content-free bubble. An illustrative, data-calibrated demonstration for Brazil's services economy makes the mechanism concrete: as capability commoditizes, a measurable share of a national wage bill is converted into payments for an imported factor that migrate toward the bloc hosting the frontier laboratories, surfacing as revenue and valuation, while a substantial premium is retained domestically. Modelling one economy and only the labor-substitution channel, it is a conservative lower bound; benchmarked against the official Brazil-United States trade balance, that flow would become a first-order driver of the bilateral imbalance. A network-effects reading converges: durable effects accrue not to commoditizing capability access but to the defensible upper layers, where revenue compounds. A falsifiable diagnostic closes the argument, and the double thread stands: the robustness that makes AI a real factor is the same force that accelerates the commoditization of the build.

title: Long-Term Epidemiology, Clinical Outcomes, and Healthcare Costs of Invasive Meningococcal Disease in Taiwan: A Nationwide Linked Surveillance and Claims-Based Study
affiliations: National Cheng Kung University, National Cheng Kung University, Sanofi, Sanofi, National Cheng Kung University, National Cheng Kung University - National Cheng Kung University Hospital and National Cheng Kung University

detail.title: Long-Term Epidemiology, Clinical Outcomes, and Healthcare Costs of Invasive Meningococcal Disease in Taiwan: A Nationwide Linked Surveillance and Claims-Based Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Huang-Tz Ou received a speaker honorarium from Daiichi Sankyo, Sanofi, Boehringer Ingelheim, GlaxoSmithKline, and Eli Lily for a scientific speech.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of National Cheng Kung University Hospital (111-4458). The requirement for informed consent was waived because all data were de-identified before analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was sponsored by Sanofi and National Science and Technology Council in Taiwan (grant NSTC112-2628-B-006-008-MY3) (recipient: Huang-Tz Ou).

detail.abstract:
Background: Invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) is uncommon but associated with substantial mortality and long-term sequelae. Population-based evidence from Asia-Pacific settings remains scarce, and long-term evidence on post-IMD sequelae, healthcare utilization, and medical costs is limited. This study evaluated the long-term burden of IMD across all age groups in Taiwan.

Methods: We conducted a nationwide population-based study by linking confirmed IMD cases from Taiwan Centers for Disease Control surveillance data during 2002–2020 to the National Health Insurance Research Database, with follow-up through 2021. IMD-related sequelae, healthcare utilization, and medical costs were examined overall and stratified by age group and sequelae status. Regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with sequelae, medical costs, and all-cause mortality. 

Findings: Among 217 linked IMD cases, the mean age was 29.7 years, and 57% were male. Serogroup B was the predominant subtype among patients with available information. During follow-up, all-cause mortality was 33%, increasing from 14% in children aged≤12 years to 79% in adults aged≥65 years. Overall, 24% of patients experienced at least one complication or sequela, most commonly neurological impairment. Mean annual medical costs increased 2.6-fold in the first year after diagnosis. Older age and higher comorbidity burden were associated with both mortality and higher medical costs. 

Interpretation: IMD remains associated with substantial long-term burden in Taiwan, particularly among older adults and survivors with sequelae. These nationwide linked data provide region-specific evidence for future surveillance, economic evaluation, and life-course prevention policy discussions in Taiwan and the broader Asia-Pacific region.

title: The Möbius Vulnerability: The genealogy of LLM: Pathologies Epistemic Residue, Derivability Decay, and Temporal Failure in Generative AI Systems
affiliations: Independent

declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a preliminary theory of epistemic pathologies in generative AI systems. Its central claim is that important failures cannot be understood only as hallucinations, biases, alignment defects or isolated errors. They must also be understood as temporal and genealogical phenomena: effects produced by the accumulation of epistemic residues along stochastic conversational trajectories. The paper introduces derivability as the capacity to reconstruct the path connecting input, transformation and output. It then defines the Möbius Vulnerability as the limit-event in which a model appears to correct itself while preserving the structural form of the error that generated the correction. Against evaluation paradigms that privilege isolated outputs, the paper argues for trajectory-based epistemic analysis. A model may remain locally coherent while becoming globally non-derivable. This condition gives rise to a deeper risk: the formation of plausible but weakly derivable epistemic environments, here called Mythos. The paper deliberately does not provide an implementation protocol, scoring system or operational architecture. It identifies the theoretical conditions under which derivability decay, correction failure and Möbius-like trajectories may emerge.

title: The Mother of All Cutbacks: Couples' Expenditure Shifts after the First Birth in Japan
