detail.abstract: This paper examines how first childbirth reshapes the within-couple distribution of private consumption in Japan. Using panel data from the Japanese Panel Survey of Consumers and a staggered event-study design, I find that first birth triggers a marked and persistent decline in wives' private expenditure while husbands' expenditure changes much less, shifting resources within the household toward the husband. The effect is largest for women who are active on the labor market, for wives with lower pre-birth earnings, and for couples where the husband is among lower earners prior to birth. The evidence suggests that some of the most vulnerable groups face the most negative outcomes regarding a factor that is sometimes overlooked: who gets to spend how much?

title: The Economic Value of Sample Correlation Information in Minimum-Variance Portfolios
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - Lingnan (University) College

detail.title: The Economic Value of Sample Correlation Information in Minimum-Variance Portfolios
detail.abstract: High-dimensional Global Minimum-Variance (GMV) portfolios require deciding when estimated dependence improves risk control rather than amplifies estimation error. We study this trade-off by separating the diversification value of sample correlations from the noise they introduce into portfolio weights. We decompose GMV weights into an inverse-variance benchmark and an orthogonal correlation correction. This decomposition identifies a marginal correlation signal, a local risk cost, and an oracle value of correlation information. The signal-cost representation leads to the Correlation-Screened Minimum-Variance (CSMV) portfolio estimator, which applies a signal-to-noise calibration rule to admit correlation corrections only when their estimated signal is large relative to split-sample noise. We further define Incremental Correlation Information Value (ICIV), an ex-ante measure of when sample correlations are likely to reduce risk. Monte Carlo designs with block, factor, time-varying, and crisis dependence show that CSMV stabilizes sample-covariance portfolios while retaining useful dependence information, and that ICIV aligns with oracle correlation value and true next-period variance reductions. Empirical evidence from U.S. equities shows that CSMV delivers the lowest out-of-sample volatility, particularly in high-dimensional universes, while ICIV-based sorts and predictive regressions identify states associated with larger realized risk reductions. The findings show that correlation information has economic value when its reliability is assessed before portfolio formation.

title: BrainBridge: Foundation-Model-Anchored Multi-View Fusion under Degraded Overlap for EEG, MEG, and fMRI
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: BrainBridge: Foundation-Model-Anchored Multi-View Fusion under Degraded Overlap for EEG, MEG, and fMRI
detail.abstract: Multi-view learning with neural recordings is challenging because EEG, MEG, and fMRIprovide heterogeneous and only partially overlapping views of the same stimuli. In practice,the overlap between modalities further degrades after subject and stimulus matching, makingcross-viewfusion and conversion harder than native within-viewretrieval.We study this problemin a foundation-model-anchored setting where each modality is aligned to frozen CLIP imageembeddings, and ask whether shared targets alone are sufficient to produce compatible crossmodalneighborhoods. Using THINGS-EEG2, THINGS-MEG, and THINGS-fMRI, we builddeterministic manifest-backed splits that separate native full-retrieval from pairwise and threewayshared-pool conversion. We then introduce BrainBridge, a multi-view fusion frameworkwith modality-specific encoders and a joint three-way contrastive objective that adds sameimagecross-view pressure among EEG, MEG, and fMRI embeddings. In subject-specificexperiments, independently trained encoders degrade as the shared candidate pool becomes morerestrictive, indicating that foundation-model anchoring alone does not guarantee robust crossviewcompatibility under degraded overlap. By contrast, the joint three-way objective improvesthe mean matched three-way raw conversion score in all six directional pairs relative to thematched baseline (+2.60 to +4.96 CLIP 2-way points) while preserving competitive retrievalperformance. These results position BrainBridge as a concrete approach to multi-view fusion onlow-quality, partially overlapping neural views.

title: The Potential and Utility of Land Value Taxation: A Theoretical Framework and Simulation for China
affiliations: Syracuse University, CEPR and Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: The Potential and Utility of Land Value Taxation: A Theoretical Framework and Simulation for China
detail.abstract: This paper develops an analytical framework for examining land taxation in the context of contemporary urban economies. We study the case of China by way of model-based simulations, comparing two scenarios where revenue losses from consumption taxes are replaced by either higher income taxes or higher land taxes. We calibrate the model to 2015 data and find that higher income taxes cause large losses in output and income, while higher land taxes lead to substantial gains that increase with the share of land in net wealth.

title: Coastal Sustainability and Environmental Resilience in France: A Decadal Assessment of Littoral Dynamics Using Satellite Images

detail.title: Coastal Sustainability and Environmental Resilience in France: A Decadal Assessment of Littoral Dynamics Using Satellite Images
detail.abstract: French coastal systems are characterized by strong environmental gradients and increasing anthropogenic pressures, resulting in rapid land cover transformations across coastal landscapes. This study investigates land cover dynamics along the northern, western, and southern French coasts using Sentinel-2 summer image time series acquired between 2015 and 2025. The research aims to identify the most dynamic coastal regions and determine where land cover transitions are most pronounced. A harmonized workflow was developed in GRASS GIS for preprocessing Sentinel imagery, generating seasonal composites, classifying land cover using a Random Forest (RF) supervised algorithm, and detecting changes through time. All imagery was processed using CORINE Land Cover (Level 1) classification nomenclature and projected to Lambert-93 (EPSG:2154). Comparative analyses were performed among the three coastal regions using statistical indicators of change intensity, persistence, and transition rates. The results reveal substantial regional differences in coastal dynamics, with the southern Mediterranean coast exhibiting the highest transformation rate (22.9% of total area changed, at 2.29% yr-1), followed by the northern English Channel coast (18.6%; 1.86% yr-1) and the western Atlantic coast (14.2%; 1.42% yr-1). Urbanization and natural vegetation loss were identified as dominant transition types across all regions. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of Sentinel-2 time series and open-source GRASS GIS methods for long-term coastal monitoring and provides a reproducible framework for large-scale assessments of coastal land cover dynamics in Europe.

title: Longitudinal Trajectory Phenotyping for Chronic Kidney Disease Progression: A Machine Learning Approach Across Chinese and Asian Community-Based Cohorts
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU), Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU), , Minnan Normal University and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU)

detail.title: Longitudinal Trajectory Phenotyping for Chronic Kidney Disease Progression: A Machine Learning Approach Across Chinese and Asian Community-Based Cohorts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

As a retrospective analysis of de-identified data, the ethics committee granted a waiver of informed consent.

detail.abstract:
Background: Traditional prediction models for chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression often disregard the longitudinal nature of renal function decline, potentially missing critical prognostic information embedded in trajectory patterns. 

Methods: We employed latent class mixed modeling to identify distinct estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) trajectory phenotypes using data from three cohorts comprising 7,845 participants from China (CHARLS, Guangzhou Nursing Home) and Asia (LASI). External validation was conducted using a leave-one-cohort-out cross-validation approach. The primary outcome was CKD progression, defined as a sustained 25% eGFR decline or progression to eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m². 

Results: Four distinct trajectory phenotypes were identified with progressively worsening outcomes. Compared to Phenotype I (stable), adjusted hazard ratios for CKD progression were 2.05 (95% CI, 1.62-2.59) for Phenotype II, 3.12 (95% CI, 2.45-3.97) for Phenotype III, and 4.88 (95% CI, 3.84-6.20) for Phenotype IV. The trajectory-based model demonstrated superior discrimination compared to conventional models (5-year AUC: 0.84 vs 0.76, P < 0.001), with a net reclassification improvement of 24.1% (95% CI, 17.2-31.0%). Performance remained robust across different cohorts and age subgroups. 

Conclusions: Machine learning-derived CKD trajectory phenotypes provide a novel, clinically actionable approach to risk stratification that significantly improves prediction of disease progression. These findings support implementation of trajectory-based assessment in routine clinical practice.

title: Neoadjuvant versus Adjuvant PD-1 Blockade Integrated with Chemoradiotherapy for Locoregionally Advanced Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: A Real-World Comparative Study

detail.abstract:
​Background: The optimal sequencing of PD-1 blockade with chemoradiotherapy for locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma (LA-NPC) remains uncertain. We compared neoadjuvant immunotherapy (neo-IT) and adjuvant immunotherapy (adj-IT) regarding survival, safety, and cost-effectiveness.

Methods: This retrospective study included 492 patients with newly diagnosed LA-NPC treated between 2019 and 2023, including 285 who received neo-IT and 207 who received adj-IT. The median follow-up was 46.77 months (interquartile range [IQR], 38.80–58.87 months). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) were used to balance baseline characteristics. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS); secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), locoregional recurrence-free survival (LRRFS), distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS), safety, and cost-effectiveness.

Findings: After adjustment, neo-IT and adj-IT achieved comparable PFS, OS, and DMFS. However, neo-IT was consistently associated with improved LRRFS across IPTW-adjusted (HR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.25–0.95; P = .04), PSM-adjusted (HR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.21–0.91; P = .023), and multivariable analyses (unadjustment: P = .019; PSM: P = .024). Grade 3–4 adverse events were comparable (35.8% vs. 40.2%; P = .446), whereas neo-IT showed a lower Time Toxicity Score (1.25 vs. 2.80; P < .001). Neo-IT was also the dominant economic strategy, with lower mean total costs ($26,395.92 vs. $33,634.45) and a 100% probability of cost-effectiveness.

Interpretation: In this real-world cohort, neo-IT was associated with improved locoregional disease control, lower treatment burden, and superior cost-effectiveness while maintaining comparable long-term survival. These findings support prospective randomized studies to define the optimal immunotherapy sequence in LA-NPC.

title: Geographical Inequalities and Factors Associated with Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care Readiness in Ethiopia: A National Bayesian Spatial Analysis
affiliations: Wachemo University

detail.title: Geographical Inequalities and Factors Associated with Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care Readiness in Ethiopia: A National Bayesian Spatial Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no specific funding for this work.

detail.abstract:
Background: Maternal and neonatal survival depends not only on access to health facilities but also on the capacity of those facilities to provide timely, high-quality emergency obstetric and newborn care (EmONC). Despite substantial investments in maternal and newborn health and expansion of emergency obstetric services in Ethiopia, persistent gaps in facility readiness continue to limit the delivery of life-saving care. Previous national studies have largely focused on service availability or individual readiness components, with limited assessment of multidimensional emergency readiness and its geographical variation. We developed a Comprehensive Emergency Readiness Index (CERI) and assessed its national distribution, geographical variation, inequality, and facility-level factors associated with emergency obstetric and newborn care readiness using nationally representative health facility data from Ethiopia.

Methods: We conducted a nationally representative cross-sectional study using data from 776 health facilities included in the 2021 Ethiopia Service Provision Assessment. A latent Comprehensive Emergency Readiness Index (CERI) was constructed from essential emergency obstetric and newborn care medicines, equipment, and clinical guidelines using structural equation modelling. National estimates accounted for facility sampling weights. Geographic variation was examined using spatial autocorrelation analyses, and Bayesian hierarchical spatial regression models based on the stochastic partial differential equation approach with integrated nested Laplace approximation were fitted to evaluate associations between facility characteristics and emergency readiness. Model performance was compared using the deviance information criterion, widely applicable information criterion, conditional predictive ordinates, and predictive accuracy measures.

Results: The nationally weighted mean CERI was 57.4 (SE 2.6), compared with an unweighted mean of 70.6 (SD 36.0). CERI varied substantially across regions, ranging from 27.8 (95% CI 15.9–39.6) in Addis Ababa to 62.5 (50.9–74.1) in Amhara, with moderate national inequality (Gini coefficient 0.374; coefficient of variation 0.510). General hospitals demonstrated the highest readiness (89.1, 95% CI 86.0–92.2), whereas medium clinics had the lowest (5.6, 95% CI 1.3–9.9). Government-managed facilities had higher readiness (78.5, 95% CI 75.0–82.0) than private-for-profit facilities (10.5, 95% CI 5.2–15.9). The Bayesian hierarchical spatial model incorporating both regional and spatial random effects provided the best overall model fit (DIC 2516.49). After accounting for spatial dependence and regional heterogeneity, greater provider availability (posterior mean 4.64, 95% CrI 1.02–8.27) and oxytocin availability (posterior mean 9.96, 95% CrI 7.52–12.40) were positively associated with CERI, whereas medium clinics had substantially lower CERI than the reference facility category (posterior mean −55.37, 95% CrI −70.09 to −40.61). Residual spatial autocorrelation was no longer evident after model adjustment (Moran's I −0.013; P=0.770).

Conclusion: Emergency obstetric and newborn care readiness remains unevenly distributed across Ethiopian health facilities, with substantial geographical and facility-level variation and moderate national inequality. title: Climate-Sensitive Energy Poverty during the European Energy Crisis: Heating-Price Shocks, Pre-Crisis Trajectories and Regional Heating Demand
affiliations: Cracow University of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Climate-Sensitive Energy Poverty during the European Energy Crisis: Heating-Price Shocks, Pre-Crisis Trajectories and Regional Heating Demand
detail.abstract: This paper examines why the European energy crisis produced different energy-poverty outcomes across countries and regions. We argue that the social consequences of heating-price shocks depend on two factors: pre-existing vulnerability and climate-related heating needs. Using an annual panel of 24 European countries over 2007–2024 and complementary NUTS-2 regional data, we combine country-specific pre-crisis energy-poverty trends, heating-energy price shocks, and heating degree days.The results show that energy poverty rose above the path implied by pre-crisis trends during 2021–2024. These deviations were larger in countries with less favourable pre-crisis trajectories. Heating-energy price shocks were also more strongly associated with energy poverty in countries with higher structural heating demand. This relationship is weaker when prices are measured using a broad energy-price index rather than a heating-specific index. At the regional level, colder-than-usual NUTS-2 regions tended to report higher energy poverty within the same country and year.The findings show that energy-price shocks do not translate uniformly into household hardship. Their effects depend on inherited vulnerability and the heating needs under which households experience them. Energy-poverty monitoring and crisis preparedness should therefore account for pre-crisis trajectories, heating-specific prices, and regional differences in heating demand.

title: Mixed-Frequency Forecasting of Monthly Electricity Demand: A Regime-Aware Framework​
affiliations: Tianjin University, College of Management and Economics and China Center for Social Computing and Analytics and Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS)

detail.title: Mixed-Frequency Forecasting of Monthly Electricity Demand: A Regime-Aware Framework​
detail.abstract: Abstract ：Accurate monthly electricity demand forecasting is challenged by the changing of economic prosperity, production behaviors and weather conditions. Multi-benchmark tests revealed that forecasting failures cluster synchronously across models, occurring during three exogenous states: moving holiday shifts, acute climate anomalies, and cross-industry transmission under extreme tail conditions. To address this, utilizing high-dimensional mixed-frequency data from a province in China, we propose REDS (Regime-aware Elastic Dynamic Scheme), a framework integrating variable selection, non-linear state extraction, and multi-scale inter-industry network learning to dynamically model regime shifts and cross-sectoral transmission. Empirical results show that REDS could not only improve overall forecasting accuracy but also suppresses the clustered propagation of forecasting failures during extreme regimes. This study offers a mechanism-driven framework for managing regional energy uncertainties and enhancing grid resilience.

title: Sovereign AI without Models: Weaponized Interdependence at the Cognitive Layer
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Sovereign AI without Models: Weaponized Interdependence at the Cognitive Layer
detail.abstract: States that host none of the frontier artificial intelligence laboratories increasingly frame their predicament as a loss of sovereignty and prescribe ownership-of models, compute, and data-as its remedy. The article argues that this framing misconstrues both the problem and the available strategies. Extending Farrell and Newman's theory of weaponized interdependence, it identifies a new hub type: the capability-gradient hub, whose centrality derives from a compounding technological lead rather than network topology, and whose panopticon observes intentions rather than transactions. The United States' Genesis Mission is read as hub formation, binding frontier cognition to the American scientific estate; the June 2026 suspension of two frontier models-cognition halted while compute ran on-demonstrates that the cognitive layer is separately weaponizable. Scope conditions are specified against the open-weight diffusion objection. Japan, weakest at the cognitive layer yet holding lower-stratum chokepoints, exemplifies the recommended strategy: managed interdependence with named terms.

title: The Enduring Value Of Holding Ourselves To Our Enduring Values: A Reflection Honoring The OECD’s Guidelines For Multinational Enterprises On Responsible Business Conduct
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School

detail.title: The Enduring Value Of Holding Ourselves To Our Enduring Values: A Reflection Honoring The OECD’s Guidelines For Multinational Enterprises On Responsible Business Conduct
detail.abstract: This lecture was given at the 50th Anniversary OECD Global Forum on Responsible Business Conduct.  In keeping with the occasion, the lecture underscores the importance of remembering our long-held principles at a time when they are under threat.  Since their adoption in 1976, the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct have articulated — with long-standing, bipartisan support by the United States — the principles of responsible business conduct that best facilitate sustainable economic development and support democracy.  The Guidelines encourage multinational enterprises to seek profit by selling safe, useful products and services while respecting the legitimate expectations of all affected by their conduct, including workers (direct and in their supply chain), consumers, communities of operation, and the environment we all depend upon.  The Guidelines encourage competition on the basis of quality and innovation, in a marketplace governed by the rule of law, and discourage corruption and kleptocracy that undermines economic progress and democracy.  Importantly, the Guidelines require corporations to recognize their duty to better the lives of the people most indispensable to corporate success — their workers — by paying living wages, giving them safe and dignified working conditions, and listening to their voices.  It may seem hypocritical to commemorate the Guidelines when so many corporations and governments seem to be turning away from these animating principles.  But there is something worse than hypocrisy; that is losing sight of the principles that allow the many to hold the powerful accountable for the duties they owe to the many.  The Guidelines thus stand as a valuable expression of the widely shared, durable values of the most democratic and market-oriented societies on Earth and valuable benchmarks against which to measure the conduct of not just multinational enterprises, but government leaders.  This lecture thus urges OECD governments and the global business community to try to live up to the Guidelines and advances several ideas that the OECD could embrace to make progress toward that goal during this dangerous and uncertain time.

title: Knowledge Management Support Policies and Practices for Policymaking in the Islamic Consultative Assembly
affiliations: Imam Hossein University, Imam Hossein University and Imam Hossein University

detail.title: Knowledge Management Support Policies and Practices for Policymaking in the Islamic Consultative Assembly
detail.abstract: In parliamentary settings, the quality of policymaking depends on the extent to which accumulated knowledge, evidence, and experience are accessible and effectively utilized. Despite the importance of this issue, there is no comprehensive understanding of the knowledge management support policies and practices employed in the policymaking process of the Islamic Consultative Assembly of Iran. Accordingly, the present study aimed to identify the policies and practices through which knowledge management supports policymaking in the Islamic Consultative Assembly of Iran. This applied study adopted a qualitative approach and was conducted using Glaserian grounded theory. Data were collected through 27 semi-structured interviews with current and former members of parliament, experts from the Islamic Parliament Research Center, parliamentary committee experts, parliamentary staff, and university faculty members. The data were analyzed through constant comparison, open coding, and theoretical coding. The findings indicated that knowledge management support for policymaking requires the establishment of policies and practices in the areas of knowledge governance, policy memory, enhancement of knowledge trustworthiness, knowledge translation and packaging, expert networking, integration of knowledge resources, and institutional learning. The results suggest that the principal challenge facing the parliament is not a shortage of information, but rather the absence of institutional mechanisms for transforming fragmented knowledge into knowledge that can be used in decision-making.

title: Regime Failure and Workaround Formation: A Theory of Economic Transition

detail.title: Regime Failure and Workaround Formation: A Theory of Economic Transition
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of economic transition in which regimes persist while they remain the least-maintenance viable architecture under resource constraints. A regime is defined not as a date range, ideology, or policy label, but as a stabilising architecture that absorbs systemic stress at tolerable maintenance cost. The central mechanism is stabiliser-transmitter reversal: the anchor that once reduced volatility eventually becomes the channel through which stress is transmitted. Agents exposed to that transmission adopt costly workarounds. If adoption generates network benefits and raises systemic capacity, a workaround can become a viable architecture before the incumbent anchor fully collapses. Transition occurs when that workaround becomes the least-maintenance viable architecture available to the system manager. The model generates four main results: inefficient regime persistence, endogenous transition through workaround scaling, under-adoption relative to the social optimum, and a delayinformation tradeoff. Higher adoption frictions delay transition, but observed adoption under high friction is more informative about the domain of the future regime because costly adoption screens low-quality domains. The paper also defines a breakdown region in which no architecture is viable under the prevailing resource envelope, distinguishes transition from breakdown, and states the comparative statics implied by the model under explicit single-crossing and survivallikelihood-ratio conditions. A short application to technology-regime precursors illustrates the model but is explicitly separated from empirical proof.

title: Protection Against Air Pollution in International and EU Environmental Law
affiliations: NATIONAL KAPODISTRIAN UNIVERSITY OF ATHENS

detail.title: Protection Against Air Pollution in International and EU Environmental Law
detail.abstract: The study examines the legal framework for addressing air pollution at both international and EU levels. It explores major multilateral environmental agreements, such as the Geneva Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution and the Montreal Protocol, alongside the EU Directive 2008/50/EC on air quality. The analysis focuses on principles of prevention and restoration, while assessing the relationship between air pollution law and climate change law. The study highlights legislative contributions to reducing pollutant emissions, case law on air quality management, and progress toward cleaner air. Recommendations include enhancing cooperation and promoting innovative measures.

title: Cross-National Diversity and Environmental Sustainability: Global Evidence and Organizational Mechanisms for Achieving the SDGs
affiliations: Singapore Management University, Chulalongkorn University and

detail.title: Cross-National Diversity and Environmental Sustainability: Global Evidence and Organizational Mechanisms for Achieving the SDGs
detail.abstract: This study investigates how cross-national diversity within top management teams (TMTs) influences corporate environmental sustainability. Drawing on a large and globally representative panel dataset of 3,798 publicly listed firms across 81 countries over an 18-year period, we employ a multi-method empirical strategy that integrates fixed effects panel regressions, a Difference-inDifferences (DiD) design, and an Instrumental Variables (IV) approach to address endogeneity and strengthen causal inference. We find that greater TMT cross-national diversity is significantly associated with improved environmental performance, as evidenced by lower carbon emissions and reduced carbon intensity. Our analysis further demonstrates two key organizational mechanisms that contribute to this relationship: (1) increased adoption of sustainable operations and responsible supply chain practices, and (2) stronger institutionalization of environmental priorities via sustainability-oriented governance structures. These findings underscore the strategic importance of leadership diversity in advancing environmental responsiveness and offer insights for firms and policymakers committed to achieving SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions).

title: The Rise of Green Regions: Do Leaders Matter?
affiliations: ,  and Syracuse University

detail.title: The Rise of Green Regions: Do Leaders Matter?
detail.abstract: The paper studies the emergence of environmental policies and green places, where regional governments are strategic actors in the green transition. We build a tractable quantitative spatial general equilibrium model in which regions with heterogeneous sizes, income, and environmental awareness compete to attract users of sustainable transport modes through environmental subsidies. We show that environmental awareness interacts with regional size to generate asymmetric policy adoption. Early adopters reshape the diffusion process: regions with large populations or high awareness emerge as green leaders that stimulate subsequent adoption through interregional competition. Once fully green, however, these leaders slow the transition of follower regions. An empirical application to French regions shows that completing the green transition requires a large increase in environmental expenditure, from negligible observed levels to about 13% of existing local tax revenues. It also reveals asymmetric leadership spillovers: early entrants not only accelerate adoption but also raise environmental policy in other regions, while early green transitions mainly delay convergence with limited effects on policy intensity.

title: The Moderating Role of Financial Development in the Human Capital-Growth Nexus: Evidence from Middle Income Countries
affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law

detail.title: The Moderating Role of Financial Development in the Human Capital-Growth Nexus: Evidence from Middle Income Countries
detail.abstract: This study investigates the moderating role of financial development in the relationship between human capital and economic growth in middle-income countries. Using panel data from the World Development Indicators (WDI), the study employs Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Fixed Effects (FE), Random Effects (RE), Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), and MEDSEM analysis. Human capital is measured through a PCA-based Human Capital Index (HCI) and the World Bank Human Capital Development Index (HCD), while financial development is proxied by domestic credit to the private sector. The findings reveal that both human capital and financial development positively and significantly influence economic growth. The interaction term between human capital and financial development is also positive and significant, indicating that financial development strengthens the growth-enhancing effect of human capital. Furthermore, mediation analysis shows that financial development partially transmits the impact of human capital on economic growth. The study concludes that human capital and financial development are complementary drivers of economic growth and recommends simultaneous investment in education and financial sector development to achieve sustainable economic growth in middleincome countries.

title: Keeping the House in the Family: Non-Market Transfers and the Supply of American Homes
affiliations: University of Cincinnati

detail.title: Keeping the House in the Family: Non-Market Transfers and the Supply of American Homes
detail.abstract: A large share of American homes change hands without a market. Using 144 million deed records covering the universe of recorded residential transfers from 2007 to 2023, this paper provides the first national deeds-based accounting of intra-family housing transfers. After stripping out trust retitling and same-person co-owner changes, families moved nearly 20 million homes between relatives over this period -- one family transfer for every 3.6 market sales -- almost always at a recorded price of zero. These transfers are not a staging step toward sale: three in five family transferred homes have not sold on the open market a decade later. A simple model shows that when heirs inherit a below-market property-tax assessment along with the house, as permitted by California's Propositions 13, 58, and 193, families keep homes that the market values more. California's Proposition 19, which abruptly ended assessment inheritance for non-occupant heirs in February 2021, provides a natural experiment to examine the effect of this tax wedge on family transfers. Family transfers surged 31% above counterfactual in the four months before the effective date and then fell to a new, persistently lower level: a donor-weighted synthetic control reveals a 2022-2023 decline of 33%, which decreases to 26% after adjusting for the elderly population. Net of California's own market-sale slump, the missing flow is roughly 58,000 deeds per year. The homes that exited the family channel have not yet surfaced as estate sales, indicating deferred successions rather than immediate listings. Our results suggest that family transfers are not outside the housing market but are one of its allocation mechanisms and property-tax rules can shift scarce homes from price-based matching to lineage-based retention.

title: Remittance Dependency and Agricultural Stagnation in Nepal: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of 75 Districts

detail.title: Remittance Dependency and Agricultural Stagnation in Nepal: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of 75 Districts
detail.abstract: Nepal receives remittances equivalent to over 25% of GDP, yet agricultural productivity has stagnated across much of the country. This study examines whether migration-intensive districts are associated with below-average agricultural yields, using district-level cross-sectional data linking CBS Nepal 2021 Census migration indicators with MoALD 2022/23 cereal yield data across all 75 districts. We construct two composite indicesthe Remittance Dependency Index (RDI) and Remittance Vulnerability Index (RVI)using Principal Component Analysis on CBS microdata. Cross-sectional OLS regression finds RDI positively associated (β=0.019, p=0.004) and RVI negatively associated (β=-0.025, p=0.010) with cereal yield, controlling for literacy (R²=0.204). Variance Inflation Factor analysis reveals severe multicollinearity for poverty rate (VIF=894), which is excluded from the preferred specification. Moran's I on OLS residuals is 0.511 (p=0.001), confirming significant spatial dependence. Spatial lag (ρ=0.823, p<0.001, AIC=123.2) and spatial error (λ=0.849, p<0.001, AIC=122.1) models, estimated on the complete 75-district sample, confirm that geographic proximity dominates yield outcomes. After spatial correction, RDI remains significant (SLM: p=0.010; SEM: p=0.010) while RVI attenuates to insignificance (SLM: p=0.177; SEM: p=0.904), indicating that the structural vulnerability signal is largely geographic in origin. A four-quadrant paradox taxonomy classifies 11 core Paradox Zone districts with robustness confirmed across threshold specifications and border district exclusion. All findings are associations; panel data with within-district variation over time would be required for causal identification.

title: Fundamentals in Management Causal Discussions
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU) - Research School of Finance, Actuarial Studies and Applied Statistics

detail.title: Fundamentals in Management Causal Discussions
detail.abstract: We propose a novel framework of extracting fundamental characteristics from textual data based on causal sentence structures. Preserving the causal relationship by separately extracting topics from cause and effect parts of sentences result in improved information processing compared to simple topic analyses. Peer firms identified from this causality-based topic analysis show strong return comovement both at the monthly level and around earnings announcements. Returns of smaller firms, more central firms, firms with higher market beta and idiosyncratic volatility can be predicted by their peers' returns. Fundamental news seems to travel more from bigger firms to their smaller, less transparent peers with simpler operations, and from earlier announcers to their later announcing peers. Evidence supports the efficacy of considering causal sentence structures in extracting information.

title: Relative Income Misperceptions: Cross-Country Patterns in Europe
affiliations: European Union - JRC-Ispra, European Commision,  and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna di Pisa

detail.title: Relative Income Misperceptions: Cross-Country Patterns in Europe
detail.abstract: We study voters' relative income misperceptions among over 19,000 respondents across all 27 countries of the European Union. To our knowledge, ours is the largest such study to date. We document that voter income misperceptions are widespread and share key characteristics across EU countries, with most respondents misperceiving their relative income by more than one decile. The pattern reflects a "middle class bias," with more (less) affluent respondents more often displaying a negative (positive) bias. Further, average misperceptions are negative in all EU countries. At the country level, average misperceptions decrease with GDP per capita. At the individual level, older, more educated and urban residents exhibit less bias. We further implement a randomized information treatment informing respondents of their household's actual relative income. While our results indicate that misperceptions exist and exhibit similar patterns and correlations across the EU, the treatment effects are more dispersed. In some countries, people who learn they are wealthier than previously thought decrease their demand for redistribution, while in others they do not change or want more redistribution.

title: Inflation and Corporate Credit Risk: Global Evidence
affiliations: The University of Sydney - Discipline of Finance, University of Sydney Business School and

detail.title: Inflation and Corporate Credit Risk: Global Evidence

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, forthcoming

detail.abstract: We provide novel international evidence that inflation is positively associated with corporate credit risk on average. A one-standard-deviation increase in inflation is associated with a 21 basis-point increase in next-year CDS spreads. Importantly, this relationship is convex: it is negative or weak at low inflation levels, but is much more positive in high-inflation environments. The positive relation between inflation and credit risk is stronger for firms with greater refinancing vulnerability and more rigid operating cash flows, and in countries with more inflation-responsive monetary regimes and weaker institutional environments. Our findings are consistent with opposing roles for debt rigidity and operating rigidity.

title:
Why Automation Stalls:
A Dual-Layer Theory of AI Deployment Constraints
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
Why Automation Stalls:
A Dual-Layer Theory of AI Deployment Constraints

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares the following: - No financial relationships with AI companies, regulatory bodies, or organizations whose interests could be affected by this research - No consulting arrangements or advisory board positions that would create conflicts of interest - Research conducted independently without external funding pressures

detail.abstract: Why does AI automation systematically fall short of its technically feasible potential? This paper develops a dual-layer theory of AI deployment constraints to explain the deployment gap — the persistent discrepancy between what is technically achievable and what is actually deployed at production scale. Drawing on Massenkoff and McCrory's (2026) finding that AI's observed task coverage remains a fraction of its theoretical feasibility, and McKinsey's (2025) documentation that only 6% of AI-adopting organizations qualify as high performers with meaningful EBIT impact, we argue that this gap reflects two structurally distinct layers of constraint. At the market layer, we formalize two legal-political distortions absent from standard factor-cost comparisons: the Zero Rights Defense Discount (ZRDD), which depresses effective labor cost below the nominal wage through rightsenforcement failures; and the Accountability Liability Premium (ALP), which inflates effective AI deployment cost above the nominal price through the near-total absence of AI legal personhood. Together, these produce a dual wedge rendering nominally viable substitution economically irrational under current institutional configurations. G At the organizational layer, we develop Deployment Boundary Theory (DBT), extending Cohen and Levinthal's (1990) absorptive capacity framework with three non-substitutable constraints — accountability (R), coordination (C), and dynamic maintenance (D). Critically, the R constraint is exogenously determined by legal institutions rather than internal organizational learning, and may rise rather than fall as deployment scales. We formally define the deployment gap  as the set of task–organization pairs that are nominally substitution-advantaged but institutionally blocked, and derive three testable predictions: the Legal Channel Hypothesis, the Competitive Externality Hypothesis, and the Non-Monotonic Labor Protection Hypothesis. Empirical identification strategies exploiting the phased implementation of the EU AI Act (2026–2028) are proposed for each.

title: Export Taxes and Cross-Sector Spillovers

detail.title: Export Taxes and Cross-Sector Spillovers
detail.abstract:
This paper studies optimal export taxation in a multi-sector open economy when the government faces constraints on the set of feasible policy instruments. While existing models typically assume that export taxes can be imposed in all sectors, this paper considers a constrained environment in which the government can tax exports in only one sector.

In this setting, the optimal export tax generally deviates from the standard inverse foreign import demand elasticity benchmark. The reason is that export taxation in a single sector induces labor reallocation toward untaxed sectors, generating general-equilibrium spillovers in wages and export prices across sectors. As a result, the government faces a trade-off between the direct terms-of-trade gain from the higher export price in the taxed sector and indirect terms-of-trade effects due to export price changes in other sectors.

The paper characterizes the constrained-optimal export tax in closed form and shows that it depends not only on the foreign import demand elasticity, but also on the strength of cross-sector spillovers induced by labor mobility.

title: U.S. Treasury Investors Are Long in AI
affiliations: London Business School, Stanford Graduate School of Business and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: U.S. Treasury Investors Are Long in AI
detail.abstract: The U.S. federal government's tax revenue is highly sensitive to long-run productivity growth but its mandatory spending commitments are not. As a result, U.S. Treasury investors have acquired a long position in AI. Using the CBO's 30-year budget projections, elasticities, and interest rate pass-through estimates, we find that 0.1 pps. of extra productivity growth raises the fundamental value of U.S. Treasurys by $1.19 trillion (3.7% of the market value), implying a 63 basis point decline in nominal Treasury yields. A larger 0.5 pps. acceleration raises the fundamental value by $5.7 trillion (17.8% of the market value).

title: Stereotypes in the Machine: Gender and Racial Bias in LLM-Generated Financial Advice
affiliations: , Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business, University of Macau and Lingnan University

detail.title: Stereotypes in the Machine: Gender and Racial Bias in LLM-Generated Financial Advice
detail.abstract: We conduct a large-scale controlled experiment of large language models (LLMs) acting as financial advisors. We find that LLMs systematically recommend lower equity allocations to female and Asian clients compared to otherwise identical White males. This bias persists and even intensifies for financially sophisticated clients, and the recommended portfolios are less efficientrejecting rational statistical discrimination in favor of stereotyping. While higher model intelligence mitigates these biases, model scale, standard safety alignment, and explicit debiasing prompts prove ineffective. Our results suggest that without advanced reasoning capabilities, AI advisors risk institutionalizing wealth disparities by projecting demographic stereotypes onto investment decisions.

title: The Market Disciplinary Effect of Asset Write-off: Theory and Empirical Evidence from Goodwill Impairment
affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology (shenzhen), National University of Singapore (NUS) - Sustainable & Green Finance Institute (SGFIN) and

detail.title: The Market Disciplinary Effect of Asset Write-off: Theory and Empirical Evidence from Goodwill Impairment
detail.abstract: We study the effect of subsequent write-off tests on myopic managers' investment decisions. Write-off tests discipline overinvestment when the likelihood of adverse events is high, but can otherwise cause more severe underinvestment. Hence, tightening impairment stringency improves firm value when the likelihood of adverse events is high, but destroys firm value when that likelihood is low. With intermediate levels of likelihood, firm value is hump-shaped in impairment stringency. To test the theory, we exploit an increase in goodwill impairment stringency following goodwill-related restatements by peer firms audited by the same auditor office, and we adopt a stacked difference-indifferences design to control for any generic effects of peer restatements. Firms facing more stringent goodwill impairment reduce M&As relative to other types of investment, as well as in absolute amounts. The valuation of treated firms improves only during periods of high recession expectations or when facing high distress risk.

keywords: Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS); Nagoya Protocol; Genetic Resources; Equitable Benefit-Sharing; Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs); Traditional Knowledge; Science Equity; Biodiversity Governance; Digital Sequence Information (DSI); Bioprospecting

detail.abstract: Global governance of digital sequence information (DSI) has concentrated almost exclusively on publicly accessible repositories, leaving a commercially significant share of genetic data generated within private, proprietary biodiscovery platforms largely outside multilateral benefit-sharing frameworks. Drawing on over two decades of practitioner experience in Nagoya Protocol implementation, the DSI Multilateral Mechanism, and bilateral Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) negotiations across Africa, this commentary argues that bilateral ABS agreements remain one of the key mechanisms providing the legal specificity and enforceability needed to govern biodiversity genetic resources (GR) and DSI, and to maintain a direct economic relationship between resource users and providers. Using case evidence from Basecamp Research's operational ABS partnerships across more than 30 countries, together with national implementation experience in Malawi and Cameroon, we show that bilateral frameworks generate accountability and sustained investment that multilateral, voluntary mechanisms structurally lack. We address the principal counterargument to this position that benefit-sharing obligations impede emergency research and show that post-pandemic reforms reinforce rather than undermine the case for benefit-sharing. We further examine the governance challenge posed by AI-driven biodiscovery, where provenance-linked training data offers a model for extending ABS compliance into algorithmic and AI-derived value chains. We conclude that bilateral and multilateral mechanisms are complementary rather than competing architectures, and that operationalising Article 10 of the Nagoya Protocol, alongside mandatory DSI provenance tracking, offers a practical path to closing the governance gap under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. We position Africa not as a passive subject of DSI governance debates but as an active architect of the equitable frameworks needed for a sustainable global bioeconomy. Executive Summary Bilateral Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) agreements under the Nagoya Protocol remain a vital mechanism for the fair and equitable use of genetic resources and associated digital sequence information (DSI), particularly in commercial research contexts and for privately held DSI databases. While multilateral mechanisms are being proposed to manage publicly accessible DSI, they remove the direct economic relationship between User and Provider and therefore cannot fully substitute for the flexibility and contextual specificity offered by well-designed bilateral arrangements. Implementing equitable ABS requires building sovereign capability, not merely enacting legal frameworks (Dutfield, 2011); capacity-building through technology transfer, intellectual property, and academic collaboration is the foundational engine of a sustainable bioeconomy, not a charitable add-on (Nnadozie et al., 2017). Drawing on over two decades of practitioner experience including the facilitation of bilateral arrangements and service within the Nagoya Protocol and the Global Biodiversity Framework, this paper presents evidence from Basecamp Research's private, public, and community commercial research collaborations across Africa and beyond. Real-world examples from East, Central, and Southern Africa demonstrate that tailored bilateral agreements provide the most robust protection for local communities, protected areas, and academic institutions, ensuring that benefit-sharing obligations remain legally enforceable throughout the commercial research value chain. Africa is not merely a provider of genetic resources; it is an active architect of equitable biodiversity governance, developing practical ABS solutions that the global policy community urgently needs to learn from.

title: Longer stays, not more calls: rainfall-linked at-berth CO₂ at a Brazilian port
affiliations: Federal University of Maranhão, Federal University of Maranhão, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Longer stays, not more calls: rainfall-linked at-berth CO₂ at a Brazilian port
detail.abstract: This study estimates auxiliary-engine CO₂ emissions during hotelling at Porto do Itaqui, Brazil, using 6,029 vessel calls from 2020 to 2025, and evaluates Onshore Power Supply (OPS). A simplified activity-based inventory was combined with logarithmic mean Divisia index decomposition and precipitation regressions. Emissions increased from 13.4 kt to 17.6 kt (+31.4%; +11.3% from the post-pandemic 2021 baseline). Longer berth times explained 44.6% of the increase, vessel power 25.1%, and additional calls 20.0%. Liquid bulk accounted for 68.6% of emissions, and Berths 104, 106, and 108 concentrated approximately 63%. A 5 mm/day rainfall increase was associated with 3.4–5.2% longer dry-bulk stays; the evidence is associative, and OPS could avoid an estimated 134–199 t CO₂ per year linked to these delays. Under full uptake, OPS could reduce auxiliary-engine CO₂ by 84.2% (73.9–91.3% across grid factors), a technical ceiling that excludes auxiliary boilers and supports phased berth electrification.

title: Healthcare's AI Trap

detail.title: Healthcare's AI Trap

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is affiliated with Mochi Health, a telehealth company, and holds no equity in it. This paper is a conceptual and theoretical contribution that uses no company data and does not concern any company product. The author is aware of no conflict of interest bearing on the argument.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical paper involving no human subjects, patient data, or clinical intervention.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external, grant, or institutional funding.

detail.abstract: In clinical care the routine cases do double duty: under a flat fee they are the profitable cases that cross-subsidize complex care, and they are the cases on which junior clinicians become senior ones. AI automates them first, severing both supports at once. On the financing side, an AI-native entrant that serves only the routine "cream" raises the average cost of the patients left behind above the flat fee and the pool unravels (Einav and Finkelstein, 2011; Faulhaber, 1975), before AI can treat the complex patients it abandons. We solve the skimming game from primitives: the over-skimming wedge carries a business-stealing term that mere fewness cannot remove, so efficiency is restored by vertical integration of the cream with the tail, with risk adjustment (Glazer and McGuire, 2000) as the price-side cure. On the workforce side, automating the routine cases starves the pipeline that produces specialists; because expertise takes a decade to build and the option of keeping it alive is never priced, the loss can be irreversible (Arrow and Fisher, 1974), and supervision and training compete for the same seniors, giving a tipping point between a healthy steady state and a low-capacity trap. The two externalities share the same cases but are not the same problem: integrating the cream with the tail removes the financing externality and trains enough seniors to replace a provider's own retirements, yet no market structure prices the option value of training above replacement, which spills across firms, so transfers and administered prices alone do not address both margins and a separate training instrument is needed. What is specific to medicine is that the cases AI takes first are at once the money that funds hard care and the making of the people who provide it.

title: Executivism and the Parallel State

detail.title: Executivism and the Parallel State
detail.abstract: Rebuilding democratic accountability after Trump requires more than reversing executive orders or rehiring dismissed officials. The second Trump administration exploited two long-running developments: the concentration of policy authority in the presidency and the migration of public functions to the intermediary class. I call the first executivism and the second the parallel state. Together they supply concentrated command and a privately operated implementation network that a personalist president can reward, redirect, or exclude. By sorting contracts, grants, data access, and public interfaces toward compliant actors, the presidency can embed a coalition in relationships costly for successors to unwind. Digital systems deepen this dependence when government cannot move, understand, or reproduce systems it formally owns. I assess such dependence through recoverability and legibility. I conclude with reforms to the civil service, procurement, Congress, judicial doctrine, and public technical capacity, sequenced to preserve service delivery while rebuilding public capacity.

title: Housing Regulation and Neighborhood Sorting across the United States

detail.title: Housing Regulation and Neighborhood Sorting across the United States
detail.abstract: In this paper, I consider the effect of minimum lot size regulation on welfare and urban structure. I construct a general equilibrium model in which households of heterogeneous incomes choose cities and neighborhoods, value affluent neighbors, and are burdened differently by regulation. The model explains two salient facts about residential income sorting: household incomes decline with residential density within cities, and this gradient is steeper in more productive cities. I provide causal evidence in support. A counterfactual deregulation exercise shows significant and progressive welfare gains for households (exceeding $2000 per household per year) that offset the losses to landowners. The exercise also reveals two surprising results. First, any productivity gains that occur from the expansion of productive cities are largely nullified by the out-migration of affluent households who prefer regulated neighborhoods. Second, deregulation does not exacerbate the neighborhood choice externality arising from the demand for affluent neighbors. These results suggest that the most important consequence of deregulating housing markets is an increase in housing affordability. Other counterfactual exercises underscore the lack of incentives for cities to unilaterally deregulate and show a significant opportunity for improved spatial targeting.

title: The Fiscal Cost of Heat Exposure: Evidence from Medicaid Spending
affiliations: University of Central Oklahoma - Department of Economics and

detail.title: The Fiscal Cost of Heat Exposure: Evidence from Medicaid Spending
detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of short-run heat exposure on Medicaid spending. We link monthly Medicaid payments, patients, and claim lines across U.S. ZIP Codes from 2018 through 2024 to daily maximum temperatures. Identification comes from within-ZIP Code variation across months of the same season and year in the number of hot days, relative to each ZIP Code's usual calendarmonth pattern. Population-weighted fixed-effects estimates show that an additional day above 80°F increases monthly Medicaid payments by 0.25 percent, with effects reaching about 1.9 percent for days above 100°F. The increase operates primarily at the extensive margin through more patients and claims. Effects are 30 to 60 percent larger in poorer ZIP Codes and in areas with larger Black, young-child, and older-adult populations. Illustrative projections based on scenarios of continued global warming imply $2.1 billion to $2.7 billion in additional annual Medicaid spending by mid-century.

title: When Rights Become Access: Abortion Reform and Missing Girls in Nepal
affiliations: Binghamton University and Binghamton University

detail.title: When Rights Become Access: Abortion Reform and Missing Girls in Nepal
detail.abstract: Reforms that expand reproductive rights change behavior only when they change effective access. We study Nepal, which legalized abortion in 2002 to reduce unsafe procedures, and ask when and where legal access affected the sex composition of births in a society with son preference. We combine quasirandom variation in firstborn sex with the staged rollout of abortion services and predetermined connectivity to city services in a triple-difference design. The rollout separates two margins. During the initial first-trimester rollout, later-birth hazards declined where services were reachable, but the male- and female-birth responses were not statistically distinguishable, and the sex composition of births did not change. Once access expanded to include second-trimester services, medication abortion, and midlevel providers, the annual probability of a female birth fell while male births did not decline. Nationally, the probability of a female birth fell by 0.49 percentage points, and the female share of later births in firstborn-girl families fell by 2.83 percentage points. The responses were concentrated within two hours of a city. Within this radius, the female birth probability and the female share declined by 1.30 and 6.52 percentage points, respectively. Back-of-the-envelope calculation maps the national composition estimate to an annual flow equivalent of about 11,900 missing girls at birth, or 1.91 percent of all births.

title: Factors Influencing the Utilization of Malaria Prevention and Case Management Services among Vulnerable Populations in Four Health Districts of Cameroon (Mokolo, Maroua 3, Doumé and Mifi): A Mixed-Methods Study
affiliations: Impact Santé Afrique (ISA),, Impact Santé Afrique (ISA),, Government of Cameroon - Ministry of Public Health Cameroon and

detail.title: Factors Influencing the Utilization of Malaria Prevention and Case Management Services among Vulnerable Populations in Four Health Districts of Cameroon (Mokolo, Maroua 3, Doumé and Mifi): A Mixed-Methods Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors declare no financial or personal relationships with other people or organizations that could inappropriately influence this work. There are no conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was obtained from the National Ethics Committee for Human Health Research of Cameroon (CNERSH), reference N° 2024/03/1653/CE/CNERSH/SP. All participants provided written or documented oral informed consent prior to enrolment. Participation was voluntary, and participants were informed of their right to withdraw at any time without consequence.
declarations.funderStatement: Expertise France, within the "Equité Accès Palu" project.

detail.abstract:
Background: Malaria remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Cameroon, with a disproportionate burden on vulnerable populations. Despite the implementation of free interventions — long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) and intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) — service utilization remains insufficient in certain contexts.

Methods: A convergent mixed-methods study was conducted from January to June 2024 in four health districts (Mokolo, Maroua 3, Doumé, Mifi) across three regions of Cameroon. The quantitative component included 633 vulnerable individuals (pregnant/breastfeeding women, caregivers of children under five, internally displaced persons, refugees, indigenous populations, persons with disabilities) selected through stratified sampling. Data were collected using the Malaria Behaviour Survey and analyzed by multivariable logistic regression. The qualitative component combined 12 focus group discussions and 16 in-depth interviews, analyzed using thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke).

Findings: Four independent determinants were identified in multivariable analysis. Health district was the strongest predictor of IPTp knowledge: residents of Mokolo were 20 times less likely to have adequate knowledge than those in Mifi (aOR = 0·05; 95% CI: 0·008–0·30). The 35–44 age group was associated with: a more favourable attitude towards IPTp (aOR = 5·79; 95% CI: 1·30–25·74), while widowhood was unfavorably associated (aOR = 0·037; 95% CI: 0·003–0·51). Women paradoxically showed less adherence to gender-equitable values than men (aOR = 0·07; 95% CI: 0·009–0·56). Secondary education or above was associated with a less favourable attitude towards LLINs (aOR = 0·11; 95% CI: 0·02–0·68). Qualitative data revealed a three-step care-seeking pathway (self-medication, traditional medicine, delayed formal care) and four categories of barriers: financial, geographical, sociocultural, and service quality-related.

Interpretation: Utilization of malaria services is driven more by contextual and relational factors than by individual characteristics. Interventions should be territorialized, target specific social vulnerabilities (widowhood, gender) and incorporate gender-transformative approaches to improve equitable access to care.

title: Commodity Price Uncertainty and Macroeconomic Dynamics
affiliations: Institute for Advanced Studies, Institute for Advanced Studies (IHS) and Institute for Advanced Studies (IHS)

detail.title: Commodity Price Uncertainty and Macroeconomic Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper constructs and analyzes a new measure of industrial metal price uncertainty, the metal uncertainty index (MUI), following and extending the methodology of Jurado et al. (2015), which defines uncertainty as the unpredictable component of future outcomes. The index is constructed from spot and futures prices of five industrial metals-copper, aluminium, nickel, zinc, and lead-together with a broad set of macroeconomic, financial, and commodity-market variables that characterize developments in the global metal sector. We conduct a range of empirical analyses for industrial production, equity markets, metal prices, and the real effective exchange rate of the US dollar, including impulse response functions and forecasting exercises for the global economy, the United States, and the euro area. To account for potential nonlinearities, we employ a threshold vector autoregressive (TVAR) model that distinguishes between low-and high-metal-uncertainty regimes. In addition, we incorporate alternative uncertainty measures, including financial uncertainty and  geopolitical risk, to complement the role of metal-specific uncertainty. The impulse response analysis reveals that the effects of metal uncertainty shocks are strongly regime dependent. Specifically, the magnitude, persistence, and, in the case of stock markets, even the direction of responses differ across low- and high-metal-uncertainty regimes, with the effects generally being more pronounced during periods of elevated metal uncertainty. The only notable exception is the real effective exchange rate of the US dollar, whose response is stronger in the low-uncertainty regime. More broadly, the responses to shocks in MUI differ from those associated with financial uncertainty suggesting that the two indices capture distinct underlying sources of uncertainty. We further evaluate the forecasting performance of models incorporating the MUI alongside other uncertainty measures under both linear and nonlinear specifications. The results show that models including the MUI frequently outperform competing alternatives, particularly for the global economy, across a range of forecast horizons and evaluation criteria. Moreover, TVAR models often rank among the best-performing specifications, underscoring the importance of accounting for regime-dependent dynamics in forecasting macro-financial variables. Overall, the findings indicate that metal uncertainty contains valuable information, enhancing both our understanding of macro-financial transmission mechanisms and the accuracy of forecasts, particularly when nonlinearities are explicitly incorporated.

detail.title: Gangnam Style Investment: Smart Finance of Rich-Neighborhood Investors
detail.abstract: Using a unique dataset of trading accounts from a major securities company in South Korea, this paper shows individual investors from Gangnam District, the most affluent neighborhood in Seoul, effectively respond to the market shock and outperform their peers. Individual investors in Gangnam intensively buy stocks when prices plunge and strategically realize profits as markets rebound demonstrating superior market timing ability. Moreover, they tend to retain stocks bought at market lows while selling holdings of pre-shock purchases, leading to a portfolio restructuring during the recovery phase. We also find that Gangnam investors exhibit high similarity in investment capital flows and portfolio composition, implying the existence of a well-developed local information-sharing network within the community. The results remain consistent after controlling for individual investor characteristics including asset size and investment experience. Our findings suggest that investors in rich neighborhoods exhibit distinct investment behavior driven by advantages in information access and sharing.

title: The Role of Trading Network in China's Corporate Bond Market
affiliations: Guanghua School of Management, Peking University and Nankai University

detail.title: The Role of Trading Network in China's Corporate Bond Market
detail.abstract: We document how a regulatory intervention on trading networks reshaped trading behavior, liquidity, and bond pricing in China's interbank corporate bond market. Using a proprietary dataset covering all transactions of non-financial corporate bonds, we analyze the effects of an exogenous regulatory shock in April 2013 that disrupted preestablished trading relationships. Our findings show that institutions more exposed to regulated accounts experienced a sharp contraction in trading activity following the intervention. Relative to less exposed institutions, they exhibited significantly lower same-day trade offsetting, reduced inventory holdings, and declines in trading volume. Sell-side prices declined more than buy-side prices, consistent with forced liquidation under liquidity pressure. Finally, we show that institutions trading less concentrated bonds adapted more effectively by re-routing trades toward alternative counterparties.

title: Do Firms Do Good Only When Watched? Media Exposure, ESG Ratings, and Reputational Herding
affiliations: Seoul National University

detail.title: Do Firms Do Good Only When Watched? Media Exposure, ESG Ratings, and Reputational Herding
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether ESG-related media exposure affects how publicly disclosed ESG information is reflected in external ESG ratings. Using S&P 500 firms from 2011 to 2023, we combine Refinitiv ESG ratings, ESG-related news coverage, and AI-generated ESG scores from 10-K filings. We find that greater media exposure is associated with shorter observed lags in the relation between 10-K-based ESG measures and external ratings: recent disclosures matter more in high-media firms, while longer lags persist in low-media firms, especially in the environmental and social pillars. We further show that high-media firms exhibit stronger adjustment toward peer benchmarks, consistent with reputational herding. Taken together, this paper highlights media’s role in shaping the external recognition of ESG disclosures and firms’ incentives to adjust toward peer benchmarks.

title: "Jurisdictional Havens": The Geography of Indigenous Identity in Mexico
affiliations: and

detail.title: "Jurisdictional Havens": The Geography of Indigenous Identity in Mexico

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: We argue that subjects living in "jurisdictional havens"-areas where rulers face competition from other rulers due to overlapping jurisdictions-enjoy prerogatives unavailable to those outside them. We employ this mechanism to explain the geographic distribution of Indigenous identity in Mexico today. Using a grid-cell design and the location of colonial authorities between 1520 and 1820, we find that the overlapping domains of royal and religious authorities exhibit, since 1800, more Indigenous pueblos, higher rates of Indigenous language use, Indigenous last names, and communal land tenure than comparable non-haven areas. To address endogeneity, we compare within-grid localities, conduct placebo tests based on historical relocations of authorities' headquarters, and match on observables. Additional evidence from colonial-era lawsuits, office valuations, and the eventual location of subnational borders is consistent with greater inter-ruler competition in havens. Taken together, our findings show how certain institutional configurations, and not just geography, create bargaining spaces for subaltern populations to capitalize on.

title: Four Claims Tested on One Landscape: A Self-Falsification Study in Topological Data Analysis
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Four Claims Tested on One Landscape: A Self-Falsification Study in Topological Data Analysis

detail.abstract: This article takes four claims from the author's own prior work on topological degradation metrics, tests each against a control on a single real substrate, and reports that three of the four do not survive. The substrate is a fire-prone landscape in the Sierra de Ancares, northwestern Spain, for which a published 100-member random forest ignition ensemble and a static predictor stack are available, and for which ERA5-Land reanalysis supplies the meteorology from which two established fire indices are computed. The first claim, that one-dimensional persistent features are near the detection threshold on this landscape, was an artifact of a truncated download: the complete ensemble puts H1 prevalence at seventeen percent rather than three. The second claim, that zero-dimensional persistence declines monotonically along a spatial ignition gradient at a rank correlation of unity, is close to tautological, because the gradient variable is the node count rescaled and total persistence scales with node count; normalized, the relationship reverses. The third claim, that a negative Latent Yield indicates intrinsic sub-random structure, fails because the sign of that quantity inverts between two defensible null models, as companion work demonstrates on two independent citation benchmarks. The fourth claim, that the magnitude of a negative Latent Yield measures a property of the system, fails outright: a two-by-two control shows the negative reading persists when the attribute autocorrelation is destroyed, when the spatial embedding is destroyed, and when both are, establishing that the quantity reports the difference between a nearest-neighbour graph and its degree-preserving rewiring rather than anything about the landscape. What survives is a single result, and it survives precisely because it depends on none of the machinery that failed: on a network whose node set is held fixed at 389, total zero-dimensional persistence tracks dead fuel moisture across the fire season at a rank correlation of 0.964 with p equal to 0.00045, and is flat against ignition probability across one hundred ensemble members. This article is a companion to a methodological treatment of construction, null, and autocorrelation sensitivity, and supplies the empirical case that the treatment argues in the abstract.

title: Diagnostic Thresholds, Written Consent Requirements, and the Utilization of Scarce Organs
affiliations: and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - University of California, San Diego

detail.title: Diagnostic Thresholds, Written Consent Requirements, and the Utilization of Scarce Organs
detail.abstract:
This paper explores how diagnostic thresholds and a written consent requirement affect decision making between patients and transplant surgeons regarding the use of deceased donor kidneys. Combining administrative data on the universe of organ donors and transplant recipients in the United States, we show that age-based discontinuities within the Expanded Criteria Donor system (ECD), which was in place from late 2002 to late 2014, led to 4.0 and 5.4 percentage point differences in the rates at which otherwise indistinguishable kidneys were discarded. A discontinuity within the subsequent presentation of the Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) led to a 2.6 percentage point difference. We present evidence that diagnostic thresholds have nuanced effects on decision making and information acquisition; procurement biopsy rates, for example, rose substantially at the ECD system’s age-based discontinuities. We further show that written consent requirements triggered within the ECD and KDPI labeling systems substantially reduced the number of potential recipients to whom kidneys were offered prior to being discarded. This channel can explain the majority of the increased rate at which “High-KDPI” kidneys are discarded under the current system.

title: The Contingency of Persistence: Construction, Null, and Autocorrelation Sensitivity in Topological Inference on Relational Data
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Contingency of Persistence: Construction, Null, and Autocorrelation Sensitivity in Topological Inference on Relational Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a named inventor on United States provisional patent applications concerning topological methods related to those discussed in this article. The disclosure is made in the interest of transparency; the analysis rests on publicly available datasets and openly documented procedures.
