detail.abstract: A persistence diagram, and any scalar derived from it, is routinely treated as a property of the data it summarizes. That treatment is unsafe. A persistence-derived summary is not a property of a relational system alone. It is a property of a tuple: the system, the construction by which a filtered complex is built from it, the null model against which structure or excess is judged, and the spatial or graph autocorrelation of the filtration values. This article demonstrates three dependency axes on real substrates spanning spatial and non-spatial, physical and social domains. On a groundwater depletion surface, four defensible pipeline constructions move the analysis from no signal to strong signal, and on a citation graph, four filtration constructions move total zero-dimensional persistence across a factor of thirty. On a fixed citation graph, a persistence-derived reserve metric changes sign between a degree-preserving null and an Erdos-Renyi null. A within-substrate control that permutes the spatial positions of one surface while holding its value distribution fixed removes a negative reserve reading entirely, isolating autocorrelation as the driver rather than any intrinsic property of the system. This article proposes a sensitivity index that makes the contingency reportable, gives an algorithmic protocol for constructing the admissible family over which it is computed, and states plainly which of its properties are demonstrated and which are conjectural. The stability theorem for persistence diagrams bounds the effect of perturbing a filtration function. It does not bound the effect of choosing a construction, of choosing a null, or of ignoring autocorrelation. That gap is the subject of this article.

title: Does Immigration Relief Affect Labor Market Outcomes? Evidence from Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals

detail.title: Does Immigration Relief Affect Labor Market Outcomes? Evidence from Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impacts of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) on individuals’ labor market outcomes using a Regression Discontinuity Design. I estimate the Intent to Treat (ITT) impact of DACA before the legal challenge to DACA in 2017. I find that the potentially eligible DACA population earned a significantly high income when the data is considered till 2017. I further compare my ITT estimates with other studies.

title: When Not to Trade: Leakage-Aware Selective Machine Learning for Factor Rotation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: When Not to Trade: Leakage-Aware Selective Machine Learning for Factor Rotation
detail.abstract: Machine-learning trading systems are often evaluated as always-on predictors: every period, a model is trained, a signal is produced, and a portfolio is formed. This paper studies a different question: when should a machine-learning strategy refuse to trade? Financial return prediction is exposed to non-stationarity, temporal distribution shift, selection bias, transaction costs, and backtest overfitting. Under such conditions, a model's apparent validation advantage may not justify deployment. I propose a leakage-aware selective alpha deployment framework for factor and sector rotation. The framework separates model fitting, validation calibration, and out-of-sample testing through a rolling-origin protocol. At each decision date, the strategy estimates whether a candidate machine-learning signal improves over a transparent fallback benchmark on a pre-specified validation window. The signal is deployed only when the validation improvement exceeds a calibrated threshold; otherwise, the strategy abstains and falls back to a benchmark portfolio. I formalize the selective strategy as a predictable portfolio rule, derive its return and mean-variance utility decomposition, provide a validation-error deployment bound, and show how null-calibrated gates control false deployment under placebo signals. In the baseline sector-rotation experiment, selective gradient boosting improves net Sharpe from 0.55 to 0.78, reduces maximum drawdown from-39.0% to-21.4%, and cuts turnover by more than half relative to its always-trade counterpart. The paper contributes a practical protocol for reducing leakage and deployment risk in machine-learning-based quantitative strategies.

title: No-Poach Agreements
affiliations: University of Cambridge and Duke University

detail.title: No-Poach Agreements
detail.abstract:
We study no-poach cartels using a wage-posting model that puts worker poaching at the center of labor market competition. Even when just two out of ten employers in a local labor market collude, wages fall by almost 5% market-wide. The reason is that no-poach agreements suppress competition along the job ladder, with spillovers to non-colluding firms. We then compare no-poach agreements to two other forms of anti-competitive conduct in the labor market: noncompete agreements and wage fixing. No-poach agreements have by far the largest negative wage effects.

title: Immigrants' Legal Status and Firms: Evidence from the 2007 EU Enlargement
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland and Northwestern University

detail.title: Immigrants' Legal Status and Firms: Evidence from the 2007 EU Enlargement
detail.abstract:
We study how firms and workers adjust when previously restricted migrants gain full and portable work rights in a labor market with substantial informality. We exploit the 2007 EU accession of Bulgaria and Romania, which granted unrestricted work rights to Italy's largest migrant group. Using matched employer–employee administrative data and an IV-DID design, we find that firms suddenly and persistently shift employment composition toward EU07 workers, compressing the native employment share without reducing native hiring or increasing separations. We don't detect any significant change in wages for either natives or EU07 workers. For migrants, this null effect reflects offsetting compositional shifts as newly observed and incumbent EU07 workers enter the formal workforce with different wage trajectories. Consistent with a shift in bargaining power toward workers, EU07 migrants experienced significant gains in job mobility and job security. Overall, the evidence suggests that removing legal restrictions reshaped firms’ personnel choices and altered migrants’ employment relationships, improving their outside options, bargaining position, and access to more secure jobs.

title: Interdependence or Contagion? An Econometric Analysis of Stablecoin Resilience in Periods of Market Stress

detail.title: Interdependence or Contagion? An Econometric Analysis of Stablecoin Resilience in Periods of Market Stress
detail.abstract: This paper tests whether stablecoins exhibit nancial contagion during market stress or merely persistent interdependence. Using daily Coin Metrics data for 20222025 for six stablecoins (USDT, USDC, TUSD, BUSD, GUSD and DAI), we show that a naive comparison of correlations is biased, exactly as Forbes and Rigobon (2002) warned: the rise in crisis-period correlations is almost entirely explained by a jump in volatility. After the correct Forbes Rigobon heteroskedasticity adjustment, and independently under a DCC-GARCH model, the systemic-contagion hypothesis is not supported for any of the three crises (UST/LUNA, FTX, SVB). The only persistent elevated link, the USDCDAI pair, reects a direct collateral link between the assets rather than panic transmission. A Markov-switching model endogenously identies a high-volatility regime that captures the known crises, formalising the regime-dependent nature of interdependence. A logistic regression with an exogenous stress denition conrms the absence of signicant cross-asset transmission channels. Additional copula tail-dependence and DieboldYilmaz connectedness analyses conrm that no hidden tail or network contagion channel is detected. The results bear on macroprudential supervision and the assessment of stablecoin systemic risk.

title: Retreating from Science: The Long-Run Effects of the 1970s U.S. Military Disinvestment from University Research
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business, Johns Hopkins University - School of Government & Policy and Duke University

detail.title: Retreating from Science: The Long-Run Effects of the 1970s U.S. Military Disinvestment from University Research
detail.abstract:
Between 1945 and 1970, the U.S. Department of Defense was one of the country's largest funders of university research, and the most important in the physical sciences and engineering. Political pressures subsequently led to this funding declining nearly two-thirds by the mid-1970s and never fully recovering. We show that these cuts were felt across the U.S. research system, with ensuing declines in university scientists, PhD production, and research output. Early career scientists who were DoD-funded in 1970 were more likely than peers to leave universities, with many moving to industry. Though some became more likely to patent, in the aggregate, this appears to have reduced science-linked innovation in related technologies and compressed U.S. leadership in formerly DoD-driven fields. These effects extend to outcomes more closely related to military objectives: fewer PhDs entered the defense industrial base, and an initial increase in science-linked defense patenting in the most exposed technology areas gave way to a long-run decline.

title: Human Enhancement Technologies: A Survey Experiment on Private Demand and Governance Preferences
affiliations: , ,  and Catholic University of Milan

detail.title: Human Enhancement Technologies: A Survey Experiment on Private Demand and Governance Preferences
detail.abstract:
When a new technology promises large private benefits but may impose social costs that markets do not price, demand need not reveal how citizens want it governed. We examine this using a nationally representative U.S. survey experiment (N=5,556) on human enhancement technologies (HET). The experiment randomizes benefit domain, mechanism, heritability, purpose, and risk across vignettes; for each respondent’s assigned vignette, we elicit stated adoption, preferred regulation, and ethical and societal concerns. Overall, about 53% would adopt. Framing the technology as enhancing rather than restorative lowers adoption by about five percentage points, as much as a severe side-effect profile. About 28% would not adopt at any benefit. This refusal is driven overwhelmingly by the enhancing framing rather than by risk, consistent with a non-compensatory constraint for a substantial subgroup. Most who would adopt still favor strict regulation, and most who would never adopt do not wish to forbid others from doing so. Productivity enhancement generates the most ethical concern of any attribute but attracts the least regulation, and respondents favor subsidizing rather than taxing its adoption, consistent with a concern about access rather than safety. Private demand is therefore an unreliable guide to the governance citizens want, and the divergence we document provides a basis for regulators seeking to align the direction of technical change with societal values and priorities.

title: Supply Chain Risk, Trade and Economic Fragility
affiliations: , , University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Economics

detail.title: Supply Chain Risk, Trade and Economic Fragility
detail.abstract:
We study how equilibrium patterns of production, trade, and input sourcing in complex supply chains are shaped by aggregate risk. We develop a quantitative multi-country model with multi-sourcing across stages. We show that sourcing shares equal an input’s expected output elasticity — its expected marginal contribution to output across states of the world. Risk has a positional effect on sourcing and welfare, operating through offsetting cross-stage complementarity and within-stage substitutability; which one dominates is a quantitative question. An increase in a country’s own risk always lowers its welfare; risk elsewhere has ambiguous, sometimes positive, effects through relative prices. We also show analytically that risk attenuates comparative advantage, as countries shift sourcing away from their most productive suppliers. Quantifying the model for 50 countries and 3 production stages, we show that supply-chain complexity lowers volatility for the riskiest countries, and rising Chinese-origin risk reallocates production and lowers welfare unevenly across the chain.

title: Exorbitant Privilege of the Periodic Table? Geoeconomics, Endogenous Centrality and Strategic Minerals for the Green Transition
affiliations: Imperial College London, University Paris Dauphine-PSL and

detail.title: Exorbitant Privilege of the Periodic Table? Geoeconomics, Endogenous Centrality and Strategic Minerals for the Green Transition
detail.abstract:
Trade networks underpinning the energy transition are endogenous economic objects, and their structure is a source of market power. Using bilateral trade data for thirteen electrification metals over 1995–2023, we show that trade in these materials has reorganised into a hub-and-spoke system centred on China, in sharp contrast to the diffuse, multilateral structure of fossil fuels. This centrality did not follow from resource endowments: China holds few of the underlying reserves. It was built through processing investment, industrial policy, and commodity-targeted development finance—an equilibrium outcome rather than a geographical accident. We formalise this in a stylised model in which a country chooses how central to become, and show that centrality maps into pricing power: the world price response to a strategic supply cut is stronger when the network is more concentrated and downstream demand and fringe supply are more inelastic. Constructing text-based, commodity-specific supply shocks and estimating local projections, we find that supply contractions in critical metals raise US and EU consumer prices by roughly twice as much as comparable fossil-fuel shocks, and more persistently. Centrality is therefore not merely descriptive: it creates leverage over global prices. The green transition reduces strategic dependence on hydrocarbon exporters but reconstitutes it around mineral supply chains.

title: The Changing Reality of Care: Effects of Institutional Changes and Third-Party Actors on The Experiences of Migrant Caregivers in Israel
affiliations: Tel Aviv University and Tel Aviv University - Department of Political Science

detail.title: The Changing Reality of Care: Effects of Institutional Changes and Third-Party Actors on The Experiences of Migrant Caregivers in Israel

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: This article aims to advance debates on migration governance by analyzing the structural contradictions of Israel's care migration regime over the past 25 years. Using a mixed-methods design, combining a survey of 141 caregivers with in-depth follow-up interviews, the study traces how bilateral labor agreements, regulatory reforms, and recruitment chains have reshaped conditions across arrival cohorts since the mid-1990s. The analysis shows that while formal reforms projected modernization, the system remained anchored in informal brokerage, escalating recruitment fees, and delegated enforcement. Building on these findings, we conceptualize Israel's regime as a form of hybrid migration governance: the state symbolically regulates migration while outsourcing recruitment, monitoring, and enforcement to transnational intermediaries. This configuration produces what we call "designed precarity", a structurally maintained condition where legal protections coexist with persistent exploitation. By foregrounding caregivers' lived experiences, the article demonstrates how state outsourcing does not dismantle coercive practices but reorganizes them through diffuse and networked forms of control. Situating the Israeli case within global debates on care chains and migration infrastructures, we argue that neoliberal outsourcing embeds dependency and vulnerability within transnational labor provision while sustaining the façade of regulatory progress. Because Israel's population is on average younger than many Western democracies, its long-standing reliance on migrant care offers an early warning model from which other aging societies can learn as they confront similar demographic and institutional pressures.

title: The Price of Political Ties: Reputational Risk and the Strategic Divestment of Corporate PACs
affiliations: Stanford University, , Stanford Law School and Stanford University

detail.title: The Price of Political Ties: Reputational Risk and the Strategic Divestment of Corporate PACs
detail.abstract:
Political contributions generate access and influence for firms, but their public visibility exposes firms to reputational risk. We study how firms adjust their political spending when the reputational cost of political ties rises sharply. To identify this response, we exploit fatal school shootings and mass shootings as exogenous shocks to the salience of gun violence in the United States. We implement a staggered difference-in-differences design on a panel of corporate PAC contributions to U.S. House candidates, 2000–2024. We find that corporate PACs divest selectively and temporarily following gun violence shocks. Contributions to Republican candidates fall by 70.3% after fatal school shootings in competitive districts and return to baseline within nine months, with no substitution toward Democratic candidates. A parallel penalty of 60.9% emerges for Republicans in safe Democratic districts but is absent in safe Republican districts. Mass shootings generate similar perturbations in corporate contributions. These patterns indicate that firms withdraw only where the reputational risk of continued association is high or its strategic value is low. The observed divestment appears across industries and is stronger for firms with greater consumer exposure. Our findings reveal that firms treat political ties as time-varying liabilities, temporarily withdrawing visible financial support when issue salience spikes and resuming once public attention fades, leaving firms’ long-run political investment intact. Since public pressure is limited and dissipates quickly, and corporate divestment is transient rather than durably reallocated, the underlying financial incentives facing policymakers remain unchanged in the long run, sustaining the policy status quo.

title: Optimal Currency Strategies Under Deviations From Interest Parity
affiliations: and Netspar

detail.title: Optimal Currency Strategies Under Deviations From Interest Parity
detail.abstract:
This paper examines optimal currency demands for global equity and bond investors in a large cross-section of developed and emerging markets over the 1975-2023 period. It extends the framework of Campbell et al. (2010) by incorporating both optimal portfolio-risk minimizing currency exposures, accounting for empirically measured hedging costs arising from deviations of Covered Interest Parity (CIP), and optimal expected-return-driven currency demands based on non-zero expected excess currency returns arising from empirically measured deviations of Uncovered Interest Parity (UIP). The analysis shows that the main conclusions of their portfolio risk-minimizing framework hold for this larger and longer panel of countries and that they are robust to deviations from CIP. Specifically, it is optimal for portfolio risk-minimizing equity investors to hold exposures to the U.S. dollar and the euro while avoiding exposure to all other currencies, whereas bond investors should hedge all currency exposures. In contrast, observed deviations from UIP are sufficiently large and persistent among currencies with high average relative interest currencies, especially Emerging Markets currencies, to generate expected return-driven currency demands that offset, and in some cases reverse, portfolio-risk minimizing demands, even for investors with low risk tolerance. The average excess returns on those currencies are large enough to compensate investors for their substantial return volatility and strong positive covariance with equity returns.

title: Spreading Out Across Expanding Idea Space
affiliations: University of Massachusetts at Amherst - College of Social and Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and University of Essex

detail.title: Spreading Out Across Expanding Idea Space
detail.abstract:
Over nearly two centuries, US inventions have become increasingly dissimilar: not just fewer head-to-head collisions between inventors, but growing distance between neighboring inventions. We document this secular decline in similarity using validated neural language models applied to the full text of claims in over 11 million US patents (1836–2023), corroborated by a 98% decline in patent interference rates, a measure of independent simultaneous invention. Measuring this correctly requires validation, since different representations of the same patent text can yield opposite conclusions about whether inventions are converging or spreading out. Our validation framework, the first systematic comparison for patent text, selects among these representations. We develop a spatial competition model in which inventors choose locations in idea space. The model explains spreading out and connects it to several independently documented patterns — rising R&D investment per inventor, increasing patent values, weakening knowledge spillovers, and declining research productivity. The mechanism is spatial; as inventors spread out to capture new territory, inventions become more valuable but also more costly for others to absorb. In doing so, the model turns spillover intensity, innovation step size, and research productivity from fixed primitives into outcomes of inventor positioning. A calibrated decomposition attributes roughly 40% of the long-run decline in US research productivity to these spatial forces, alongside traditional explanations such as fishing out and the burden of knowledge. Where inventors stand relative to each other in idea space matters as much for growth as how many of them there are.

title: Volatility Disagreement in the Options Market
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, Yale SOM and

detail.title: Volatility Disagreement in the Options Market
detail.abstract:
We construct a novel stock-level measure of volatility disagreement as the cross-sectional dispersion of realized variance forecasts built from heterogeneous information sets and machine learning models. Sorting single-name delta-hedged straddles on this measure yields a long-short return of −5.14% per month, robust to known option return predictors and not subsumed by disagreement about first moments or the variance risk premium. A one-standard-deviation increase in volatility disagreement is associated with a 30% rise in option position opening. The cross-sectional patterns of our disagreement measure align with recent theoretical advances of beliefs and pricing of variance claims. Evidence on attention, ownership, and arbitrage costs is more consistent with mispricing than risk compensation.

title: Life Insurance as a Random Variable: Path Enumeration and The Probability Distribution of the NPV
affiliations: Polytechnic University of Valencia

detail.title: Life Insurance as a Random Variable: Path Enumeration and The Probability Distribution of the NPV

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study. The research is purely mathematical and does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or personal data; all numerical illustrations use the published Illustrative Life Table (Bowers et al., 1997).
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The present value of the future net liabilities of a life insurance contract is a random variable, not a scalar. This paper constructs its exact probability distribution by path enumeration: the direct sum over all admissible trajectories, each with its deterministic discounted cash flow and its probability. The method completely separates the biometric component of the policy from its financial mechanics, so that both can be modelled independently. For an individual contract with a single transition to a terminal state we obtain, in continuous time, the exact density of the net present value (NPV), and we show that its mean is the classical prospective reserve: the usual actuarial valuation is thereby characterized as the first moment of that distribution. Discretizing time leads to the path enumeration algorithm, which operates directly on the mortality table and yields the complete NPV distribution of any finite-horizon multistate contract; from it, all moments, quantiles and risk measures are read off without further computation. Again, its mean coincides with the value given by classical actuarial mathematics. An endowment contract with a life annuity illustrates the method: the classical reserve is confirmed as the mean, the standard deviation is 32% of the total nominal premiums, and the 99.5% Solvency II VaR exceeds sixteen annual premiums. In addition, the explicit form of the NPV density under Gompertz-Makeham mortality is derived.

title: Who Wants to Break Up Big Firms? Harm, Fairness, and the Demand for Antitrust
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and

detail.title: Who Wants to Break Up Big Firms? Harm, Fairness, and the Demand for Antitrust
detail.abstract:
The rise of superstar firms has made dominant companies central to modern economic life, and antitrust enforcement is one of the main policy tools for regulating their market power. Public opinion can shape the political and regulatory environment in which antitrust enforcement takes place, yet there is little direct evidence on what drives these preferences. We conduct a pre-registered information-provision experiment with 4,000 American households. Respondents were told about one of five real antitrust cases and randomly assigned to information treatments designed to study four potential drivers of support for antitrust enforcement: perceived market share, perceived consumer harm, perceived unfair competition, and perceived negative image. All four treatments moved the beliefs they were designed to affect, but their effects on demand for antitrust differed sharply. Information about consumer harm had the most systematic effects: it increased plaintiff support and support for break-up and conduct remedies, with effects remaining visible one month later, and also spilled over to broader support for antitrust policies. By contrast, and contrary to expert forecasts, information about market share had no meaningful effect on demand for antitrust enforcement. The findings suggest that the public thinks like economists in one key respect: they do not care about market share per se, but respond instead to consumer harm. One factor outside the core economic framework, perceived unfair competition, also matters, though its effects are more limited in scope. We discuss implications for policymakers and regulators.

title: What is the status of integration of rehabilitation and assistive technology into national strategies in the WHO European Region? A descriptive cross-sectional study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Lucerne, University of Lucerne, University of Lucerne, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Lucerne

detail.title: What is the status of integration of rehabilitation and assistive technology into national strategies in the WHO European Region? A descriptive cross-sectional study
detail.abstract: Background: Integrating rehabilitation and assistive technologies (AT) into national health strategies is essential to achieving equitable, effective, and sustainable health systems and to achieve Universal Health Coverage.,Objectives: To identify and document the current status of integration of rehabilitation and AT into national strategies and to analyze the integration in available strategy documents.,Methods: This descriptive cross-sectional study collected quantitative and qualitative data. All 53 WHO/Europe member states were invited to participate in an online survey regarding the integration of rehabilitation and AT into their national strategies and were asked to provide related policy documents for analysis. Descriptive analysis was conducted on the quantitative data, while thematic analysis was applied to the free-text responses and the analysed documents.,Result: 39 survey responses were received from 27 countries. Of these, 18 countries reported that rehabilitation is integrated into a national strategy, seven indicated it is not, and four were uncertain. AT integration was reported in 15 countries, with five reporting no integration. Overall, 39 documents from 16 countries were eligible for analysis and comprised five document types: strategies (n=12), strategic frameworks and policy proposals (n=4), action plans (n=9), situation assessments (n=9) and programs (n=5).,Conclusion: Findings reveal limited integration of rehabilitation and AT, hindered by low policymaker awareness and a lack of leadership. Existing strategy documents offer models for integration, and the study provides recommendations to inform policy, support advocacy, and guide resource use.

title: From Extraction to Continuity: Circular Material Governance, and Precision Resource Stewardship in NewVistas
affiliations: Quaid-i-Azam University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Extraction to Continuity: Circular Material Governance, and Precision Resource Stewardship in NewVistas
detail.abstract: This paper formalizes Agency 22, Materials, as the constitutional standards governor of long-term raw-material continuity within the NewVistas LAW/PLAT system. Unlike conventional resource regimes that prioritize extraction volume, commodity exports, speculative ownership, or centralized mining scale, Agency 22 is designed to preserve the physical material base required for buildings, utilities, transportation systems, manufacturing, robotics, server infrastructure, fuel-cell systems, polymers, glass, cement tiles, stainless steel components, and steward enterprises. Its purpose is not to maximize mining, but to secure resilient material continuity for a cooperating of approximately fifty communities and five million people. The paper develops a recovery-first framework in which material demand is governed through the hierarchy of reuse, repair, remanufacture, recovery, recycling, substitution, precision extraction, and balanced strategic import. Waste streams are treated as artificial ore deposits, including stainless steel scrap, copper, aluminum, electronics, batteries, catalysts, polymers, glass, obsolete machinery, fuel-cell components, and precision equipment. As recovered and recycled supply expands, required primary extraction declines, extending the effective material horizon. Where virgin extraction becomes necessary, Agency 22 favors precision methods over mass excavation. The paper emphasizes PCD drilling, directional drilling, drill-and-ream systems, robotic extraction, remote operation, surface-based human supervision, digital hole records, assay records, material passports, and backfill documentation as alternatives to open-pit mining, drill-and-blast systems, and hazardous underground labor. Extraction becomes admissible only when tied to TOK-validated physical demand, binding off-take, safety certification, Agency 22 standards, and digital proof. The paper also preserves NewVistas constitutional boundaries. Agency 22 does not own resources, operate mines, finance equipment, hold custody, trade commodities, accumulate reserves, or collect transition funds. Title, finance, custody, execution, accounting, proof, and audit remain separated across the proper NewVistas rails. The result is a no-reserve, no-deficit, contractor-executed, recovery-first material governance system that transforms raw materials from speculative commodities into long-horizon civilizational continuity assets.

title: Mapping of National Laws, Collective Agreements and Jurisprudence Concerning Work-Related Psychosocial Risks, Workplace Bullying and Work-related Stress in the EU27

detail.title: Mapping of National Laws, Collective Agreements and Jurisprudence Concerning Work-Related Psychosocial Risks, Workplace Bullying and Work-related Stress in the EU27

detail.abstract: There have been numerous changes in the European world of work in recent decades. The globalisation of markets, deindustrialisation and expansion of the tertiary sector are some of the shifts that have contributed to profound changes in the nature of work and the environment in which it is performed. Alongside these changes work-related psychosocial risks (PSR) have been exacerbated. This development has been subject to increasing attention in the public debate, in research and in policy responses, at both the European and the national level.

title: Too much of a Good Thing? Safe Assets, Spillovers, and Fiscal Policy Coordination
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), European Stability Mechanism, Banca d'Italia and European Stability Mechanism

detail.title: Too much of a Good Thing? Safe Assets, Spillovers, and Fiscal Policy Coordination

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Stability Mechanism Working Paper No. 78
publicationDetails.journalName: European Stability Mechanism (ESM) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Are public debt levels too high and convenience yields too low, or is the opposite true? Safe asset issuers have market power, which incentivises them to restrict issuance to raise the convenience yield earned on foreign-held debt. Yet, these governments also tend to over-issue, failing to internalise the fiscal cost they impose abroad by lowering demand for other countries’ bonds and, thus, their convenience yields. We develop a model of financially integrated economies and show analytically that the relative strength of these opposing incentives depends on public expenditure (which exacerbates the fiscal externality) and bond substitutability (which reduces governments’ bond market power). Calibrating the model to the euro area over the period 2015-2023, we find the fiscal externality to dominate: non-cooperative governments that ignore spillovers issue too much debt, on the order of 5% of GDP, compared to a cooperative benchmark. Introducing common debt mitigates the market power distortion, but exacerbates the fiscal externality and can thus improve the non-cooperative equilibrium when market power is the dominant distortion.

title: Restricted Correlation Framework (RCF): A Licensing Protocol and Technical System for Protecting Software Methodology from AI Extraction

detail.title: Restricted Correlation Framework (RCF): A Licensing Protocol and Technical System for Protecting Software Methodology from AI Extraction
detail.abstract: We present the Restricted Correlation Framework (RCF), a licensing protocol and technical system designed to protect software methodology from extraction by large language models (LLMs) and automated analysis systems. Existing open-source licenses-MIT, Apache 2.0, GPL-were designed before LLMs existed. They regulate copying and distribution but provide no mechanism to address a new class of intellectual property threat: the correlation and replication of methodology through AI training, where not a single original token need survive the translation between programming languages. RCF introduces three contributions. First, a legal layer: the RCF-PL license distinguishes Visibility rights (reading, auditing) from Usage rights (replication, AI training), establishing a licensing primitive absent from existing frameworks. Second, a mathematical layer: surprisal-weighted correlation over Program Dependence Graphs (PDGs), a language-invariant representation that survives translation between programming languages. Third, a proof layer: p-value and E-value statistics analogous to BLAST in bioinformatics, turning similarity scores into court-grade evidence of shared origin. We define a closed semantic alphabet Sigma that every language normalizer must implement, making cross-language fingerprinting possible by construction. We describe the methodology canary-a designed, functionally-neutral idiosyncrasy that serves as near-zero false-positive evidence of methodology extraction. RCF is implemented as an open-source TypeScript and Python package with 1,362+ npm downloads and active deployment in production systems.

title: Role of Higher Education Institutions in Promoting Green Communities

detail.title: Role of Higher Education Institutions in Promoting Green Communities

detail.abstract: Higher Education Institutions (HELs) plays an important role in evolving environmentally responsible citizens and developing the sustainable practices within society. HELs possess the potential to influence attitudes, behaviors and sustainable decision-making through knowledge creation, policy development and community engagement. The paper explores the contribution of HELs for the development of green communities by curriculum integration, campus sustainability initiatives, research innovations, outreach projects and student participation. Taking over the insights from global and national practices, the study emphasizes the transformative role of universities and college in strengthening the ecological awareness. Finally, the paper deals with a strategic, multi stakeholder approach within HELs that accelerates significantly the transition on environmentally conscious societies.

reference: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-10
title: Intergenerational Mobility in Late Qing Dynasty: Evidence from Northeast China
affiliations: University of Chicago - Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility, University of Chicago - Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility and New Economic School (NES)

detail.title: Intergenerational Mobility in Late Qing Dynasty: Evidence from Northeast China

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-10
publicationDetails.journalName: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines intergenerational mobility across social classes during the late Qing dynasty employing a remarkable data set from Liaoning province in Northeast China. We identify two distinct epochs with markedly different mobility dynamics. Before 1850, mobility patterns exhibited stability and convergence toward a steady state. The second epoch, beginning around 1850, was characterized by unstable intergenerational class dynamics that persisted until the dynasty's collapse. The transition between epochs coincides with the Opium Wars and Taiping Rebellion, demonstrating how the footprints of major crises in the late Qing era can be traced in mobility dynamics. Employing Markov-chain measures and two alternative mobility conceptsthe persistence of class origin across generations and intergenerational class movement-we document that intergenerational mobility increased over the period. However, this aggregate increase masked a decline in upward mobility alongside a rise in downward mobility-disparate patterns that resonate with broader theories of political instability.

title: The Struggle Between The Geographical Indications Act And Lifestyle Industries

detail.title: The Struggle Between The Geographical Indications Act And Lifestyle Industries
detail.abstract: India is in a very strange and paradoxical place in the global panorama of cultural appropriation of Intellectual Property. It is a repository of civilisations that showcases cultural diversity in a staggering manner, with hundreds of different weaving techniques, metallurgical crafts, performing art forms and material cultural practices, many of which are the sole inheritance of the specific tribal and artisanal communities but the major piece of legislation under which the Indian state claims to safeguard these expressions in the commercial domain, the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999, was not a law for cultural protection, but rather a trade law statute, shaped by India's obligations under Article 22 of the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS). It is neither from the loops of Kutch nor the dhokra furnaces of Bastar but from the vineyards of Bordeaux and the cheese caves of Parma. This paper argues that that structural origin story is not incidental, it is determinative of the Act's limitations. It is pertinent to mention that the GI Act, 1999 is structurally inadequate.

title: Correlated Weights: Partial Pooling for Synthetic Control with Multiple Outcomes
affiliations: Texas Tech University

detail.title: Correlated Weights: Partial Pooling for Synthetic Control with Multiple Outcomes

declarations.ethicsApproval: no patients or participants it's public data, theory and computer code

detail.abstract: A study that applies the synthetic control method to several outcomes faces an unacknowledged choice. Fit each outcome its own donor weights, or impose one common set on all of them. The right answer often lies between the two, and this paper makes the middle ground available. The estimator gives each outcome its own weights while penalizing their dispersion around a common centroid, so that the penalty lambda spans a family with existing practice at its corners, with separate fits at lambda = 0 and common weights at lambda = infinity. Because short pre-treatment panels make cross-validation brittle, no single lambda is selected. The estimator aggregates across the family with exponential weights earned by leave-one-out prediction. Aggregation stabilizes estimation and yields the paper's central diagnostic, the mass profile, the data's own answer to how much the outcomes share donor structure. Regret theory caps the price of aggregating and characterizes when the interior's guarantee undercuts both corners'. Placebo inference reruns the entire pipeline, tuning included, in every permutation. Python and Stata implementations accompany the paper.

title: Foreign Direct Investments in EAEU Member States in 2025

detail.title: Foreign Direct Investments in EAEU Member States in 2025
