detail.title: Estimating the Human Development Impacts and Economic Returns from an Adolescent Cash ‘Plus’ Programme in Kenya: An Economic Modelliing Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used only secondary, de-identified data and did not involve human participants. Approvals were obtained for the KDHS from The DHS Program (ICF/USAID) and for the VACSs from the Centers for Disease Control and Together for Girls. County-level administrative data were obtained from the Government of Kenya. No ethical approval was required for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was funded by the UK Research and Innovation Global Challenges Research Fund (UKRI GCRF) Accelerate Hub [ES/S008101/1 to LC], and the Wellspring Philanthropic Fund [Grant no. 18757 to WR, LC, & ET]. The funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

detail.abstract: The Government of Kenya plans to scale-up an adolescent-focused cash ‘plus’ programme to improve educational attainment and delay adolescent pregnancy. We aimed to estimate the programme’s impacts, economic returns, and cost-effectiveness using model-based economic evaluation. We modelled the delivery of conditional cash transfers ‘plus’ adolescent clubs, community conversations, parenting support and psychosocial support to poor adolescents in nine selected counties from 2026 to 2029. Two scenarios were compared: a baseline in which intervention variables remained constant at 2025 levels, and an immediate scale-up sustained throughout 2026-2029. Human development impacts were simulated using an integrated modelling framework. Gains in years of schooling were projected with an education transition model, while reductions in adolescent pregnancy, child marriage, and experiences of violence were estimated with a deterministic age–cohort transition model. Economic returns to schooling were calculated with Mincerian earnings functions. Model parameters were derived from rigorous impact evaluations, nationally representative surveys, and Kenya’s national social registry. The four-year intervention, costing US$46.1 million, is projected to reach 140,000 adolescents, and compared with the baseline, generate an additional 74,900 (+7%) years of schooling; and avert 1,420 (-8%) adolescent pregnancies, 1,500 (-11%) child marriages, 2,970 (-3%) experiences of sexual violence, and 21,800 (-8%) experiences of emotional/physical violence. Furthermore, the intervention is projected to generate US$318 million in discounted lifetime labour earnings, representing a seven-fold return on investment. The estimated cost was US$567 per additional year of schooling, and US$109 when benefits across multiple outcomes were considered, comparing favourably with other adolescent education interventions. Findings were robust to sensitivity analyses, with a >98% probability that returns exceeded programme costs. These findings suggest that scaling up an adolescent focused cash ‘plus’ programme could substantially improve adolescent human development, while delivering strong economic returns and good value for money.

title: Robust Revelation in Competing Mechanisms with Endogenous Exclusive Agency
affiliations: McMaster University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Robust Revelation in Competing Mechanisms with Endogenous Exclusive Agency
detail.abstract: This paper studies competing mechanism games with endogenous exclusive agency, where principals announce mechanisms and agents select and communicate with at most one principal. The standard revelation-principle argument is hard to apply because agents may need to report information about rival mechanisms, creating an infinite-regress problem. The analysis focuses on equilibria in which communication with non-deviating principals is ex-post optimal, and it imposes robustness with respect to continuation equilibria after unilateral deviations. Within this disciplined class, market-information communication can be reduced to the identity of the deviating principal. A Weak Revelation Principle represents robust quasi ex-post equilibrium allocations by truthful equilibria in EPIC extended direct mechanisms. A Strong Revelation Principle gives an operational test: it suffices to check BIC direct deviations against the EPIC direct mechanisms used by non-deviators, allowing the continuation selection most favorable to the deviator. The results turn revelation into a tractable robustness criterion for exclusiveagency environments in which ex-post or dominant-strategy communication with non-deviators is economically natural.

title: The Broken Energy Ladder: Household Drudgery, Fragmented Transition, and Rural Structural Barriers in India
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur and Shiv Nadar University

detail.title: The Broken Energy Ladder: Household Drudgery, Fragmented Transition, and Rural Structural Barriers in India
detail.abstract: The Energy Ladder Hypothesis proposes that rising household income drives a progressive shift from traditional energy sources to cleaner modern energy. Building on this hypothesis, this paper reconceptualises energy deprivation as energy-based domestic drudgery-a household production constraint grounded in Becker's (1965) theory of time allocation. It also introduces two novel empirical constructs. The Broken Ladder Hypothesis posits that the consumption-drudgery gradient diverges across the rural-urban divide. The Fragmented Transition Hypothesis posits that cooking-energy and electricity drudgery respond asymmetrically to rising consumption. Using pooled data from India's Time Use Surveys of 2019 and 2024, and covering 278,284 nationally representative households, we deploy surveyweighted probit models and a Fairlie nonlinear decomposition technique. Results confirm the energy ladder in the Indian context but reveal it to be simultaneously broken and fragmented. The consumption gradient for cooking-energy drudgery is more than eight times that for electricity drudgery. The Fairlie decomposition reveals that over half of the rural-urban cooking drudgery gap is structurally unexplained by observable household endowments, while the electricity gap is fully explained. The results call for enhanced supply-side infrastructure investment, sustained refill subsidies for marginalised households, and a gender-responsive clean energy policy in India.

title: Adaptive Sovereign Balance Framework (ASBF): Functional Configuration as an Independent Object of Macrofinancial Diagnosis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Adaptive Sovereign Balance Framework (ASBF): Functional Configuration as an Independent Object of Macrofinancial Diagnosis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses only publicly available macroeconomic and institutional data; no human subjects or participant data were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
Existing instruments for sovereign vulnerability assessment — reserve adequacy metrics, debt sustainability analysis, balance-sheet mapping, early warning systems — operate at the level of individual components or sectors of the sovereign balance. This paper proposes that macrofinancial stability is a relational, not additive, property: it resides in the joint functional configuration of the sovereign balance rather than in any component considered separately. The Adaptive Sovereign Balance Framework (ASBF) operationalises this configuration through a four-step sequence — function, obligation, resource margin, adequacy — applied to five functional contours of the sovereign balance: international reserves, the sovereign wealth fund, the fiscal system, monetary coordination, and economic diversification. Two indices summarise the resulting diagnosis: SVI^S, measuring the overall adequacy deficit across contours weighted by systemic importance, and SVI^P, measuring the rate at which that configuration is deteriorating or improving.

The framework is tested on Kazakhstan, 2005–2023, a small open commodity-dependent economy with a managed exchange rate and a sovereign wealth fund. Three independent non-parametric tests — Mann-Whitney U (p = 0.0017), Fisher's exact test (p = 0.028), and a permutation test (p = 0.014) — show that SVI^P is significantly elevated in years preceding identified crisis episodes relative to calm years. A structured comparison against IMF Article IV consultation reports across three crisis episodes (2008–2009, 2014–2016, 2020) documents a recurring diagnostic gap: in each case, SVI^P registered rising systemic pressure in the year preceding crisis onset, while component-level surveillance instruments — ARA, DSA — reported individually adequate conditions or did not translate observed sectoral risks into a system-level reading. In 2007, SVI^P reached +1.020, the highest value in the sample, while reserves and external debt were both assessed as comfortable; the banking crisis materialised within two years. An illustrative out-of-sample check for 2016–2023 shows internally consistent quadrant transitions with no false positive signals.

The paper argues that this gap is architectural rather than a surveillance failure: existing instruments are well-calibrated to their own diagnostic objects — the reserve buffer, the debt trajectory, a vector of leading indicators — but none is designed to estimate the functional adequacy of the sovereign balance as an integrated system. The contribution of ASBF is accordingly not the construction of another composite index, but the operationalisation of sovereign balance configuration as an independent diagnostic object; SVI is one implementation of that broader framework. Limitations of the pilot specification — a single-country sample of 19 annual observations, theory-derived rather than statistically estimated thresholds and weights — are discussed alongside the conditions for falsifiability and the research programme required for cross-country generalisation.

title: Tax Transparency as an Anti-corruption Mechanism: The Case of Uzbekistan

detail.title: Tax Transparency as an Anti-corruption Mechanism: The Case of Uzbekistan

declarations.funderStatement: This article is based on the MOCCA project (Multilevel Orders of Corruption in Central Asia) that has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie grant agreement No. 101085855

detail.abstract: This article examines the interaction between anti-corruption law and tax law by analyzing tax transparency mechanisms within Uzbekistan's recent legal and institutional reforms. The study adopts a theoretical and policy-oriented legal analysis rather than an empirical approach, focusing on newly developing legal frameworks and institutional structures. It argues that tax transparency mechanisms can function as effective anticorruption instruments only when supported by coherent legal rules, procedural consistency, and sufficient institutional capacity. The analysis evaluates reforms in four key areas: asset declaration, beneficial ownership transparency, whistleblower protection, and information exchange. The findings demonstrate that despite important recent reforms, significant legal and institutional deficiencies remain. Asset declaration lacks comprehensive legislative regulation and practical implementation; beneficial ownership transparency remains limited in scope; whistleblower protection is narrowly focused; and information exchange mechanisms face both domestic and international shortcomings. The article concludes that legal reform alone is insufficient to ensure effective anti-corruption outcomes. Sustainable progress requires stronger institutional capacity and gradual, proportionate implementation that balances transparency objectives with the protection of individual rights, particularly privacy.

title: Graph Neural Networks and Knowledge Graphs for Clinical Reasoning: A Review of Architectures, Applications, and Open Challenges

detail.title: Graph Neural Networks and Knowledge Graphs for Clinical Reasoning: A Review of Architectures, Applications, and Open Challenges

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author has no personal or financial relationships with any organizations that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or patient data. All data used in this research were obtained from publicly available datasets (BUSI - Breast Ultrasound Images Dataset). Therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Clinical decision-making increasingly draws on structured relational knowledge that links symptoms, laboratory findings, diagnoses, medications and outcomes across heterogeneous data sources. Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a natural computational substrate for reasoning over such relational structures, while knowledge graphs (KGs) provide the curated or data-derived schema that encodes clinical semantics. This review synthesises recent progress at the intersection of these two paradigms, focusing on their combined application to clinical reasoning tasks such as diagnosis prediction, risk stratification, treatment recommendation and pharmacovigilance. We examine the principal GNN architectures adopted in the clinical domain, including graph convolutional networks, graph attention networks, relational graph convolutional networks and heterogeneous graph transformers, and describe how they are coupled with electronic health record data, medical ontologies and biomedical literature to construct task-specific knowledge graphs. Representative studies spanning 2013 to 2025 are compared according to data source, architecture, task and reported finding. The review further considers interpretability mechanisms that expose evidentiary subgraphs to clinicians, and discusses persistent challenges relating to data heterogeneity, missingness, temporal dynamics, fairness and clinical validation. We identify emerging directions, including the fusion of GNNs with large language models, federated and privacy-preserving graph learning, and dynamic knowledge graphs that evolve with longitudinal patient trajectories. The review concludes that while GNN-KG integration demonstrably improves predictive accuracy and offers a pathway toward explainable clinical artificial intelligence, translation into routine practice requires closer attention to prospective validation, regulatory scrutiny and clinician trust.

title: Severe Cognitive Impairments and Long-term Care in Germany
affiliations: Paris Dauphine University, Max Planck Society for the Advancement of the Sciences - Munich Center for the Economics of Aging (MEA), German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), DIW Berlin, German Institute for Economic Research and Paris Dauphine University

detail.title: Severe Cognitive Impairments and Long-term Care in Germany
detail.abstract:
Germany experiences an increase in LTC recipients, due to population ageing but also to reforms which made LTC benefits easier accessible for individuals with cognitive impairments. Previous studies documented the cost of long-term care, and how it evolved. However, less is known about the specific case of elderly people suffering from cognitive impairment. Thus, we measure the economic costs of cognitive impairment, which include extensive medical, nursing care and at-home long-term care. We use the SHARE, the Survey on Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, Wave 9. We observe 4% of elderly people living at home with severe cognitive impairment (SCI) (Langa et al. (2017) definition). These individuals are 30% more likely to receive any care, and obtain on average 6 more hours of formal care and 6 more hours of informal care per week. The main driver is not the cognitive impairment per-se but the limitation in activities of daily living (ADLs) which SCI leads to. Thus, once controlling for ADLs, SCI does not explain any additional probability to use care. However, because people with SCI are more likely to have ADLs, the annual cost of their care is estimated to 10,000 euros per year per individual on average.

title: The U.S. Mortality Crisis as a Preston Curve Reversal
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania, Yale University, Boston University - Department of Global Health, University of Pennsylvania and University of Minnesota - Minneapolis

detail.title: The U.S. Mortality Crisis as a Preston Curve Reversal
detail.abstract:
U.S. life expectancy stagnated and declined in the 2010s despite continued growth in real per capita income. We use Preston curves to characterize this pattern as a change in the relationship between income and longevity. Using state-level data from 1980 to 2019 and county-level data from 2000 to 2019, we estimate population-weighted Preston curves relating life expectancy to logged real per capita income. From 1980 to 2010, U.S. states followed the classic Preston curve pattern: rising income was accompanied by rising life expectancy. Counties followed the same pattern from 2000 to 2010. From 2010 to 2019, however, states and counties continued to become richer while life expectancy stagnated or declined. The curves shifted right without shifting up and became steeper, indicating decoupling and divergence: increases in aggregate resources over time no longer produced broad longevity gains, and, in any given year, inequality in life expectancy by income grew. These patterns are robust to alternative temporal anchors around the Great Recession and to substituting education for income. They also appear across sex and racial groups. County-level decompositions are broadly consistent with arguments that longevity has fallen due to widely shared exposures to social deterioration, which may account for the Preston curve reversal. Collectively, we show that the recent U.S. mortality crisis reveals a weakening—and growing inequality—in the conversion of aggregate resources into longevity gains. We conclude that the recent U.S. mortality crisis could be understood not only as a story about particular causes of death, but also as a weakening of institutional and social translation.

title: The Intervention Persistence Anomaly: A Resolution through Thermodynamics and Trade-off Redistribution
affiliations: Southern Luzon State University, Southern Luzon State University

detail.title: The Intervention Persistence Anomaly: A Resolution through Thermodynamics and Trade-off Redistribution
detail.abstract: The persistence of Earth system degradation across five decades, despite sustained intervention under Commoner's Four Laws of Ecology, constitutes an anomaly the prevailing paradigm cannot assimilate without fundamental theoretical revision. No formal mechanism within the collective body of ecological, Earth system, and sustainability science accounts for why coordinated, science-informed intervention fails to arrest redistribution displacement at the system level. This study formally designates this unresolved pattern the Intervention Persistence Anomaly and resolves it through Trade-Off Redistribution, a thermodynamic framework establishing that open systems continuously transform and redistribute matter, energy, and constraint through available pathway architectures. The anomaly is resolved through three interlocking conditions: the Conservation Condition, establishing that every material gain within the Anthroposphere draws from finite Earth stocks governed by the First Law; the Entropic Condition, establishing that every act of intervention is itself a physical process generating entropy under the Second Law; and the Architectural Disruption, identifying the disruption of naturally evolved redistribution architecture as the cumulative mechanism the existing paradigm cannot see. TOR provides the diagnostic instrument Phi = R_O/R_Opt to assess whether intervention genuinely restores redistribution balance or merely displaces stress to subsystems not yet under observation.

title: What Difference does an IG Make? Leadership, Professional Background, and the Allocation of Oversight Activity among Federal Inspectors General, 2001-2025
affiliations: Virginia Tech and Virginia Tech - Center for Public Administration and Policy

detail.title: What Difference does an IG Make? Leadership, Professional Background, and the Allocation of Oversight Activity among Federal Inspectors General, 2001-2025
detail.abstract: Inspectors General (IGs) are appointees meant to provide independent oversight of federal agencies, yet relatively little empirical research examines how leadership shapes the oversight IG offices perform. Using new data drawn from semiannual reports issued by 24 federal agency IG offices from 2001 to 2025, this paper analyzes variation in the two sides of IGs' dual missions: audit functions, measured by reports issued, and investigative functions, measured by investigations closed. Four findings emerge. First, IG confirmation status and tenure are not consistently associated with oversight activity. Second, leadership transitions are associated with short-term declines in reporting activity. Third, IG professional backgrounds are associated with how oversight work is allocated across audit and investigative functions. Fourth, oversight activity declines over time, with a sharp additional decline in 2025. These findings provide new descriptive evidence linking IG leadership to the allocation of oversight activity and document a significant recent disruption in federal oversight.

title: Monopsony and Backloaded Compensation: Theory and Evidence from Public Accountants
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Economics and Goethe University Frankfurt - University of Zurich

detail.title: Monopsony and Backloaded Compensation: Theory and Evidence from Public Accountants
detail.abstract:
In monopsony models, wage markdowns induce deadweight loss and are therefore inefficient. Yet markdowns also arise in models with backloaded efficiency pay, where they are designed to induce effort among early-career workers and are thus efficient. To reconcile—and empirically distinguish—these two mechanisms, we build a dynamic model incorporating labor market power and endogenous effort. Estimating a team production model on novel data on U.S. public accounting firms, we find evidence of both: markdowns for junior workers and markups for senior ones reflect incentive-providing backloading, while monopsony power induces a ‘lifetime’ wage markdown of 15%.

title: ESG Disclosure Intensity and Dupont Performance: NLP Evidence from a Frontier Market
affiliations: , Strathmore Business School, University of Nottingham Business School and

detail.title: ESG Disclosure Intensity and Dupont Performance: NLP Evidence from a Frontier Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or primary data collection requiring ethics board approval; all data were derived from publicly available corporate annual reports.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Purpose. This study examines whether ESG disclosure intensity is associated with financial performance, and whether investment efficiency mediates this relationship, among firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE). 

Methodology. ESG disclosure intensity (ESGI) is measured from the annual reports of 60 NSE-listed firms over 2010 to 2024 using fine-tuned RoBERTa pillar classifiers. Financial performance is decomposed through the DuPont framework, and investment efficiency is tested as a mediator. Estimation uses pooled OLS, fixed-effects, and entity-and-year fixed-effects models, with lagged regressors and two-step system GMM for robustness.

 Findings. ESG disclosure intensity shows no detectable association with return on equity, net profit margin, or total asset turnover, and investment efficiency does not mediate the relationship. A power analysis shows the study can rule out, with 80% power, ROE effects larger than 0.056 per standard deviation, so the result is an informative null rather than an underpowered one. 

Research limitations/implications. The sample covers a single frontier market close to its full listed population, which constrains power and generalisability. The measure captures the intensity of ESG communication rather than its substantive quality. 

Originality. The study bounds the disclosure-to-performance relationship documented in developed and Chinese markets: it does not extend to an East African frontier market when disclosure is measured by intensity rather than third-party ratings. It also documents an exact algebraic identity between the equity multiplier and leverage, with implications for DuPont-based ESG research using hand-reconstructed data.

title: The Labor Market Impacts of GLP-1s
affiliations: University of Copenhagen, , University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics, Rockwool Foundation Research Unit and Duke University - Stanford School of Public Policy

detail.title: The Labor Market Impacts of GLP-1s
detail.abstract:
We estimate the causal impacts of GLP-1 treatment on labor market outcomes using linked Danish administrative data and a matched stacked difference-in-differences design. We compare patients who initiate GLP-1 treatment during the first two years of Semaglutide availability to observably similar patients who initiate four years later. We find that GLP-1 treatment reduces long-term sickness leave by 17.3%. We estimate total fiscal benefits of GLP-1 initiation of approximately 1.3–1.5% of annual labor income per employed individual. We do not detect statistically significant or economically meaningful impacts on income, labor force participation, or employment over four years.

title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Merger Simulations
affiliations: Northwestern University - Department of Economics, Northwestern University, Northwestern University, Cornerstone Research and American University - Department of Finance and Real Estate

detail.title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Merger Simulations
detail.abstract:
Prospective merger simulations are a commonly used tool in industrial organization and antitrust, but evidence about their accuracy and predictive ability is limited. We study 101 mergers in consumer packaged goods and compare the realizations of price changes with predictions from merger simulations. In our sample of consummated mergers, predicted price changes from merger simulations are typically larger than realized ones. Despite the overprediction, we find that full merger simulations are more effective than both structural presumptions and approximations of the merger effect at identifying mergers with large price changes.

title: Oligopsony and Collective Bargaining
affiliations: University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration - Department of Economics, Duke University and Ohio State University (OSU) - Economics

detail.title: Oligopsony and Collective Bargaining
detail.abstract:
Employers facing limited labor market competition may suppress wages below socially optimal levels. Unions can counteract wage suppression through collective bargaining, though they may also push wages above the socially optimal level and lead to job rationing. We estimate a structural model of labor supply, labor demand, and Nash-in-Nash bargaining over wages between local teacher unions and school districts in Pennsylvania’s K-12 public school system from 2013 to 2019. We compare negotiated equilibrium wages and employment to oligopsony wage posting and social planner scenarios. On average, oligopsony reduces wages 7 percent below the social optimum, while collective bargaining raises wages 8 percent above it. Averages mask substantial district-level heterogeneity driven by bargaining power variation. Twenty-eight percent of school districts have salaries lower when public schools are unionized than when they are not due to cross-district externalities, where high salaries at one school cause hiring reductions that increase labor supply elsewhere.

title: In Sickness and in Health: Retirement Responses to Spousal Health Shocks
affiliations: University of Texas at El Paso, Sungkyunkwan University and George Mason University - School of Policy, Government, and International Affairs

detail.title: In Sickness and in Health: Retirement Responses to Spousal Health Shocks
detail.abstract:
Health shocks are a major driver of retirement. However, the existing literature on this topic tends not to consider the marital context in which retirements occur. Using the 1992-2022 Health and Retirement Study and staggered difference-in-differences methods, we investigate how spousal health shocks impact retirement transitions. We also investigate whether these effects differ by gender and health insurance status. We consider multiple definitions of health shocks, including self-reported health declines, additional diagnoses, hospitalizations, increases in out-of-pocket medical spending, and functional deterioration. Our results suggest that the probability of retirement increases by 1.2 to 1.3 percentage points (12 to 13 percent) after a spouse’s new health condition diagnosis or hospitalization. These retirements tend to occur earlier than anticipated. They also tend to be concentrated among women and respondents with employment-based health plans that include retiree coverage for their spouse.

title: Estimating the Economic Effects of Federally Funded R&D
affiliations: , Government of the United States of America - Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Government of the United States of America - Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Dartmouth College and Government of the United States of America - Congressional Budget Office (CBO)

detail.title: Estimating the Economic Effects of Federally Funded R&D
detail.abstract:
In recent years, there has been Congressional interest in changing various policies related to research and development (R&D). Recent legislation has included provisions that would modify federal funding for R&D investments and tax provisions affecting the after-tax price of R&D. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has developed analytical frameworks for estimating how changes in R&D investments affect the economy and the federal budget. This paper describes the agency’s current analytical framework for modeling the economic effects of changes in federal funding for R&D, focusing on two distinct approaches that CBO has developed: an R&D capital stock approach and an R&D components approach.

title: Better Together? The Impact of Cash Transfers and Couples' Financial Planning on Household Dynamics and Economic Outcomes
affiliations: The World Bank,  Poverty, Health, and Nutrition Division of the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), Cornell University and University of Southern California - Center for Economic and Social Research (CESR)

detail.title: Better Together? The Impact of Cash Transfers and Couples' Financial Planning on Household Dynamics and Economic Outcomes
detail.abstract:
Households' most consequential economic decisions are usually made jointly, yet behavioral interventions are typically targeted to individuals and optimized to overcome intra-personal constraints. We use a randomized controlled trial to study whether behavioral interventions targeted to couples can overcome interpersonal constraints related to intra-household decision-making. In rural Liberia, we layer a facilitated joint financial planning exercise atop a large unconditional cash transfer, assessing effects relative to cash only and a pure control. Relative to cash only, adding planning increases the amount of the transfer spent on productive investment and consequently improves economic outcomes by 0.16 standard deviation units. However, for households with the highest ex-ante conflict risk, these gains come at the cost of additional intimate partner violence.

title: Estimating Trends In Mental Distress Using Survey Data
affiliations: University of Virginia - Frank Batten School of Leadership and Public Policy

detail.title: Estimating Trends In Mental Distress Using Survey Data
detail.abstract:
One way of examining how mental health has changed over time is to use information available in large national surveys. While these survey-based measures are valuable in principle, and have been widely employed in prior research, a number of challenges may limit their practical usefulness or require considerable care in their application. This study uses data on U.S. 18-64 year olds from five major household surveys over the period 1999-2019 to investigate three specific questions. First, do different measures or the same indicator from different data sets consistently show how mental distress has changed over time? Second, how does the performance of single-item measures compare to those of psychometrically validated screeners based on multiple questions? Third, what are the benefits or potential costs of using different functional forms of these measures? The answers to these questions are as follows: 1) the estimated trends vary, often dramatically, across measures and, for the same indicator, across data sets and, as a result, some proxies provide a misleading understanding of how mental health has changed over time; 2) the single-item measures do as well or better than those based on multiple questions; 3) no single functional form demonstrates clear superiority over the others. After demonstrating these points, lessons are elucidated for researchers attempting to use survey data to examine trends in mental health.

title: Inference with AI-Generated Covariates
affiliations: and Stanford University - Department of Management Science & Engineering

detail.title: Inference with AI-Generated Covariates
detail.abstract:
Empirical researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to extract structured features, such as sentiment scores, classifications, and expectations, from unstructured data and treat these generated features as observed covariates in downstream estimation. This practice can invalidate inference when systematic, input-dependent errors in generated features, such as hallucination and look-ahead bias, distort the downstream moment conditions. Even after correction, generated features remain noisy proxies whose error profiles differ across models and prompts. We introduce AI-Powered Inference (AI-PI), a method-of-moments framework for valid and efficient inference that combines three components: a moment-specific bias correction based on a small human-labeled calibration set; adaptive weights that optimally combine multiple model-prompt pairs; and an optimal calibration-set design that concentrates costly human labels where the generated features are least reliable. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the AI-PI estimator, allowing for data-adaptive labeling designs, cross-fitted LLM-pipeline tuning, and overidentified GMM. Simulations confirm substantial gains over naive LLM regressions and over debiasing without optimal weighting or labeling design. In an application to news-based sentiment and stock returns, AI-PI produces stable conclusions where naive analyses vary substantially across LLM and prompt choices, with a confidence interval roughly half as long as using the human-labeled data alone.

title: Firm Exit and Financial Frictions
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania and Duke University

detail.title: Firm Exit and Financial Frictions
detail.abstract:
Governments often intervene to prevent firm closures during crises, fearing that financially constrained but viable firms may fail. We develop a firm dynamics model with incomplete financial markets and show how financial frictions generate excessive firm exit. A key statistic governing this dynamic inefficiency is the marginal propensity to exit with debt. Using confidential U.S. Census data, we estimate the relationship between debt and exit and use it to discipline the model. The calibrated model implies that eliminating financial frictions reduces firm exit from 9.3% to 5.0% and generates welfare gains of 3.6% in consumption-equivalent terms. We show that the welfare costs of financial frictions rise sharply during financial crises but change little during standard productivity recessions. Finally, we compare government-guaranteed loans and grants, quantifying the trade-off between fiscal cost and effectiveness in preventing excessive exit.

title: Life After Divorce: Effects of Joint Custody on Parents and Children
affiliations: , , , Yale University, Stockholm University, IZA Institute of Labor Economics, Stockholm University - Department of Economics, Ifo Institute,  and

detail.title: Life After Divorce: Effects of Joint Custody on Parents and Children
detail.abstract:
Divorce reshapes family life, yet little is known about one of its most consequential features: the allocation of child custody. We study the impact of joint versus sole custody on both parents and children using rich administrative data from Sweden linked to over 25 years of newly-collected court custody rulings. To address selection concerns, we exploit random assignment of custody disputes to judges who differ sharply in their propensity to grant joint custody. For fathers, joint custody substantially raises earnings and improves mental health, consistent with sustained paternal involvement enhancing labor market attachment and psychological well-being. In contrast, there are no measurable labor market or mental health effects for mothers. Turning to children, joint custody increases standardized test scores and school quality without affecting mental health outcomes. Joint custody increases fathers’ chances of remarriage, keeps separated parents in closer geographic proximity, and has no effect on intimate partner violence allegations against either partner. These findings inform longstanding debates over the role of child custody in shaping post-divorce family life.

title: Sharpening Economic Interpretation with HARS
affiliations: and Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

detail.title: Sharpening Economic Interpretation with HARS
detail.abstract:
We develop a unified framework that combines shock volatility with sign and narrative restrictions and provides the theoretical foundation for the computationally efficient sampler HARS. HARS preserves the heteroskedastic likelihood and can be combined with any posterior simulator for the heteroskedastic model. In monetary policy, oil market, and fiscal policy models, the same restrictions deliver substantively different economics once shock heteroskedasticity is accounted for. Homoskedastic SVARs put uncertainty in the wrong place, pushing shock-scale variation into impulse-response uncertainty. Heteroskedasticity sharpens dynamic responses, alters economic conclusions, and restores 90% credible intervals as a practical standard for economic inference.

title: Policy Thresholds as Growth Barriers: Theory and Evidence from a Payroll Tax Notch
affiliations: , University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - Department of Economics and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Policy Thresholds as Growth Barriers: Theory and Evidence from a Payroll Tax Notch
detail.abstract:
Discrete policy thresholds are pervasive in tax and regulatory systems and can substantially distort behavior. We show that notches acting as barriers to mobility within a distribution generate distortions extending far beyond the threshold. The same mechanism biases conventional difference-in-differences estimators, and we propose a new methodology to recover causal effects. Applying the method to the abolition of a size-based payroll tax notch, we find that the notch reduced the number of firms above the threshold by 18 percent and lowered treated firms’ employment, capital stock, and value added by 10 percent, whereas conventional difference-in-differences estimates imply negligible effects.

title: AI-Driven Smart Badminton Stadiums as Instruments of Managerial Lease Accounting Obfuscation: CAS 21 Manipulation, Hidden Leverage, and CEO Performance-Vested Stock Option Valuation Distortion in China
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: AI-Driven Smart Badminton Stadiums as Instruments of Managerial Lease Accounting Obfuscation: CAS 21 Manipulation, Hidden Leverage, and CEO Performance-Vested Stock Option Valuation Distortion in China
detail.abstract: The accelerating deployment of AI-enabled smart badminton stadiums across China-facilities integrating IoT sensor networks, edge-compute nodes, real-time player-tracking systems, and dynamic court-allocation platforms-has generated a novel class of mixed-use infrastructure arrangement whose lease classification under Chinese Accounting Standards No. 21 (CAS 21, the domestic equivalent of IFRS 16) is both technically contested and managerially discretionary. This paper investigates two interrelated hypotheses. First, we examine whether CEO-controlled lease classification decisions for smart stadium infrastructure constitute intentional earnings management through the strategic exploitation of CAS 21's identified-asset and substantive-substitution-right criteria, enabling firms to retain significant fixed infrastructure commitments off the balance sheet as operating-lease or service-contract arrangements rather than recognizing right-of-use (ROU) assets and corresponding liabilities. Second, we analyze how the resulting balance-sheet obfuscation distorts the valuation of CEO performance-vested stock options (PVSOs), which are tied to EBITDA, return-on-assets (ROA), and leverage-ratio performance conditions that are systematically inflated or deflated by the lease classification choices the CEO controls. Employing a panel of 63 A-share and Hong Kong-listed sports-infrastructure entities with smart stadium assets (2019-2024, n = 378 firm-years), we document that CEO-controlled CAS 21 classification choices suppress reported net debt by a mean of RMB 284 million per firm-year and inflate EBITDA-based performance metrics by 16.8-23.4% conditional on PVSO moneyness. Using a modified Black-Scholes framework augmented with stochastic performance-condition paths, we demonstrate that PVSO fair values are overstated by a mean of 31.7% relative to values computed on adjusted financials, with the overstatement increasing convexly in the proportion of PVSO vesting conditions linked to EBITDA and leverage metrics. These findings establish a material agency conflict at the intersection of AI infrastructure accounting and executive compensation design, with significant implications for compensation committee governance, auditor scrutiny, and CAS 21 enforcement by the Ministry of Finance.

title: Empires in the Mirror of Time A Hybrid Short Story on Empire Cycles and Actionable Lessons for Modern Governance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Empires in the Mirror of Time A Hybrid Short Story on Empire Cycles and Actionable Lessons for Modern Governance
detail.abstract: Why do large-scale political systems repeatedly experience cycles of expansion, strain, and reconfiguration? Empires rarely collapse suddenly; they fail when routine pressures—fiscal strain, legitimacy loss, distorted information, and overextended commitments—interact faster than institutions can adapt. This book examines a millennium of large-scale governance systems to identify recurring failure modes and the conditions under which decline can be slowed, managed, or redirected. Blending historically grounded narrative scenes with a practical governance playbook, it introduces a Five Machines framework—governance, fiscal systems, security, information, and legitimacy—that allows leaders to diagnose institutional stress before crisis becomes unavoidable. Drawing lessons from medieval federations, industrial empires, Cold War superpowers, and today’s networked world, the book translates historical patterns into stress tests, early-warning indicators, and reform roadmaps applicable to modern states, alliances, platforms, and critical infrastructure systems. Its goal is prevention: improving institutional resilience without requiring catastrophe to justify reform.

title: Learning and the Efficiency of Expert Referrals
affiliations: Emory University - Department of Economics and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Learning and the Efficiency of Expert Referrals
detail.abstract:
Buyers of complex goods and services often rely on the advice of expert intermediaries who are themselves imperfectly informed about the quality of the available options. How well do these intermediaries learn about that quality and act on it? We study this question in the setting of referrals from primary care physicians (PCPs) to specialists, using data on 4.5 million joint replacement surgeries for Medicare beneficiaries. We first document substantial heterogeneity in specialist quality and costs within geographic markets, and we present design-based evidence showing that PCPs adjust their referrals specifically based on the outcomes of their own patients. We then employ a structural learning model of PCP referral choices to quantify the losses from informational frictions and to simulate possible reallocations with improved information. Beyond learning, the model also accounts for limitations on possible reallocations due to habit persistence and capacity constraints. We find that about one-quarter of patients would be referred to a different specialist in the absence of informational frictions, with small but meaningful improvements in patient outcomes.

title: Financial and Real Effects of Fiscal Risk
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS), Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and Bank for International Settlements (BIS) - Monetary and Economic Department

detail.title: Financial and Real Effects of Fiscal Risk
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the macroeconomic and financial effects of fiscal risk shocks using a novel identification from bond yields. We first recover country-specific fiscal risk shocks from a daily Bayesian VAR model in sovereign and safe corporate bond yields, identified via contemporaneous sign restrictions that capture portfolio rebalancing away from government debt toward private safe assets. We then estimate the effects of these shocks using a local-projections framework applied to a monthly panel of twelve economies. Fiscal risk shocks generate stagflationary dynamics. Inflation and inflation expectations rise on impact, while industrial production increases only temporarily before declining persistently. Sovereign yield curves steepen, exchange rates depreciate and equity prices fall. These effects are significantly stronger when monetary policy remains accommodative-leading to persistently negative real interest rates-and when sovereign risk premia are already elevated.

title: Global Financial Transparency and Offshore Wealth Accumulation
affiliations: School of Economics and Business, NMBU, University of Oxford - Oxford University Centre for Business Taxation, Aix Marseille University and University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics

detail.title: Global Financial Transparency and Offshore Wealth Accumulation
detail.abstract:
This paper uses administrative data to analyze wealth flows from Norway to offshore tax havens before and after a major improvement of global financial transparency: automatic exchange of bank account information between tax authorities. We present three results suggesting that the policy is a significant deterrent of offshore tax evasion: First, taxpayers who become wealthy are much less likely to shift wealth to offshore banks. Second, when wealth does flow to offshore banks, it is much less likely to reduce domestic tax payments. Third, there is no increase in the use of complex ownership structures for offshore wealth flows.
