title: The Civil War Origins of Fiscal Policing: Evidence from the District of Columbia
affiliations: and Duke University School of Law

detail.title: The Civil War Origins of Fiscal Policing: Evidence from the District of Columbia

declarations.funderStatement: The Fuller-Perdue Endowment Fund at Duke Law School

publicationDetails.detailsText: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Series Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The rise of “fiscal policing” in the United States—the use of fines, fees, and forfeitures to extract revenue from civilian populations—is widely described in previous scholarship as a relatively recent development with roots in post-1970s municipal austerity policies. A smaller literature argues that the revenue-extracting function of American policing can be traced earlier to slave patrols before the Civil War and Reconstruction-era Black Codes in the South. But this Article is the first to show that fiscal policing in the North has roots a century deeper than the austerity account recognizes, and an origin distinct from the Southern institutions documented in prior scholarship. We demonstrate this through a case study of the nation’s capital, drawing on an original dataset compiled from the annual reports of the Metropolitan Police of the District of Columbia from 1862 to 1877—the first systematic quantitative analysis of these records—to show that revenue extraction was not a subsequent corruption of the Metropolitan Police’s original crime-control purpose but a core feature of its institutional design from the outset. We supplement the quantitative data with contemporary newspaper accounts, congressional and city-council debates, and correspondence between the governing Board of the Metropolitan Police and the military and civilian authorities that shared jurisdiction over the city. Congress established the Metropolitan Police by statute in August 1861, less than four months after the Civil War began, in direct response to the population surge, jurisdictional uncertainty, and disorder that the war had already produced in the capital.


Our key finding is that the Metropolitan Police generated surplus revenue from its first full year of operation, and this fiscal logic not only continued but intensified after the war. Fine revenue nearly doubled from $32,532 in 1862 to $61,944 in 1865—the year the Board first declared the force a net revenue-producing institution, boasting to Congress that there was “probably no other community in our country whose police system produces a net revenue to its finances.” Revenue receded with wartime conditions but remained above the 1862 baseline in 1877, and fine cases rose from 31.9 percent of all arrests in 1862 to a peak of 45.5 percent in 1867, two years after the war ended. We explain this pattern through two mechanisms. The first is wartime state-building: extending Charles Tilly’s account of how war forges extractive institutions, we show that the Civil War simultaneously created the governance and security crisis that necessitated a new police force and—by exhausting congressional appropriations on military spending—ensured that the force was designed to generate the revenue its own survival required. The second is bureaucratic autonomy: like other nascent administrative agencies, the Metropolitan Police Board had an existential incentive to demonstrate its value to skeptical principals, and it quickly recognized that surplus revenue from fines, forfeitures, and licensing fees was the performance metric most legible and persuasive to Congress and the city councils that controlled its budget—more so than improvements in public safety, which were harder to achieve and measure. The enforcement burden also fell unevenly—across national origin, race, gender, and civil-military status—in ways that shifted during and after the war. These findings relocate the origins of American fiscal policing from the late twentieth century to the 1860s, reveal a Northern and federal pathway that is distinct from Southern institutions previously studied—notably the literatures on slave patrols and Reconstruction-era Black Codes, and provide historical context for contemporary debates over the constitutional limits of fines, fees, and forfeitures. More broadly, the Article models what can be gained by studying the United States as a post-conflict society, bringing to American legal history the theories and methods that political scientists have long used to study civil wars and state-building in other countries.

title: Corporate Emissions Targets as Demand Signals for Supply Chain Coordination
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business, , Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and

detail.title: Corporate Emissions Targets as Demand Signals for Supply Chain Coordination
detail.abstract: We examine whether corporate emissions reduction targets influence investment in climate solutions beyond the announcing firm. We hypothesize that emissions targets can function as forward-looking demand signals, shaping suppliers' expectations about future procurement needs for low-carbon inputs and technologies. Using granular supply-chain data and controlling for industry time trends, we find that suppliers increase their climate solution activity following emissions target announcements by their direct customers. The results are directionally stronger when the customer relationship is more economically important and when suppliers face greater uncertainty. Notably, supplier responses remain statistically positive even for targets with limited ex-ante credibility, consistent with the cheap talk equilibria in which costless signals remain informative when sender and receiver preferences are sufficiently aligned. To address endogeneity and capture broader spillovers, we implement a Bartik-style instrumental variable strategy that combines country-level climate concern with supplier-industry exposure to countries through customer-industries, and find evidence that targets influence supplier investment beyond directly linked customer-supplier relationships. These findings suggest that corporate emissions targets can generate market-wide demand signals that reallocate investments toward climate solutions.

title: The Development of Eye Gaze System to Write Arabic Letters Using Image Processing and Deep Learning Algorithms
affiliations: British University in Egypt, British University in Egypt and Nottingham Trent University

detail.title: The Development of Eye Gaze System to Write Arabic Letters Using Image Processing and Deep Learning Algorithms
detail.abstract: Diseases such as Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease, and Locked-in Syndrome (LIS) result in near-total paralysis of voluntary muscles, severely limiting conventional modes of communication. Eye muscles, however, often remain functional, providing a potential channel for hands-free communication through eye movements. Eye-gaze-based text entry systems have been developed to exploit this preserved function, with most implementations focused on English, while Arabic—owing to its cursive and context-dependent script—remains underexplored. In this study, we present a novel system for Arabic text entry using eye-gaze movements, integrating computer vision and deep learning techniques. The system operates in two main stages: (1) detection and tracking of eye movements, achieved by initial face detection using Haar Cascade classifiers, pupil localization via Binary Large Object (BLOB) analysis, and mapping of eye positions to a screen cursor using homography; and (2) recognition of Arabic letters from eye trajectories using deep learning models. Three architectures were evaluated for letter recognition: VGG16, ResNet, and a custom convolutional neural network (CNN) optimized for Arabic letter classification. The system further incorporates a usability evaluation framework to categorize letters based on writing difficulty into three levels: easy, medium, and hard. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous eye-gaze-driven Arabic letter recognition and highlight the potential for developing accessible, low-cost communication tools for individuals with severe motor disabilities. This work provides a foundation for gaze-based Arabic writing input and contributes to the broader field of assistive communication technologies.

title: Corporate Culture and Climate-Related Disclosure Informativeness
affiliations: Macquarie University, Monash University and

detail.title: Corporate Culture and Climate-Related Disclosure Informativeness
detail.abstract: This study examines whether and how corporate culture affects the informativeness of climaterelated disclosures. We conceptualize disclosure informativeness as an information-efficiency outcome, which captures the extent to which climate risk disclosures convey decision-relevant information with minimal redundancy and processing cost. To operationalize this construct, we use large language models to generate firm-specific, information-efficient summaries of climate risk disclosures and calculate the ratio of the summary length to original disclosure length. Using a sample of U.S. companies from 2005 to 2020, we document a positive association between strong corporate culture and climate disclosure informativeness. Mechanism analyses indicate that firms with strong corporate cultures exhibit superior climaterelated performance and greater internal climate reporting capacity. Cross-sectional tests show that the effect of corporate culture is stronger when internal formal governance and external monitoring are weaker, and when information asymmetry is higher, consistent with corporate culture acting as an informal substitute governance mechanism. Overall, our findings highlight corporate culture as a key internal determinant of informative climate disclosure.

title: Physics-Informed Monte Carlo Data Augmentation for Robust Raman-Based Skin Cancer Classification Under Small-Sample Constraints
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Vietnam National University Hanoi

detail.title: Physics-Informed Monte Carlo Data Augmentation for Robust Raman-Based Skin Cancer Classification Under Small-Sample Constraints
detail.abstract: Raman spectroscopy provides a rapid, label-free, molecular fingerprint of skin tissue and is an attractive candidate for non-invasive skin cancer screening. However, the clinical translation of machine-learning classifiers built on Raman data is hampered by the scarcity of labelled spectra: assembling large, histopathologically confirmed cohorts is slow, expensive, and ethically constrained, and models trained on small datasets overfit and generalise poorly across patients and instruments. Conventional data-augmentation strategies (additive Gaussian noise, random scaling, spectral mixing, and generative adversarial networks) enlarge the training set but do not guarantee that synthetic spectra remain physically plausible, and can inject artefacts that degrade rather than improve robustness. Here we propose a physics-informed data-augmentation framework in which synthetic Raman spectra are generated by Monte Carlo modelling of light transport in a multilayer optical model of human skin (implemented with MCML and COMSOL), constrained by literature-derived optical properties and biochemically grounded Raman band signatures for basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), melanoma, and benign tissue. The physically simulated corpus is combined with limited experimental spectra to train a hybrid one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) with a Transformer encoder. We describe the complete acquisition protocol (RamuLaser-Vial785, 785 nm, 400–3400 cm⁻¹, 2 cm⁻¹ resolution), preprocessing pipeline, augmentation model, network architecture, cross-validation design, and evaluation metrics, and we pre-register the analysis plan and hypothesised performance trends. This manuscript is a methodological framework: no measured patient spectra are reported, and all data-like figures are explicitly labelled as illustrative simulations. The framework is designed to be evaluated on a prospective multi-centre Vietnamese cohort (target 1,200 spectra) and is intended to establish whether physics-informed augmentation improves small-sample generalisation relative to noise- and GAN-based baselines.

title: Betting on Established Heuristics to Fight Climate Change: Making Emissions Binding in Energy Performance Certificates
affiliations: Audencia Business School

detail.title: Betting on Established Heuristics to Fight Climate Change: Making Emissions Binding in Energy Performance Certificates
detail.abstract: Can policymakers exploit established heuristics to price emission externalities? We test this using France's 2021 Energy Performance Certificate reform, which made GHG emission ratings binding on the final EPC grade previously determined solely by energy ratings. Using over one million house sale transactions (2014-2025), pre-reform, we document that heuristic pricing existed only for energy ratings. Post-reform, for properties whose grade is now set by the emission rating, heuristic pricing shifts to emission rating thresholds with comparable magnitude, while energy-based discontinuities disappear when not binding. The results support anchoring binding regulation to a salient, pre-existing heuristic to accelerate emission pricing at low policy cost. We further document evidence consistent with emission pricing influencing sellers' renovation decisions, using both renovation audit recommendations and post-reform shifts in the distribution of emission ratings as proxies.

title: The Grapes of Delay: The Changing Drivers of Global Food Prices
affiliations: and International Hellenic University

detail.title: The Grapes of Delay: The Changing Drivers of Global Food Prices
detail.abstract: This study examines the dynamic relationship between global food prices, maritime freight markets, oil prices, supply-chain stress, and geopolitical risk using monthly data spanning 1998-2026. Motivated by the growing importance of logistics disruptions in the post-pandemic era, the analysis investigates whether food inflation has shifted from a traditionally energy-driven process toward a more logistics-and supply-chain-centered regime. The empirical framework combines Vector Autoregression (VAR), Vector Error Correction Models (VECM), structural-break tests, and regime-dependent estimations. The findings indicate that global food prices respond more persistently to supply-chain stress than to direct geopolitical shocks. In particular, shocks captured by the Global Supply Chain Pressure Index (GSPI) generate gradual and long-lasting increases in food prices, highlighting the growing role of logistics fragmentation, transportation bottlenecks, and operational disruptions in shaping modern food inflation dynamics. Structural-break tests identify significant changes in the transmission mechanism during major global crises, particularly in the post-pandemic period. Commodity-level evidence further reveals substantial heterogeneity, with cereals, meat, and dairy products exhibiting stronger responses to logistics disruptions than vegetable oils and sugar. Overall, the results suggest that while oil prices and freight markets remain relevant, global food inflation is increasingly influenced by broader supply-chain pressures and resilience constraints. These findings carry important implications for food security, logistics policy, and inflation monitoring in an increasingly fragmented global economy.

title: LLM and Multi-Agent Systems in Algorithmic Trading: Taxonomy and Research Agenda

detail.title: LLM and Multi-Agent Systems in Algorithmic Trading: Taxonomy and Research Agenda
detail.abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) and multi-agent systems (MAS) in algorithmic trading has accelerated sharply since 2023, producing a fragmented literature spanning natural-language processing, reinforcement learning, and market microstructure. This paper provides the first structured taxonomy of this emerging field, organising existing work along five orthogonal dimensions: the functional role of the LLM within the trading stack (signal generation, research synthesis, execution, or risk oversight); the information modality processed (text, tabular, time-series, or multimodal); the learning paradigm (zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning from market feedback); the system architecture (single-agent versus coordinated multi-agent); and the evaluation standard applied (in-sample, out-of-sample backtest, or live market). Applying this taxonomy to more than forty papers published between 2019 and 2026, the survey identifies four open research gaps: the absence of a rigorous, cost-adjusted benchmark for LLM-generated signals; the underexplored failure modes of MAS under adversarial or illiquid conditions; the tension between prompt-engineering flexibility and reproducibility; and the near-complete absence of rigorous testing in non-US markets. The paper closes with a ten-question research agenda intended to guide empirical work over the next three years.

title: When Opposites Negotiate: The Effect of Mismatched Extraversion on Negotiation Outcomes Across Communication Media
affiliations: Singapore Management University - Yong Pung How School of Law and

detail.title: When Opposites Negotiate: The Effect of Mismatched Extraversion on Negotiation Outcomes Across Communication Media

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was obtained by Singapore Management University's Institutional Review Board (IRB-22-093-A051(822).
declarations.funderStatement: This research is supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore, under its Tier 2 Academic Research Fund Tier 2 (SSH 2021-2025), T2EP40221-0016 and its Tier 1 Academic Fund (22-SOL-SMU-085) .

detail.abstract: The link between individual characteristics and negotiation success used to be widely doubted within negotiation scholarship. This view has been challenged in the last two decades, when there has been a revived interest in the impact of personality differences. At the same time, negotiation research has examined the effect of communication media on outcomes. Conflicting results have emerged on whether face-to-face interaction is the most optimal medium for achieving good outcomes. It has also been posited that the outcome hinges more on the individual than the communication mode since individuals are able to adapt their communication behavior to different media. Consequently, it is pertinent to explore the influence of individual characteristics on their use of the communication medium and the consequent negotiation outcome. This study explores the interface between the personality trait of extraversion, communication media and negotiation outcomes. It examines four hundred participants' negotiation experiences across four communication media-face-to-face interaction, videoconferencing, audio calls, and text messaging. Through a mixed-method approach, this article synthesizes both the quantitative findings and qualitative insights from a multiple case study. It finds that in-person negotiators' value creation was significantly lower than video and audio modes amongst dyads with mismatched extraversion levels. Furthermore, face-to-face interaction had a polarizing effect on the negotiators' mismatched extraversion levels, creating an impasse that prejudiced their joint value creation. The abundance of visual and non-visual channels, coupled with real-time interaction at a quick pace, energized the extravert and accentuated his extraverted behavior. The introvert, who became increasing exhausted by the need to monitor multiple cues, reacted adversely in terms of deteriorating emotions and declining cooperativeness. In sharp contrast, the audio medium, having only a verbal cue channel, seemed to have an equalizing effect on the negotiators' mismatched extraversion by regulating the pace of conversation, "muting" the impact of extraverted behavior on the introvert, and enabling negotiators to focus and interact calmly, thus contributing to high levels of value creation. The overall findings provide a rich understanding of how negotiators with opposing extraversion personalities respond and interact differently in face-to-face, video and audio communication media, thus highlighting the need for future research to gain a deeper understanding of how dyadic negotiations between “opposites” are affected by communication media.

title: Order Timing in the Nanostore Setting
affiliations: Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management, Arizona State University (ASU) - Supply Chain Management and University of Colorado at Boulder

detail.title: Order Timing in the Nanostore Setting
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Millions of nanostores act as the direct link between consumer goods suppliers and consumers at the bottom of the pyramid. Suppliers have traditionally relied on direct visits by their sales representatives to collect shopkeepers' orders, which are typically delivered the following day. The precise timing of these visits gives suppliers a strategic lever to influence when shopkeepers commit to orders, with potentially meaningful consequences for order size. Because shopkeepers face liquidity constraints and interact with multiple suppliers on any given day, the intra-day moment at which an order is collected shapes what operational information is available at the time of commitment, how much demand uncertainty remains, and how much of the day's cash has already been allocated. Methodology/results: We implement a multimethod approach consisting of two behavioral experiments and an empirical analysis of transactional data from a real nanostore supply chain to analyze the influence of order timing in driving ordering behavior under different product margins, competition, and initial inventory and budget conditions. We find that shopkeepers consistently order more when ordering earlier in the day (i.e., when uncertainty is greater). However, shopkeepers partially incorporate realized demand signals, and sufficiently strong demand signals can reverse the timing effect and lead to larger orders later in the day. Our behavioral model indicates that the interplay of shopkeepers' inventory holding preferences and inventory weighting behavior may lead to optimal shopkeeper behavior under certain conditions. Furthermore, we show that in a competitive setting suppliers can influence ordering behavior by strategically influencing the timing of shopkeepers' orders, regardless of the timing of other suppliers' visits. Finally, our empirical analysis covering transactions of close to 18,000 nanostores over five years corroborates the experimental findings, showing that shopkeepers order 14.2% less when visited in the afternoon and that market-wide demand signals attenuate this gap on high-demand days. Managerial implications: We provide novel insights to the behavioral operations literature, by examining the interplay of order timing, demand signals and inventory weighting in driving shopkeeper behavior at the bottom of the pyramid. Suppliers can leverage our findings to guide their order timing strategy, through smart workforce allocation, the use of digital ordering channels or by adjusting ordering windows based on demand signals.

title: The Four Bodies of Meaning: Rethinking the Meaning of Work Beyond the Individual

detail.title: The Four Bodies of Meaning: Rethinking the Meaning of Work Beyond the Individual

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports no financial or personal relationships with other people or organizations that could have inappropriately influenced the work reported in this study. This research was conducted independently and received no external funding.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to the study, and all interviews were recorded with their explicit permission. The findings were anonymized to protect participant privacy. Furthermore, the preliminary findings were presented to and discussed with the participants in a validation meeting to ensure accuracy and transparency.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The notion of the meaning of work is dominated by approaches that situate meaning in the individual subject’s relation to their activity. Drawing on a qualitative study of twenty-four working people using micro-phenomenology and photo-elicitation, whose inductive analysis produced 98 categories grounded in lived experience, this article proposes a shift: meaning resides neither in the task nor in subjective experience alone, but in the living articulation of four bodies: bodily, relational, ecological and technical. Two results structure the analysis: the buffering function of the relational (mezzo) level between the individual and the system, and the near-total absence of any relation to the living world in the experience of work. These results invite us to think the meaning of work beyond the individual, as participation in a larger order of meaning.

reference: Journal of Society and Polity, Volume 17, No. 2, Pp. 189-211
title: Reconstructing Mising Identity: Elite Mobility, Community Organisation, and the Politics of Recognition in Post-Assam accord Period in Assam
affiliations: North Lakhimpur University and North Lakhimpur College (Autonomous)

detail.title: Reconstructing Mising Identity: Elite Mobility, Community Organisation, and the Politics of Recognition in Post-Assam accord Period in Assam

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Society and Polity, Volume 17, No. 2, Pp. 189-211

detail.abstract: The identity movement of the mising is not a post-colonial development. However, it gained momentum during the post-Assam Accord period, which marked the end of the six-year-long antiforeigner movement in Assam. The current study investigates the evolution and complexities of the mising identity movement since 1985. There is a significant research gap in understanding the sociopolitical contexts that have shaped the identity formation and mobilisations of the mising tribe in Assam. The paper argues that the post-Assam Accord period has contributed to the rejuvenation of organised elite among missing, who have become instrumental in mobilising the mising community and pursuing its aspirations before the state. The paper mainly aims to understand the changing dynamics of elite mobility and their role in the mising Identity movement through various community organisations. To achieve this objective, the paper employs a qualitative methodology based on archival analysis. The paper highlights that the movement's success in preserving identity, political representation, and extended autonomy was possible only because of changing patterns of elite mobility and strategic shifts in their capacity to regulate and lead the community's interests through community organisations. This research contributes a new and ethnicspecific perspective to the existing body of literature on tribal elite mobility and identity in Northeast India by discussing the role of mising elite mobility and mising national organisations in mising identity in the post-Assam Accord period. The study finds that the post-Assam Accord period witnessed the emergence of an educated and organisationally mobile Mising elite that played a decisive role in reconstructing and articulating Mising ethnic identity.

title: Adaptive Behavioral Archetypes in Organizations: Introducing Manfurists and Kasturists for Leadership and Decision-Making Research

detail.title: Adaptive Behavioral Archetypes in Organizations: Introducing Manfurists and Kasturists for Leadership and Decision-Making Research

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing interests or conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study is a conceptual/theoretical study and did not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly operate in environments shaped by uncertainty, rapid change, complex collaboration, and continuous pressure for faster decision-making. While modern leadership and management theories emphasize teamwork, adaptability, and alignment, organizations often struggle to balance two competing needs: the need for critical evaluation and the need for coordinated execution. Prior research has shown that excessive consensus pressure may suppress independent evaluation and produce poor decisions (Janis, 1972), while psychologically safe environments support learning behavior and interpersonal risk-taking in teams (Edmondson, 1999). This conceptual paper introduces two adaptive behavioral archetypes: Manfurists and Kasturists. Manfurists are defined as evidence-oriented skeptical adaptation archetypes who initially resist ideas, emphasize analytical evaluation, and often become stable contributors after persuasion. Kasturists are defined as consensus-oriented adaptive alignment archetypes who rapidly synchronize with group direction and prioritize collaboration speed, belonging, and organizational harmony. The paper argues that these archetypes should not be understood as fixed personality types, but as dynamic behavioral responses shaped by psychological safety, authority pressure, perceived fairness, expertise confidence, accountability structures, emotional exhaustion, and previous workplace experiences. Building on theories of groupthink (Janis, 1972), psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999, 2018), bounded rationality (Simon, 1957), dual-process thinking (Kahneman, 2011), social identity (Tajfel & Turner, 1979), organizational culture (Schein, 2010), leadership behavior (Northouse, 2021), and team conflict (Jehn, 1995; De Dreu & Weingart, 2003), the paper develops a conceptual framework explaining how Manfurist and Kasturist tendencies may influence decision quality, innovation, accountability, technical debt, employee engagement, and leadership effectiveness. The paper also introduces two original concepts: Agreestorming and Behavioral Conversion Theory. Agreestorming refers to performative collaboration in which teams imitate brainstorming while avoiding meaningful disagreement. Behavioral Conversion Theory explains how repeated punishment, blame, exclusion, or unfairness may shift individuals from one behavioral mode to another. The paper contributes to leadership and organizational behavior literature by proposing an adaptive framework for understanding the relationship between skepticism, conformity, collaboration, and organizational learning, while providing future empirical directions for validating the model through surveys, interviews, longitudinal research, and cross-industry analysis.

reference: International Tax and Public Finance, volume 19, issue 6, 2012[10.1007/s10797-011-9208-6]
title: Auditing Internal Transfer Prices in Multinationals Under Monopolistic Competition
affiliations: Kobe University - Graduate School of Business Administration

detail.title: Auditing Internal Transfer Prices in Multinationals Under Monopolistic Competition

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Tax and Public Finance, volume 19, issue 6, 2012[10.1007/s10797-011-9208-6]

detail.abstract: This paper derives an appropriate standard price that can be used by the tax authorities of a country for auditing transfer prices in multinational firms (MNFs) for the purpose of social welfare maximization of the country. We assume that the corporate tax rate in the host country, where MNFs undertake foreign direct investment to locate their manufacturing divisions, is lower than that in the home country. Our conclusion is that the tax authorities of the home country should not always force MNFs to hold down the transfer price through a too strict audit standard if it aims to maximize social welfare of the country in the long-run equilibrium. This result implies that tax authorities face a trade-off between consumer welfare and tax revenue when determining the standard price used for auditing. One notable implication is that the tax authorities should raise the upper-limit price allowed for internal transfers as the elasticity of substitution between brands for consumers decreases.

reference: International Journal of Production Economics, volume 139, issue 1, 2012[10.1016/j.ijpe.2011.10.030]
title: Cost-Based Transfer Pricing Under R&D Risk Aversion in an Integrated Supply Chain
affiliations: Kobe University - Graduate School of Business Administration

detail.title: Cost-Based Transfer Pricing Under R&D Risk Aversion in an Integrated Supply Chain

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Production Economics, volume 139, issue 1, 2012[10.1016/j.ijpe.2011.10.030]

detail.abstract: This paper examines the economic role of transfer pricing for a vertically integrated supply chain when a risk-averse production-division manager faces uncertainty on the outcomes from R&D investment. In particular, we compare two representative cost-based transfer pricing methods: full-cost and variable-cost pricing. We construct an economic model based on the assumption that R&D investment reduces the expected fixed costs of a production factor as well as the variable production costs. We show that a firm's profit under full-cost transfer pricing is greater than that under variable-cost transfer pricing under certainty. Contrary to this benchmark result, variable-cost pricing becomes more profitable than full-cost pricing when the risk-averse manager bears relatively high risk.

title: The Constitutive Third in the Firm (Paper 4 of the series) - The Principle of Structural Realizability
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Constitutive Third in the Firm (Paper 4 of the series) - The Principle of Structural Realizability
detail.abstract:
Paper 4 of the series, following The Irreducibility of Triadic Relations (Paper 1), Triadic Structure in Law and Institutions (Paper 2), and Conservation Through the Third (Paper 3).

Across the earlier papers in this series the constitutive third appears in cosmology, in law, and in physics, where a critic may always retreat to the objection that the cases are analogies drawn between heterogeneous domains. The firm closes that retreat. Within a single genus of object, the business enterprise, the bearer of the constitutive third can be observed to migrate, as system complexity rises, from a person to a norm and then to a mechanism that administers invariance, while its constitutive function holds constant. This essay argues that the firm is therefore not a fourth illustration but a natural experiment that exhibits the multiple realizability of the third directly rather than inferring it by homology. The claim is structural and diagnostic, not prescriptive: it identifies where a constitutive third must stand for a firm to possess identity as a unit, without prescribing what concrete architecture any firm ought to adopt.

title: Measuring Effective Sovereignty Under Collapse: An Open-data Reconstruction of the Burke Sovereignty Index for Afghanistan, 2001-2024

detail.title: Measuring Effective Sovereignty Under Collapse: An Open-data Reconstruction of the Burke Sovereignty Index for Afghanistan, 2001-2024
detail.abstract: Measuring state sovereignty empirically has long confronted a core dilemma: the most consequential cases-fragile, conflict-affected, and post-collapse states-are precisely those for which data coverage is weakest and expert-survey recruitment most difficult. This paper presents an empirical test of the Burke Sovereignty Index (BSI), a seven-dimensional composite index of effective sovereignty scored on a 0-700 scale, using Afghanistan as a hard test case across five observation years (2001, 2010, 2014, 2021, 2024). The statistical component is built entirely from open, machine-accessible data (World Bank, SIPRI, UNESCO, Freedom House, RSF, IMF). The expert component is approximated through a low-cost, experimental method: a stochastic simulation of a 100-expert panel using a large language model (LLM), stratified across 10 disciplinary profiles and 5 geographic blocs representing 55 countries. The simulation generates not only point-estimate scores but also inter-rater statistics (mean, SD, CV, IQR) and propagated 95% confidence intervals for each composite total. Results show that Afghanistan spent the entire 2001-2024 period in the "existential threat" zone (BSI < 300), with only a brief and statistically uncertain crossing into "critical vulnerability" in 2014 (BSI = 307.4; 95% CI: [293.9, 320.9]). The 2021 Taliban takeover caused the largest single-period shock in the reconstruction (-93 points), and the 2024 score (174.5) reflects deepening informational and cognitive collapse. We argue that the LLM-panel approach constitutes a viable, explicitly lowcost proxy for expert survey data in cases where recruitment is infeasible, temporal or resource constraints bind, or post-shock retrospective scoring is required-while documenting its structural limitations with precision. The paper connects this methodology to an emerging literature on LLM-as-expert-substitute in political science and raises normative questions about delegating judgment to statistical systems.

title: Digitalization and Innovation in the Real Estate Sector
affiliations: and KTH Royal Institute of Technology

detail.title: Digitalization and Innovation in the Real Estate Sector
detail.abstract: Recently, digitalization has emerged as a main theme in the industry discourse in the real estate sector. In this discourse, some influencers foresee that digitalization poses disruption, even an existential threat, to the traditional actors, which are expected to make "digital transformations" to remain relevant. Others emphasize the potential of digitalization to drive efficiency, sustainability and servitization of the industry. However, the real estate sector is a mature business environment with a low rate of innovation and limited R&D resources, and it is not evident how this traditional sector reacts to the multitude of new predictions and propositions. Based on theories of innovation management, this study investigates real estate owners' sense-making and strategizing in this area: how do they seek information and prioritize which initiatives to take? Which actions are taken? How are structures for innovation management affected, within firms as well as on the industry level? The results are based on semi-structured interviews conducted with respondents responsible for digital development in large private and public real estate owners in Sweden, as well as with representatives of industry associations. Findings include that real estate firms and industry associations emphasize digitalization-related opportunities to improve efficiency and tenant satisfaction, as well as to create new services and business models. Also, real estate firms perceive that change is needed to remain competitive, and as a response, they have created digitalization strategies, formed new organizational units and recruited new people to lead digitalization efforts. Further, they have established new collaborative relationships to industry networks and competitors.

title: Holding Stocks, Trading Bonds
affiliations: Dublin City University - School of Mathematical Sciences and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Holding Stocks, Trading Bonds
detail.abstract: Why do rational investors actively trade long-term bonds? This paper solves a continuous-time exchange economy with heterogeneous CARA agents, common information, stochastic dividend growth, personal income, a stock, short-term lending, and long-term fixed-income securities. The economy is constructed to make trade difficult: in the constant-growth benchmark, heterogeneous agents do not rebalance after the initial allocation. With stochastic growth, however, shocks to expected dividends move interest rates and change the value of heterogeneous consumption plans and income hedges. In equilibrium agents hold stock positions that are constant after the initial allocation, while they trade long-term bonds dynamically. Bonds are the clean hedge because their deterministic coupons isolate discount-rate and growth-risk exposure from direct dividend cash-flow risk. The paper also develops an inaction-band implementation of frictionless bond targets, so that quadratic variation determines leading-order trading volume, and extends the mechanism to multiple stocks, multiple growth factors, and sinking funds.

title: From Record to Finding Why Tamper-proof Logs Cannot Establish Legal Oversight of Agentic AI

detail.title: From Record to Finding Why Tamper-proof Logs Cannot Establish Legal Oversight of Agentic AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Apparens, a consultancy specialising in AI governance and adversarial review, and is the author of related commercial and open works including the AI Enterprise Control Index and the supervisory-evidence ontology cited in this paper. The paper is a working paper and reflects the author's independent analysis. No external party directed or reviewed its content.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted by the author independently.

detail.abstract: A supervisor charged with overseeing an agentic AI system must, under EU law, be able to establish certain findings of fact: whether personal data of a protected class left a controlled environment, whether a human had the authority and the window to intervene, whether an information barrier held, whether a delegated authority was valid at the moment it was used. This paper asks a narrow and prior question. Under what conditions can a runtime record answer such a finding at all? It develops an evidentiary-adequacy criterion: a representation can answer a determination of this kind only if it carries two things, the legal typing that maps recorded events to the operative category, and the relation, usually provenance or authority, on which the determination's truth depends. A representation carrying neither can raise a suspicion but cannot establish a finding. The criterion is a necessity claim, not a sufficiency claim; sufficiency fails for reasons the paper makes explicit. The criterion is stated formally, its necessity is shown by construction across a defined class of determinations, the property set is shown to be minimal, and its adequacy is argued to be bounded to that class rather than universal. The determinations in scope are characterised by a stated selection rule: they are binary findings of fact about specific events and their relations, not evaluative or statistical properties such as fairness or robustness. The criterion is supported, not derived, by three independently established results that converge on the same necessity from different directions: Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety, the Good Regulator Theorem, and the trace-versus-hyperproperty boundary of runtime verification. The paper is careful to claim no novelty in that convergence; the inversion of cybernetic model-dependence onto the overseer has been made before, notably by Aguirre (2025), as an impossibility argument about control. The contribution is the criterion itself, its instantiation in EU AI Act oversight, a gap analysis showing that existing governance frameworks do not answer these determinations, and a pre-registered experiment that tests the criterion against expert judgement. The legal claim is stated conditionally. A record that is not semantically and relationally interpretable cannot serve as evidence that effective oversight under Article 14 was possible, even where it satisfies the Article 12 duty to log. The structure recurs in any domain where legal findings depend on the execution paths of autonomous systems, of which EU AI Act oversight is the worked instance.

title: The Illusion of Objectivity: Colonial Legacy, Language Bias, and the Structural Framing of the Israel-Palestine Conflict in Western Media
affiliations: International Islamic University, Islamabad - Department of Politics & International Relations

detail.title: The Illusion of Objectivity: Colonial Legacy, Language Bias, and the Structural Framing of the Israel-Palestine Conflict in Western Media
detail.abstract: This paper argues that Western media is not episodically or accidently biased in its coverage of the international conflicts particularly the Israel-Palestine conflict. The Western media bias is observed to be structural as a direct product of its colonial origins and the linguistic frameworks which are the foundations of contemporary journalism. The Western political and economic power controls the design of the global journalistic standards. This argument is further advanced with four case studies from the colonial press era to the ideological construction of objectivity, the language frameworks that surround it, the post 9/11 and war on terror coverage and the Israel-Palestine conflict. There is also a comparative analysis that follows the top western media broadcasting stations CNN, BBC with Al-Jazeera, a non-western media house. The paper carefully de-constructsthe underlying mechanisms that sustain the illusion of objectivity in western media and why it fails to apply to events outside its area of interests.

title: Building a High-Performance FP&A Function: Strategic Recommendations for Modern Organizations
affiliations: Institute of Chartered Accountants of Pakistan

detail.title: Building a High-Performance FP&A Function: Strategic Recommendations for Modern Organizations
detail.abstract: Financial Planning and Analysis (FP&A) has shifted over the past decade from a primarily historical reporting function toward a forward-looking discipline expected to inform real-time business decisions. Despite widespread investment in new systems and transformation initiatives, many organizations continue to experience inaccurate forecasts, slow reporting cycles, and FP&A teams that spend disproportionate time reconciling data rather than interpreting it. Drawing on direct professional experience across logistics, financial services, and professional services organizations, together with relevant industry research, this paper identifies five characteristics that distinguish high-performing FP&A functions: disciplined data governance, forward-looking planning, financial modeling capability, business partnering, and technology enablement. Each characteristic is illustrated with specific, real-world examples of how these practices function in operation, followed by a discussion of common implementation challenges and practical recommendations for organizations seeking to strengthen their FP&A capability.

title: Measuring Consumer Confidence beyond Surveys
affiliations: , University of Strathclyde, Glasgow - Strathclyde Business School - Department of Economics and University of Strathclyde - Strathclyde Business School

detail.title: Measuring Consumer Confidence beyond Surveys
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to measuring consumer confidence that combines more than fourteen million news articles with nearly thirteen thousand institutional documents from UK policy bodies. Using an announcement-anchored and cross-source filtering procedure we construct a joint economic vocabulary, and extract consumer sentiment only where institutional and media language overlap. The resulting index is transparent, low cost and tightly linked to policy communication, co-moving with existing survey-based confidence measures and reacting sharply around major policy and data events. Empirical evidence shows that the news-based index delivers robust gains in out-of-sample forecast accuracy relative to specifications that rely on traditional survey confidence.

title: Macroeconomic Analysis of Geopolitical Volatility: The Impact of US-Iran Conflict on India’s Aggregate Output (GDP)

detail.title: Macroeconomic Analysis of Geopolitical Volatility: The Impact of US-Iran Conflict on India’s Aggregate Output (GDP)
detail.abstract: This extensive research report investigates the economic repercussions of an escalating US-Iran conflict on India's macroeconomic stability. India, a net importer of energy and a primary recipient of global remittances, occupies a vulnerable position in the face of Persian Gulf instability. Through a detailed analysis of the Aggregate Output identity (Y = C + I + G + NX), this paper identifies five primary transmission channels: energy-driven supply shocks, remittance-induced consumption drops, trade logistical disruptions, capital flight, and fiscal burden expansion. The study employs quantitative projections to suggest that a sustained conflict could lead to a 'Stagflation trap, reducing India's annual GDP growth by 0.8% to 1.5%, while pushing inflation past the Reserve Bank of India's upper tolerance limit of 6%.

title: Refugee Absorption and Electoral Change: Evidence from the Indian Partition
affiliations: and University of Luxembourg

detail.title: Refugee Absorption and Electoral Change: Evidence from the Indian Partition
detail.abstract: The 1947 Partition of British India triggered the largest forced migration of the twentieth century, redistributing millions of refugees across newly independent India. We study whether this demographic shock left a lasting imprint on democratic politics. Combining district-level refugee shares from the 1951 Census with constituency-level electoral data covering Indian state assembly elections between 1960 and 2007, we estimate the long-run effects of refugee settlement on electoral competition. We find that constituencies exposed to larger refugee inflows exhibit higher voter turnout, narrower victory margins, and a lower likelihood of electing candidates from national parties. Instead, refugee settlement shifted electoral support toward regional parties and contributed to the long-run denationalization of political competition. Our findings show that large demographic shocks can leave enduring political legacies, reshaping patterns of political representation and party competition long after displacement itself has ended.

title: The Integrated High Performance Framework (IHPF): A Conceptual Model of Strategic Planning, Character Development, Continuous Improvement, and Courage for Sustainable High Performance

detail.title: The Integrated High Performance Framework (IHPF): A Conceptual Model of Strategic Planning, Character Development, Continuous Improvement, and Courage for Sustainable High Performance
detail.abstract: Organizations and individuals invest heavily in leadership development, strategic planning, productivity training, and executive coaching, yet sustained high performance remains elusive for many who adopt these tools. A likely reason is that the most widely used performance frameworks-SMART goal-setting, SWOT analysis, the marginal-gains philosophy of continuous improvement, Covey's Seven Habits of character-based leadership, and the psychological courage captured in Theodore Roosevelt's "Man in the Arena" address-are typically taught and applied in isolation. Each framework addresses a distinct layer of achievement (purpose, positioning, daily execution, character, and courage, respectively), but the interaction among these layers is rarely theorized. This paper introduces the Integrated High Performance Framework (IHPF), a conceptual model proposing that sustainable high performance is an emergent property of the dynamic interaction among five constructs: goal clarity, strategic alignment, continuous improvement, character development, and courageous execution. Drawing on established literature in goal-setting theory, strategic management, continuous improvement, leadership psychology, and resilience research, the paper develops the theoretical rationale for integration, situates the model relative to complementary constructs (grit, growth mindset, self-efficacy, deliberate practice, and systems thinking), and illustrates its application through five leadership case vignettes spanning higher education, international academic service, authorship, community partnership, and sport coaching. Five testable research propositions are advanced to guide future empirical validation using structural equation modeling and longitudinal designs. The paper concludes that isolated frameworks are necessary but insufficient, and that their integrationrather than any single component-may better explain why some individuals and organizations sustain excellence over time while others plateau despite comparable intelligence, resources, and effort.

title: INSTITUTIONALIZATION OF THE NATIONAL POLICY ON MEDICINAL PLANTS AND PHYTOTHERAPEUTICS IN MUNICIPALITIES OF PARANÁ
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Itaipu Binacional, Itaipu Binacional, Itaipu Binacional, Itaipu Binacional, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: INSTITUTIONALIZATION OF THE NATIONAL POLICY ON MEDICINAL PLANTS AND PHYTOTHERAPEUTICS IN MUNICIPALITIES OF PARANÁ
detail.abstract: Background: The Brazilian National Policy on Medicinal Plants and Herbal Medicines (PNPMF) aims to expand access to safe therapies and strengthen integrative practices within the Unified Health System (SUS), and its incorporation into planning instruments is a relevant indicator of municipal implementation. Objective: This study aimed to analyze the institutionalization of the PNPMF in municipalities in Paraná that joined the Plante e Colha Saúde project, proposed by Sustentec in partnership with Itaipu Binacional. Methods: This is a cross-sectional, exploratory study with a quantitative approach that analyzed federal funding transfers, Municipal Health Plans (PMS), and Annual Health Programs (PAS). Results: Of the 110 participating municipalities, 49.0% (n=54) received federal funding for PNPMF-related actions; 13.6% (n=15) mentioned the theme in the PMS and 5.4% (n=6) in both instruments. Incorporation was heterogeneous, with predominance of low (53.3%; n=8), followed by high (26.6%; n=4) and moderate (20.0%; n=3) levels. Conclusion: Strengthening inductive initiatives may increase its incorporation into planning.
